sweeps.cluster: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (DAMS; Zhou, Balakrishnan & Lipton, AISTATS 2023) and follow-ups on missingness-mechanism shift

papers.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift
papers.authors: Helen Zhou, Sivaraman Balakrishnan, Zachary C. Lipton (Carnegie Mellon University)
papers.venue_year: AISTATS 2023, PMLR vol. 206, pp. 9577-9606. arXiv:2211.02093 (v1 3 Nov 2022, v3 3 May 2023). Code: github.com/acmi-lab/Missingness-Shift
papers.verification: Fetched the full text: downloaded the arXiv v3 PDF, extracted all 32 pages locally and read Sec. 1-8 plus App. B and App. I.3. Checked the PMLR page for venue, volume and pages. The arXiv ID 2211.02093 is correct.
papers.method: Missingness is modeled as X~ = X ⊙ ξ (the mask zeros out values). The paper works mainly in the no-indicator 'underreporting' case. (a) Theorem 4.1: UCAR (underreporting completely at random) acts like dropout, i.e. an L2-type regularizer, following Wager et al. 2013. (b) Algorithm 1, the non-parametric adjustment: estimate the relative missingness rate r^{s->t} = 1 - q^t/q^s, where q is the per-feature proportion of nonzeros in each domain. Then apply a fresh random Bernoulli missingness filter at rate r^{s->t} to the labeled source data and train any model on it. This is literally artificial dropout of the source, calibrated to the target. It is a 'proper adjustment' only when m^s <= m^t elementwise; otherwise it is an 'improper' adjustment using max(r,0). (c) Algorithm 2 / Proposition 2, a closed form for the linear model: beta_t* = E[X~t'X~t]^{-1}(r^{s->t} ⊙ E[X~s'Y^s]). The target Gram matrix can come from unlabeled target data, or from source data rescaled by (1-r) (Proposition 3). (d) Theorem 6.1 gives a Hoeffding bound on the estimate of r.
papers.identification_result:
Definition 1: missingness shift means P^s(X,Y) = P^t(X,Y) = P(X,Y), while P^s(ξ|·) ≠ P^t(ξ|·).

Proposition 1 (App. B): if ξ is observed and is MCAR, or 'v-MAR' (ξ ~ Bernoulli(f(X_c)) with X_c a completely observed covariate subset; Mohan & Pearl 2021 terminology), then P^s(Y | X~, ξ) = P^t(Y | X~, ξ). The problem reduces to covariate shift on the augmented covariates (X~, ξ), so the Bayes predictor is invariant and reweighting by p^t/p^s suffices under overlap. The proof uses ξ ⊥ (X_m, Y) | X_c together with invariant P(X,Y).

Without indicators, under UCAR:
- Remarks 1-2: the optimal source linear predictor can have target risk at least Var(Y), and for the 'confounded features' example it can exceed τ·Var(Y) for any τ > 1.
- Lemma 5.1: the clean distribution is identified if the missingness rates m are known (m < 1).
- Remark 4 (non-identifiability): the missingness rates themselves are not identified from corrupted data. Counterexample: Bern(0.5) with m = 0.5 and Bern(0.25) with m = 0 give the same observed distribution.
- Remark 5: relative non-missingness rates are identified, (1-m^t)/(1-m^s) = P^t(X~≠0)/P^s(X~≠0).
- Theorem 5.2: the labeled target distribution p~^t(x,y) is identified from p~^s and r^{s->t} (requires m^s < 1).

No results for MNAR, Y-dependent or value-dependent missingness, for missingness that depends on partially observed covariates, or for any shift in P(X,Y).
papers.shift_assumptions: P(X,Y) is exactly invariant across domains; only the missingness mechanism changes. Main setting is UCAR: ξ_j ~ Bernoulli(1 - m_j), independent across features and of (X,Y), with constant unknown rates and no indicators (a missing value is recorded as 0). Secondary setting (indicators observed): MCAR or v-MAR, i.e. missingness depends only on always-observed covariates. MNAR is not treated. The Discussion lists covariate-dependent underreporting ('a doctor may choose not to perform a test based on patient state') and other graph structures as future work.
papers.source_access: Labeled corrupted source data {(X~^s_i, Y^s_i)}. The source is itself subject to missingness (m^s is generally nonzero), not fully observed. Masks are unobserved in the main UCAR setting and observed in the Proposition 1 setting.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled corrupted target covariates {X~^t_i} only (masks unobserved in the main setting). No target labels at training time. In the experiments, target labels are used only by the Oracle (trained on target) and for held-out target evaluation.
papers.experiments:
Synthetic: 10,000 samples from two DGPs ('redundant features' and 'confounded features'), with m^s = [1-ε, ε] and m^t = [ε, 1-ε] for ε from 0.05 to 0.95, 20 runs each. Models: linear, XGBoost, MLP.

Semi-synthetic: covariates from UCI adult, bank and thyroid, with synthetic labels y = βX (β ~ U(0,10)). Missingness is synthetic MCAR in both domains, in two regimes: m^s <= m^t, and arbitrary rates drawn from U(0,0.9). Split 4:1:4:1 into source train, source test, target train and target test.

Real: eICU, two hospitals (n = 3006 and n = 2663; 48-h mortality 9.7% and 10.0%), binary FIDDLE features with naturally occurring underreporting, linear models only. For cross-domain evaluation a model was trained on all of one hospital and tested on all of the other. Target labels were used only for evaluation and for the Oracle (80/20 split).

Outcome on eICU: the adjustments FAILED. The unadjusted source model had the best AUROC and AUPRC (for example H2 to H1: source 0.593, closed-form 0.540, non-param 0.555), the estimated rates did not satisfy m^s <= m^t, and MissForest imputation collapsed to the base rate. The authors attribute the failure to violated assumptions: different P(X,Y), 'selection bias (very different cohort)', label shift, and missingness that depends on covariates.

papers.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness
papers.authors: Tyrel Stokes, Hyungrok Do, Saul Blecker, Rumi Chunara, Samrachana Adhikari (NYU)
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2504.00322 (v1, 1 Apr 2025), stat.ME/stat.ML. A search result points to an OpenReview PDF headed 'Under review as submission to TMLR' that may be this paper, but OpenReview blocked the fetch, so that status is UNVERIFIED.
papers.verification: Fetched the full text: downloaded the arXiv v1 PDF, extracted the text locally and read Sec. 1-7.
papers.identification_result:
Under MNAR shift, P_T(Y | Xo, X*u, R) ≠ P_S(Y | Xo, X*u, R) even when P(Y | Xo, Xu, R) is invariant (proof in the supplement). So plain covariate-shift IW, and hence Zhou et al.'s reduction, does not apply.

Theorem 1: with a consistent nonparametric outcome regression, the reducible target MSE converges to P(R=0) × E[(E_T[Y | Xo, X*u, R=0] − plim μ̂(Xo, Xu + e, R=0))^2 | R=0]. It therefore vanishes if the imputation error e → 0, so the target error is bounded by imputation error when the regression is continuous in Xu.

The paper notes that self-censoring (Xu → R) is not nonparametrically identifiable (citing Nabi et al. 2020 and Bhattacharya et al. 2020), so identification rests on parametric assumptions of the imputation models. It proposes no partial-identification bounds or sensitivity analysis.
papers.shift_assumptions: P_T(Xo,Xu) = P_S(Xo,Xu) and P_T(Y | Xo,Xu,R) = P_S(Y | Xo,Xu,R). The mechanism P(R | Xo,Xu) differs and may be MNAR, including self-censoring. The simulation DGPs allow a direct R→Y effect. An extension allows simultaneous covariate shift. Also requires positivity/overlap of the importance weights.
papers.source_access: Full labeled sample of (Y, Xo, X*u, R), with missingness indicators observed.
papers.target_access: A subsample of (Xo, X*u, R) with no outcome. Exception: the 'leak' variants of the Bayesian imputers use target Y and are reported as a comparison. In both the simulations and the eICU application, target labels were available and used for evaluation. The authors also used them for extra diagnostics, which showed concept shift between regions.
papers.experiments:
Simulations: synthetic, factorial design with about 120,000 runs. Covers 8 DAGs (all with self-censoring MNAR), sample sizes 750-5000, missing rates 5-30%, and varying nonlinearity.

Real data: eICU with natural missingness across 57 features. South has 39,433 patients and Northeast 8,158. Section 5 names South as source and Northeast as target, but the Figure 10 caption states the reverse, an internal inconsistency. Outcome is ICU mortality, evaluated by Brier score and AUROC.

Findings: the domain-classifier propensities show almost no overlap between regions. ML imputers do somewhat better than MICE, but 'none of the methods out-perform mean imputation by a large margin'.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The second anchor paper named in the user request, and the closest MNAR treatment. It formalizes why observed-data conditionals shift under MNAR acquisition, which is the core of an N1 counterexample. It then resolves the problem by assuming a correctly specified MNAR imputation model, not by sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts
papers.authors: Patrick Rockenschaub, Zhicong Xian, Alireza Zamanian, Marta Piperno, Octavia-Andreea Ciora, Elisabeth Pachl, Narges Ahmidi
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2406.16484 (v1, 24 Jun 2024), stat.ML. No peer-reviewed venue found.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the arXiv HTML full text. Details were extracted through a summarizer, not read line by line.
papers.method: Proposes NeuMISE, a modification of NeuMiss that embeds in the missing rather than the observed dimensions. Benchmarks impute-then-regress (ICE, MICE, MIWAE, plus variants that condition on Y and variants with a mask), NeuMiss, complete-case analysis, and analytic Bayes-predictor oracles.
papers.identification_result:
Theorem 1: under a missingness shift with invariant p(Y,X), the pattern-specific Bayes predictors E[Y | X_obs, M=m] are equal across environments for all m, in general only if the shift is ignorable (MAR in both source and target). Under non-ignorable shifts (MNAR, or missingness that depends on Y), the Bayes predictor can change.

Corollary: when missingness depends on Y, imputing with Y creates an artificial shift at deployment, where Y is unavailable.
papers.shift_assumptions: p(Y,X) = q(Y,X), with the mask mechanism changing from p(M|·) to q(M|·). Mechanisms covered: MCAR, non-monotone MAR, MNAR (Gaussian self-masking) and MAR-Y (missingness depends on Y).
papers.source_access: Labeled source data (X~, Y) with the mask M observed.
papers.target_access: The deployment target provides (X~, M) without Y. Target labels are used only for evaluation.
papers.experiments:
Synthetic: d = 50 multivariate-normal covariates, n = 100k, with a nonlinear 'wave' outcome.

Semi-synthetic: 50 LBIDD covariates with an artificial outcome.

Missingness is imposed synthetically, mainly shifting from 50% missing in source to 25% in target, plus the reverse direction and a no-shift control. There is no natural-missingness evaluation.

Finding: method robustness and ranking depend on the shift type and direction. Methods that exploit informative missingness (NeuMiss, ICE+mask) degrade catastrophically after a Y-dependent shift, while MICE is more robust there.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Gives the cleanest statement of when mask-aware predictors transfer: they are invariant iff missingness is ignorable in both domains. It also shows empirically that method rankings can flip under non-ignorable shifts, which is N1's phenomenon, though only with synthetic masks.

papers.title: ICYM2I: The illusion of multimodal informativeness under missingness
papers.authors: Young Sang Choi, Vincent Jeanselme, Pierre Elias, Shalmali Joshi
papers.venue_year: ICLR 2026, per the arXiv v3 comment 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'. arXiv:2505.16953 (v1 22 May 2025, v3 2 Mar 2026). Cites Zhou et al. 2023 according to Semantic Scholar.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the arXiv HTML full text through a summarizer. The citation of DAMS comes from the Semantic Scholar citations API.
papers.method:
Double inverse-probability weighting to correct for selective modality acquisition, in two places:
- training: reweight complete cases by 1/P(complete | C) so the model estimates P_Ω(y | x1, x2) rather than the complete-case P_Ωobs;
- evaluation: apply the same IPW correction to performance metrics such as AUC.
Also corrects partial-information-decomposition (PID) estimates of a modality's unique and shared information.
papers.identification_result:
Under MAR (the missingness of modality, and of the label, depends only on observed covariates C) and positivity P(all observed | C) > 0, IPW identifies:
- the model that would be trained if all modalities were observed;
- its performance and information gain in the fully observed population.
There are no guarantees under MNAR. The authors state that MAR versus MNAR is untestable, and the appendix sensitivity check covers MCAR only.
papers.shift_assumptions: MAR given observed covariates C, positivity, and an invariant P(Y|X). The implicit target environment is one where the modality is acquired for everyone.
papers.source_access: A naturally incomplete multimodal cohort: modalities (and possibly labels) missing for some units, with masks observed and covariates C always observed.
papers.target_access: A hypothetical fully acquired population, of which no samples are available. Everything is estimated from the source by reweighting. In the real case study a temporally later test period (2018 onward) is used for evaluation with labels.
papers.experiments:
Synthetic bitwise logic tasks with MAR missingness. Semi-synthetic UR-FUNNY and Hateful Memes with 70% MAR or MNAR missingness imposed.

Real: a structural heart disease cohort (98,397 patients) with ECG and echo, where chest X-ray is naturally acquired for only 12.79% of patients. Temporal split: train 2008-2017, test 2018 onward.

Finding: the naive estimate of the chest X-ray's unique information (5%) drops to 1.8% after IPW correction.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The closest multimodal paper with natural, selective modality acquisition, for example chest X-rays ordered by clinicians. It argues that naive evaluation on the acquired or complete-case subset misstates a modality's value in the deployment population, which is the N1 thesis in mirror image.

papers.title: Prediction with Missing Data: Target Probabilities and Missingness Mechanisms
papers.authors: Pierre Catoire, Robin Genuer, Cécile Proust-Lima
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the HTML full text through a summarizer. The summarizer reports that the paper does not cite DAMS or Rockenschaub et al.
papers.method:
A conceptual and statistical framework rather than a new learner. It defines two prediction targets:
- MU (missingness-unconditional): Pr(Y | X_o = x_o);
- MC (missingness-conditional): Pr(Y | X_o = x_o, M_X = m).
It proposes a new classification of mechanisms (NIMO, NICO, MARX-YO, MARX-YM) that determines which target is consistently estimated by pattern submodels, deterministic imputation, missing indicators and similar approaches.
papers.identification_result: MC can be consistently predicted under arbitrary mechanisms, including MNAR, using pattern submodels or indicators within one stable environment. MU and MC coincide under NIMO: Y ⊥ M | X_o(m). Both targets can be consistently predicted under conditions weaker than MAR. The paper discusses 'missingness shift' across development, validation and deployment: MC, which uses pattern information, is vulnerable to a change in mechanism, while MU is not affected by it.
papers.shift_assumptions: Mainly a single environment. Missingness shift between development and deployment is discussed qualitatively in terms of which target remains valid.
papers.source_access: The development data: labeled data with missingness indicators.
papers.target_access: Deployment, discussed conceptually. In the illustration, labels are available for evaluation.
papers.experiments: Simulations, plus real emergency-department trauma data (n = 678, Bordeaux, 2017-2019; outcome ISS ≥ 15). The missingness is natural and informative: altered mental status and hypoxaemia were missing more often in severe patients.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Gives precise estimand language that N1 needs: observed-only (MU) versus mask-aware (MC) risk. It also explains why mask-aware models win in-distribution but become fragile when the acquisition policy changes.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the conceptual distinction behind N1's observed-only versus mask-aware baselines, and qualitatively names missingness shift at deployment. Does not cover artificial dropout evaluation, model ranking, sensitivity bounds or source-population selection.

papers.title: Prediction with Incomplete Data under Agnostic Mask Distribution Shift (StableMiss)
papers.authors: Yichen Zhu, Jian Yuan, Bo Jiang, Tao Lin, Haiming Jin, Xinbing Wang, Chenghu Zhou
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2305.11197 (18 May 2023). No peer-reviewed venue found.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the HTML full text through a summarizer. The summarizer found no citation of DAMS.
papers.method: StableMiss: a mask-parameterized predictor g_{φθ(M)}(X ⊙ M), with sample reweighting that decorrelates features and masks using Random Fourier Features partial cross-covariance. The aim is to learn mask-specific invariant predictors that stay robust when the mask distribution changes in ways not known at training time.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1: under MCAR or MAR, with invariant P(X,Y) and P(Y | X, M) = P(Y | X), the conditional P(Y | X_obs, M) is invariant between training and test. Theorem 2: naive parameterizations can fit training equally well yet fail under mask shift.
papers.shift_assumptions: P(X,Y) invariant, P(M|X) shifts arbitrarily and the test mask distribution is unknown, restricted to MCAR/MAR. The mask may not depend on Y or on unobserved values.
papers.source_access: Labeled training data with observed masks.
papers.target_access: None at training time (agnostic). The target is used only for evaluation.
papers.experiments: Synthetic Gaussian data, House Sales, MNIST, and a naturally incomplete Traffic dataset. Mask shifts are simulated as changes in missing rate (10-90%) and in pattern (MCAR-Ind, MCAR, MAR).
papers.relevance_to_N1: Another statement of the MCAR/MAR invariance of P(Y | X_obs, M), together with a robust-training baseline for mask shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the invariance result under MAR and robust training under mask shift. It is a possible 'nearby missingness-shift baseline' for N1's experiment 6. Does not cover MNAR or selective acquisition, source-population selection, model selection, or sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: MIRRAMS: Learning Robust Tabular Models under Unseen Missingness Shifts
papers.authors: Jihye Lee, Minseo Kang, Dongha Kim
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2507.08280 (v1 11 Jul 2025, v2 14 Aug 2025). Semantic Scholar lists an earlier title, 'MIRRAMS: Towards Training Models Robust to Missingness Distribution Shifts', and cites DAMS.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page only. The full text was not read.
papers.method: Mutual-information-based 'MI robustness conditions' turned into loss terms that encourage label-relevant, missingness-robust representations. Extends to the semi-supervised case with missing labels.
papers.identification_result: None claimed in the abstract. It is presented as assumption-free with respect to MCAR, MAR or MNAR, which means it offers no identification guarantee for the target risk.
papers.shift_assumptions: The test-time missingness distribution is unseen or unknown. No specific mechanism is assumed.
papers.source_access: Labeled training data with missingness (labels may be partly missing in the semi-supervised extension).
papers.target_access: None at training time.
papers.experiments: Tabular benchmarks. The abstract does not say whether missingness shifts were synthetic or natural.
papers.relevance_to_N1: An example of the 'new loss for robustness to missingness shift' line. The user request explicitly warns against using a new loss to paper over the identification question, so this is a baseline or foil rather than a competitor for the N1 claim.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Overlaps only as a robust-training baseline under mask shift. Provides no identification, ranking, sensitivity or uncertainty analysis.

papers.title: Multimodal domain adaptation under label shift and blockwise missing modalities
papers.authors: Zebin Wang, Ziang Dou, Molei Liu, Tianxi Cai
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the HTML full text through a summarizer. Its 'Zhou et al. (2023)' citation refers to BONMI (blockwise missing), not DAMS, so this paper is adjacent rather than a DAMS follow-up.
papers.method: Uses a reference modality that is observed in all domains to estimate the target outcome distribution from unlabeled target data. Source data are reweighted to the target label mixture before alignment ('weight before alignment'). Auxiliary modalities are aligned by target CCA and source ridge maps, then outcome likelihood ratios are transferred.
papers.identification_result: Representations are recovered up to a common rotation (Lemma 2). The outcome model is identified under label-shift and likelihood-ratio assumptions.
papers.shift_assumptions: Label shift: P(Y) varies and P(X|Y) is stable. Missingness is blockwise by domain or site, meaning each domain observes a fixed subset of modalities, rather than per-unit selective acquisition. The reference modality is always present.
papers.source_access: Multiple labeled source domains, each with a different subset of modalities. Surrogate labels are allowed.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target with the reference modality and possibly others. Target labels are 'masked during fitting and used only for final evaluation'.
papers.experiments: Simulations, plus renal cell carcinoma recurrence data. Source spans 2000-2016 (5,674 patients); target spans 2017-2022 (379 patients with all modalities). The natural blockwise pattern comes from different periods acquiring different imaging modalities.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A modality-level missingness plus domain-shift setting with honest use of target labels, but the missingness is per-domain design, not per-unit selective acquisition.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the modality-block framing and label-shift reweighting. This matters for N1 step 8, which asks whether ranking changes are explained by class-balance adjustment. Does not cover per-unit acquisition masks, MNAR acquisition, dropout-based evaluation or model selection.

papers.title: Imputation and missing indicators for handling missing data in the development and deployment of clinical prediction models: A simulation study
papers.authors: Rose Sisk, Matthew Sperrin, Niels Peek, Maarten van Smeden, Glen P. Martin
papers.venue_year: Statistical Methods in Medical Research 32(8):1461-1477, 2023. arXiv:2206.12295.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract. Journal, volume and pages come from a search snippet. Details of the simulated mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR and outcome-dependent missingness) come from the abstract and snippets, not the full text.
papers.method: Simulation comparison of multiple imputation versus regression imputation (with or without the outcome in the imputation model) and missing indicators. Covers deployment scenarios where missing data are allowed and where they are not.
papers.identification_result: None formal. Empirically, missing indicators help under informative missingness but can be harmful when missingness depends on the outcome. The best handling strategy depends on whether data may be missing at deployment.
papers.shift_assumptions: Various mechanisms, including outcome-dependent missingness. The deployment-time missingness regime can differ from development.
papers.source_access: Labeled development data with missingness.
papers.target_access: Deployment or validation data, simulated with known labels for evaluation.
papers.experiments: Simulation only.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The clinical-prediction counterpart of the ML missingness-shift work. It motivates comparing observed-only, imputation and mask-aware models under changed deployment missingness.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Partially covers N1's baseline set (imputation versus indicators under development/deployment mismatch). Does not cover identification, dropout evaluation, ranking inference or source-population selection.

papers.title: Collecting data when missingness is unknown: a method for improving model performance given under-reporting in patient populations
papers.authors: Kevin Wu, Dominik Dahlem, Christopher Hane, Eran Halperin, James Zou
papers.venue_year: CHIL 2023, PMLR vol. 209, pp. 229-242. Cites DAMS according to Semantic Scholar.
papers.verification: Fetched the PMLR abstract page. The full text was not read.
papers.method: Budgeted, targeted data collection (for example subsidized check-ups) to maximize a fixed, already-deployed model's performance on a population with 'latent missingness', meaning under-reported binary diagnoses.
papers.identification_result: Not established from the abstract.
papers.shift_assumptions: Under-reporting without indicators, as in DAMS UCAR, possibly differing across subpopulations.
papers.source_access: Records with under-reported binary diagnosis indicators.
papers.target_access: A deployment population with a budget to acquire the true values for some individuals.
papers.experiments: Simulated and real-world data (details not verified).
papers.relevance_to_N1: Treats acquisition as a decision variable in the same group of problems. It relates to N1's 'selective modality acquisition' framing, though it optimizes what to collect rather than which model to select.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Low overlap. Covers acquisition-as-intervention under under-reporting, but not model ranking, dropout evaluation or sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: Causal inference amid missingness-specific independencies and mechanism shifts
papers.authors: Johan de Aguas, Leonard Henckel, Johan Pensar, Guido Biele
papers.venue_year: UAI 2025, PMLR vol. 286, pp. 31-44. arXiv:2506.15441. Cites DAMS according to Semantic Scholar.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page. The full text was not read.
papers.method: Introduces lm-SCMs and lm-graphs: missingness graphs with labels for context-specific independencies, to capture mechanism shifts induced by missingness itself. Provides recovery criteria and doubly robust estimators.
papers.identification_result: Recovery criteria for two estimands: FATE (the effect with no data loss) and NATE (the effect under the natural, unaltered system including missingness).
papers.shift_assumptions: Missingness may itself shift downstream mechanisms (context-specific independencies).
papers.source_access: Observational data with missingness.
papers.target_access: Not a domain-adaptation setup.
papers.experiments: Simulations, plus an ADHD treatment effect application on Norwegian test-achievement data with naturally missing baseline scores.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The FATE-versus-NATE distinction is the causal analogue of N1's 'risk under full acquisition' versus 'risk under the natural acquisition policy'. It is useful for formally separating the S and M estimands.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Conceptual only: estimand separation under missingness-induced mechanism shift. Nothing on prediction, model ranking or dropout.

papers.title: Weighted Conformal Prediction Provides Adaptive and Valid Mask-Conditional Coverage for General Missing Data Mechanisms
papers.authors: Jiarong Fan, Juhyun Park, Thi Phuong Thuy Vo, Nicolas Brunel
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2512.14221 (16 Dec 2025). Cites DAMS according to Semantic Scholar.
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page. The full text was not read.
papers.method: A 'preimpute-mask-then-correct' approach: distributional imputation on the calibration set, followed by weighted conformal prediction to achieve both marginal and mask-conditional coverage.
papers.identification_result: Coverage guarantees, both marginal and mask-conditional. The mechanism generality claimed in the title is not verified beyond the abstract.
papers.shift_assumptions: General missing-data mechanisms, per the title. Details not verified.
papers.source_access: Labeled calibration data with masks.
papers.target_access: A test point with its observed mask.
papers.experiments: Synthetic and real datasets (details not verified).
papers.relevance_to_N1: A possible tool for the 'uncertainty' component, where N1 needs mask-conditional uncertainty for pattern-specific risk. Tangential to identification.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Low overlap. Covers mask-conditional uncertainty quantification, not risk-difference inference between models under acquisition shift.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
I confirmed the anchor paper against its primary sources: Zhou, Balakrishnan & Lipton, 'Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift', AISTATS 2023, PMLR 206:9577-9606, arXiv:2211.02093 v3. I extracted the full text from the arXiv PDF and read it.

**Setup.** DAMS assumes the underlying P(X,Y) is identical in source and target and only the mask mechanism changes (Definition 1). The observed data are X~ = X ⊙ ξ. The learner has labeled, corrupted source data (X~^s, Y^s) and unlabeled, corrupted target data X~^t. Target labels appear only in the oracle and in held-out evaluation.

**Main results.**
- **Masks observed (Proposition 1).** With MCAR or v-MAR masks (missingness depends only on always-observed covariates X_c), P(Y | X~, ξ) is invariant and the problem is ordinary covariate shift, so importance weighting applies.
- **Masks not observed (UCAR).**
  - The unadapted source predictor can be arbitrarily worse than predicting the mean.
  - The missingness rates themselves are not identifiable (Remark 4).
  - Relative non-missingness rates are identified from the proportions of nonzeros (Remark 5).
  - The labeled target distribution is identified from the source plus the relative rates (Theorem 5.2).
  - When m^s ≤ m^t, randomly re-masking the source at the relative rate (Algorithm 1) gives labeled data that is i.i.d. from the target. This is formally artificial dropout calibrated to the target.
  - For linear models there is a closed-form adjustment (Algorithm 2).
  - UCAR is equivalent to dropout-style L2 regularization (Theorem 4.1).
- **Experiments.**
  - Synthetic and semi-synthetic runs (UCI covariates, synthetic linear labels, synthetic MCAR masks) show gains when the assumptions hold.
  - On eICU, with two hospitals and natural underreporting, the adjustments lost to the unadapted source model.
  - The authors attribute this to cohort selection, label shift, a different P(X,Y), and missingness that depends on covariates.

**Follow-ups.**
- **Same group.** I found no later missingness-shift paper by Helen Zhou herself; her publication page ends in 2023, and the only related same-group paper is 'Evaluating Model Performance in Medical Datasets Over Time', CHIL 2023, on temporal evaluation. In the Lipton group more broadly, Akpinar, Lipton & Chouldechova (FAccT 2024) study differential feature under-reporting and fairness.
- **Direct follow-ups that cite DAMS** (Semantic Scholar citations API):
  - Stokes et al. 2025, MNAR domain adaptation via imputation.
  - Rockenschaub et al. 2024: the Bayes predictor is invariant iff missingness is ignorable in both domains, and method rankings flip under non-ignorable shift, shown with synthetic masks.
  - ICYM2I (ICLR 2026): IPW-corrected training and evaluation of a modality's value under natural MAR modality acquisition.
  - MIRRAMS (2025).
  - Wu et al. (CHIL 2023).
  - de Aguas et al. (UAI 2025).
  - Fan et al. (2025).
- **Relevant but not citing DAMS:**
  - StableMiss (2023).
  - Catoire et al. (2026), the MU vs MC targets.
  - Sisk et al. (SMMR 2023).
  - Wang et al. (2026), blockwise-missing modalities with label shift.

**Implication for N1.** Together these establish the positive side of N1's question. With invariant P(X,Y), no population selection, and acquisition that is MCAR or v-MAR, artificial dropout matched to the target mask law, or equivalently IW on (X_obs, M), identifies target risk and therefore model rankings. They also establish that under MNAR or Y-dependent acquisition the observed-data conditional shifts, so this breaks down (Stokes et al.; Rockenschaub et al.).
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
1. **Model selection is not the target.** Every paper in this cluster targets the optimal predictor, imputation quality, or a modality's informativeness. None frames the question as choosing between two fixed models using their target risk difference, or asks when the sign of ΔR_T is identified. None gives a minimal counterexample in which dropout-based evaluation on a fully observed source ranks two models in the opposite order to natural-acquisition target risk. The ingredients exist, though: Stokes et al.'s claim that P_T(Y | X_obs, R) ≠ P_S under MNAR, and Rockenschaub et al.'s Theorem 1.

2. **Population selection S and mask M are never separated.** DAMS, Rockenschaub et al. and StableMiss assume P(X,Y) is invariant. Stokes et al. assume P(Xo,Xu) is invariant, or add generic covariate-shift IW on imputed data. None models a fully observed source that is itself a selected complete-case cohort, where S = all modalities acquired, as distinct from the target's per-unit mask. DAMS's own eICU failure is attributed to exactly this confound but is not analyzed.

3. **No sensitivity analysis or partial identification for MNAR or Y-dependent acquisition.** Stokes et al. rely on correctly specified parametric MNAR imputers. ICYM2I and Rockenschaub et al. stop at MAR, and ICYM2I's sensitivity check covers MCAR only. No paper bounds P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) relative to the source with an odds-ratio or marginal-sensitivity parameter, or propagates such a bound to a model-ranking decision with bootstrap or other uncertainty.

4. **Direction and granularity.**
   - DAMS works at feature level with zero-coded underreporting, and its source is itself corrupted rather than fully observed.
   - ICYM2I runs the reverse direction: a naturally missing source with a hypothetically fully acquired target.
   - Wang et al. 2026 handle blockwise, site-level modality absence, not per-unit clinician-driven acquisition.
   - None treats the N1 setup: a fully observed multimodal source, and a deployment population where a modality is selectively acquired per unit.

5. **No test of artificial versus natural masking on real data.** No paper compares model rankings under artificial masking with rankings under natural acquisition on one real cohort while controlling for sample selection and class balance (N1 step 8). DAMS's eICU and Stokes et al.'s eICU experiments use natural missingness but do not compare against artificial masking of the same cohort, and they conflate hospital or region shift with missingness shift.

6. **Target labels and identifiability claims.** In every real-data experiment here (eICU in DAMS and in Stokes et al., the heart-disease cohort in ICYM2I, the RCC data in Wang et al.), target labels existed and were used for evaluation. Stokes et al. also used them for diagnostics. Non-identifiability arguments therefore concern the training or selection-time information set only. N1 must state that scope explicitly and cannot claim non-identifiability where target labels are public.

7. **What remains novel for N1.** Importance weighting on (X_obs, M) under MAR is already the stated remedy (DAMS Proposition 1, ICYM2I). Robust losses already exist (StableMiss, MIRRAMS). N1's defensible contribution is therefore limited to:
   - separating S from M;
   - the identification conditions and counterexample specifically for dropout-based ranking;
   - sensitivity and uncertainty for the risk difference;
   - a natural-versus-artificial ranking audit.
   If those add nothing beyond DAMS Theorem 5.2 plus Proposition 1, the result would be NO_GO per the user's criterion.

sweeps.cluster: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness (Stokes et al., arXiv 2504.00322) and closely related work on missingness shift, MNAR modality missingness, and target-risk estimation or sensitivity analysis for prediction (2021-2026)

papers.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness
papers.authors: Tyrel Stokes, Hyungrok Do, Saul Blecker, Rumi Chunara, Samrachana Adhikari (NYU Grossman / NYU)
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2504.00322 [stat.ME, stat.ML], v1 only, 1 Apr 2025. I found no peer-reviewed venue.
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract page and downloaded and read the full 24-page PDF (v1), including appendices A-D. The exact title exists.
papers.method: Two stages. (1) Impute the missing covariates separately in source and target with an MNAR-capable imputer. Candidates: joint Bayesian latent-variable models (z-model, joint model, no-outcome, no-missingness variants, each with and without 'leak' of target Y); single-imputation MICE (PMM, norm, rf, random-indicator); PVAE, not-MIWAE and GINA. (2) Train a domain classifier on (Xo, X̂u, R) to estimate importance weights P(T|Xo,X̂u,R)/P(S|Xo,X̂u,R), then fit a weighted outcome model: weighted Bayesian linear regression in the simulations, random forest on eICU. The authors describe this as reducing MNAR missingness shift to an imputation problem plus standard covariate-shift reweighting.
papers.shift_assumptions: Pure missingness shift: P_T(Y|Xo,Xu,R)=P_S(Y|Xo,Xu,R) and P_T(Xo,Xu)=P_S(Xo,Xu), with P_T(R|Xo,Xu)≠P_S(R|Xo,Xu). The extension allows covariate shift in (Xo,Xu,R) as well. The Appendix A derivation additionally uses P(R|Y,Xo,Xu)=P(R|Xo,Xu), i.e. no label-dependent missingness. Yet simulation DAGs 5-8 include R→Y edges, so the paper is internally inconsistent here. The MNAR class is self-censoring/self-masking (Xi→Ri) with latent Z confounding. The paper states this is not nonparametrically identifiable, so identification rests on the imputers' parametric assumptions. Outcome Y is never missing. Missingness is at feature level (tabular EHR), not modality level.
papers.source_access: Labeled source with its own natural or MNAR missingness: (Y, Xo, X*u, R). The source is NOT fully observed. Appendix C shows that if Y ⟂ R | Xo, Xu, then P(Y|Xo,Xu) is learnable from source complete cases alone.
papers.target_access: By the formal setup, a (sub)sample of target (Xo, X*u, R) with no Y. Target labels were nonetheless used: for all evaluation (RMSE, Brier, AUROC); inside the 'leak' imputation variants in the simulations; and in the eICU analysis, where the authors trained separate target outcome models to diagnose concept shift. So in the empirical parts target labels were available, and non-identifiability is a statement about the formal setup only.
papers.identification_result: (i) Negative result (App. A, adapting Zhou et al. 2023): under MNAR, even with invariant P(Y|Xo,Xu,R), the observed-data conditional P_T(Y|Xo,X*u,R) ≠ P_S(Y|Xo,X*u,R), because it depends on each domain's mechanism P_d(R|Xo,Xu) and on P_d(Xu|Xo). So importance weighting on observed (Xo,X*u,R) is not sufficient. (ii) Theorem 1: with a consistent nonparametric outcome regression, the asymptotic reducible target MSE equals P(R=0) times the error from plugging the imputed X̂u=Xu+e into the full-data regression. It vanishes if P(R=0)→0 or X̂u→Xu in probability, and is bounded by imputation error when E[Y|Xo,Xu,R] is continuous in Xu. My reading: this needs point imputation that converges to the counterfactual realized Xu, which is generally unattainable from observed data unless Xu is a deterministic function of observables. It is therefore a reduction, not an identification result. (iii) App. D: with consistent imputation in both domains, simultaneous covariate and missingness shift reduces to covariate shift on (Xo,Xu,R). The paper gives no bounds, no partial identification, no sensitivity parameter and no confidence intervals (only 5 random seeds on eICU).
papers.experiments: Simulations use a factorial design of about 120,000 runs over 8 DAGs (with and without R→Y), n from 750 to 5000, 5-30% missingness and nonlinearity in X, comparing 18 imputers. Missingness is SYNTHETIC self-censoring logistic MNAR, and truth is known. Findings: Bayesian joint models that use target Y ('leak') perform best; without leak they are worst; MICE-PMM/norm are strong. A GAM analysis finds source imputation error matters as much as or more than target imputation error. The real-data study is eICU-CRD, ICU mortality, 57 features. Exclusions: APACHE IVa, first ICU stay, age ≥16, unknown region, and variables with >70% missing. It compares 39,433 South and 8,158 Northeast stays; missingness is NATURAL, averaging 17.9% vs 13.4%. The text names South as source and Northeast as target, but the Figure 10 caption and Sec. 5.1 say the reverse, so the direction is ambiguous in the paper. Evaluation uses target Brier and AUROC with target labels. ML imputers (PVAE, not-MIWAE, GINA) beat MICE, but the authors conclude that 'none of the methods out-perform mean imputation by a large margin'. The domain classifier separates regions almost perfectly (a practical positivity violation). The paper does not separate cohort selection from missingness; missing entries are simply NA, with no distinction between 'not recorded' and 'not performed'.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the exact-title paper and the main MNAR comparator N1 must position against. It establishes formally that under MNAR missingness shift, P(Y|x_obs, m) differs between domains even when the full-data outcome model is invariant. That is the core reason an artificial-dropout evaluation (MCAR masks on a complete cohort) cannot in general determine target risk. Its App. C condition (Y ⟂ R | X makes complete cases valid for the full-data outcome model) is exactly the condition under which a fully observed source cohort is informative. N1 needs more than that: the target law of (X_u | x_obs, M) and of Y | x_obs, M, which this paper handles only through parametric MNAR imputation.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Overlap: (a) the non-transportability argument for P(Y|x_obs,M) under MNAR, which is essentially the core of N1's 'minimal counterexample'; (b) imputation plus importance weighting on (Xo, X̂u, R), which N1 must include as a 'close missingness-shift baseline' (impute-then-reweight) and must not relabel as new; (c) eICU with natural cross-hospital missingness as a testbed. No overlap: no model selection or pairwise risk difference, no sensitivity model or bounds on P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m), no uncertainty quantification, no fully observed source with artificial dropout, no modality-level acquisition, no separation of population selection S from mask M, and no test of whether artificial-mask rankings match natural-missingness rankings.

papers.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift
papers.authors: Helen Zhou, Sivaraman Balakrishnan, Zachary C. Lipton (CMU)
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML and downloaded the full PDF text. I read Prop. 1, the Discussion and the eICU passage directly. The PMLR venue is confirmed by a search result listing proceedings.mlr.press/v206/zhou23b; code is at github.com/acmi-lab/Missingness-Shift.
papers.method: DAMS with UCAR (underreporting completely at random: a feature is zeroed with no indicator). Algorithm 1 is a nonparametric 'missingness filter': extra masking of source data at the estimated relative rate r̂(s→t), valid only when m_s ⪯ m_t. Algorithm 2 is a closed-form optimal linear target predictor β_t = E[X̃tᵀX̃t]⁻¹(r ⊙ E[X̃sᵀY_s]).
papers.shift_assumptions: Clean P(X,Y) is identical across domains; only the missingness process differs. Main case: UCAR, per-feature Bernoulli rates m_s, m_t independent of X and Y, with indicators NOT observed. Prop. 1: if indicators ξ ARE observed and missingness is MCAR or v-MAR (dependent only on always-observed covariates), missingness shift satisfies covariate shift on the augmented input (x̃, ξ), and the optimal predictor is invariant. There are no MNAR results; the authors list covariate-dependent underreporting ('doctors take measurements as needed') as future work.
papers.source_access: Labeled source with masked covariates (X̃s, Ys). Indicators are absent in the main setting.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target X̃t. Target labels are used only for evaluation, in synthetic, semi-synthetic and eICU experiments.
papers.identification_result: Absolute missingness rates are NOT identifiable from corrupted data (Remark 4 counterexample). Relative rates r(s→t)=1−(1−m_t)/(1−m_s) ARE identifiable (Thm 5.2), so the labeled target distribution and the optimal target linear predictor are identifiable without knowing absolute rates (Prop. 2). The optimal source predictor can do arbitrarily worse on the target, even worse than predicting the mean. With indicators observed plus MCAR/v-MAR, the problem reduces to covariate shift (Prop. 1).
papers.experiments: Synthetic data and semi-synthetic UCI data (Adult, Bank, Thyroid, with a synthetic linear Y), both with SYNTHETIC UCAR masks. Real data: eICU 48-h mortality across hospitals, binary FIDDLE features, NATURAL missingness. On eICU the methods 'do not work particularly well'. The authors note they 'have no particular reason to believe that missingness shift is especially prominent between the hospitals compared to factors such as selection bias (very different cohort), label shift, or changes in prevalences', and call 'analyzing sensitivity to assumption violations' future work.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the MAR/MCAR predecessor N1 is required to compare first. Its Prop. 1 is the precise condition under which mask-aware reweighting works: with M observed and M ⟂ (unobserved X, Y) given always-observed covariates, P(Y | x_obs, m) is invariant. Its eICU discussion states N1's S-versus-M confound almost verbatim: cross-hospital performance differences may reflect cohort selection or prevalence rather than missingness shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the reduction 'observed mask + MAR on always-observed covariates → covariate shift → importance weighting on (x_obs, M)'. Any N1 reweighting baseline is this result and cannot be called new. The 'missingness filter' (extra masking of source to match target rates) is literally an artificial-dropout adaptation under MCAR, so N1's dropout baseline under MCAR is anticipated here. Not covered: MNAR, model ranking or selection, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty, modality-level acquisition, and a fully observed source.

papers.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts
papers.authors: Patrick Rockenschaub, Zhicong Xian, Alireza Zamanian, Marta Piperno, Octavia-Andreea Ciora, Elisabeth Pachl, Narges Ahmidi (Fraunhofer IKS)
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2406.16484 [stat.ML], 24 Jun 2024. I found no published venue.
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML and downloaded the PDF text. I read the abstract, Theorem 1, Sec. 6.2 (Corollary 1) and the data section directly.
papers.method: Theory on pattern-wise Bayes predictors f*_m(x_obs)=E[Y|X_obs,M=m] under missingness shift. It compares ICE, MICE, MIWAE, AE imputation, ICE+mask, NeuMiss and a proposed NeuMISE architecture against conditional and probabilistic oracles. Models are trained on the source only, with no adaptation.
papers.shift_assumptions: Definition: missingness shift means p(M|X) ≠ q(M|X). It is 'ignorable' if both source and target mechanisms depend only on X_obs (MAR). The paper studies MCAR, MAR, Gaussian self-masking MNAR, and MAR-Y (missingness depends on Y). P(X,Y) is invariant.
papers.source_access: Labeled source with ~50% (or 25%) missingness. The source is not fully observed.
papers.target_access: Target with shifted missingness (25%, 50% or 0%). Target labels are used for evaluation only; there is no transfer or adaptation from target data.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1: the pattern-wise Bayes predictors in source and target coincide for all m 'in general only if the missingness shift is ignorable'. So under MAR-to-MAR shift any consistent Bayes-predictor estimator is robust, while under non-ignorable shift the Bayes predictor can change. Corollary 1: if target missingness depends on Y and differs from source, the shift cannot be ignorable. A key remark: when source is MAR and the target is fully observed, source Y-dependence can still be ignorable. There are no bounds or sensitivity parameters.
papers.experiments: Simulation: N=100,000, d=50 Gaussian covariates, nonlinear outcome. Semi-real: LBIDD 1995 covariates (50 complete features) with an ARTIFICIAL outcome. All masks are SYNTHETIC (MCAR, MAR, self-masking MNAR, MAR-Y), with shifts 50%→25%, 25%→50% and 50%→0%. Empirically, different estimators are robust to different shifts; under MNAR none recovers the Bayes predictor, and ignoring missingness helped most when missingness was highly informative. No natural missingness is used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This gives the theoretical boundary for N1's question in its simplest form. If the natural target mechanism is MAR given the observed modalities, the pattern-wise optimal predictor is invariant, so artificial evaluation can be informative, though risk weights over patterns still change. If it is MNAR or label-dependent, the optimal predictor itself moves. The abstract states N1's model-selection motivation explicitly: 'Prediction performance in the source data may no longer be a good selection criterion'.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Pre-empts the motivation and the qualitative ignorable-versus-non-ignorable dichotomy of N1's counterexample. N1's counterexample must go beyond 'the Bayes predictor changes', for example by showing a rank reversal between two fixed models. Not covered: pairwise risk-difference selection, sensitivity or partial identification, uncertainty, natural missingness, fully observed source with artificial dropout, and S/M separation.

papers.title: ICYM2I: The illusion of multimodal informativeness under missingness
papers.authors: Young Sang Choi, Vincent Jeanselme, Pierre Elias, Shalmali Joshi
papers.venue_year: ICLR 2026, per the arXiv comments and PDF header. arXiv 2505.16953 (v3, Mar 2026).
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML and downloaded the PDF text. I read Assumption A, Assumption B, the clinical dataset section, the Appendix D MNAR passage and the Limitations directly.
papers.method: IPW correction ('double inverse-propensity weighting') of both TRAINING and EVALUATION of unimodal and multimodal models. Complete cases are reweighted by the inverse probability of observing all modalities and the label given covariates C, so that performance (AUROC, Brier) and partial information decomposition (shared, unique, synergistic information) are estimated for the fully observed population. Propensities come from logistic regression or neural networks.
papers.shift_assumptions: Assumption A: demonstrating a modality's value changes future collection, so the target population is the fully observed one. Assumption B: MAR given observed covariates C, plus positivity P(all observed | C) > 0. MNAR is explicitly not covered ('No theoretical guarantees exist under MNAR patterns'). The Appendix D 'sensitivity analysis' is only an empirical demonstration that both naive and IPW estimates are biased under MNAR, with no sensitivity model.
papers.source_access: Historical data with modality-level and label missingness (X1, X2, Y partially observed, masks M1, M2, M_Y).
papers.target_access: A hypothetical fully observed population; no target sample. Performance there is estimated by IPW on complete cases. The synthetic and semi-synthetic oracle comparisons use ground-truth full data. In the clinical study there is no ground truth for the fully observed population.
papers.identification_result: Under MAR and positivity, IPW-weighted loss and metrics on complete cases identify the full-population risk (Lemma 1, Corollary 1), and IPW-weighted marginals identify the PID terms (Lemma 2). There are no results under MNAR.
papers.experiments: Synthetic bit-wise AND/OR/XOR with MAR masks. Semi-synthetic UR-FUNNY and Hateful Memes with 70% SYNTHETIC missingness and an oracle. Real data: Columbia cohort of 98,397 adults who had both an ECG and a TTE within 1 year; the label is structural heart disease from the TTE; 12.79% have a CXR (NATURAL modality missingness); temporal split at 2018. The naive analysis attributes about 5% unique information to CXR; the corrected analysis gives 1.8%. Note that the cohort is itself selected on label acquisition (having a TTE), which is an S-type selection the paper does not separate from M.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the closest multimodal work. It states that naive evaluation under non-random modality missingness misestimates a modality's value, and it corrects evaluation by IPW. The direction is the REVERSE of N1: incomplete source to fully observed target, whereas N1 goes from a fully observed source to a naturally incomplete target. It also highlights the S-versus-M issue, since its cohort requires label acquisition.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers IPW-corrected evaluation of multimodal models under MAR modality missingness. An N1 'acquisition-aware' evaluator that is IPW over mask patterns under MAR would largely duplicate this, and plain IPW cannot be claimed as new. Not covered: MNAR sensitivity or bounds, pairwise model-selection risk difference with uncertainty, and artificial-versus-natural rank concordance.

papers.title: Prediction with Missing Data: Target Probabilities and Missingness Mechanisms
papers.authors: Pierre Catoire, Robin Genuer, Cécile Proust-Lima
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract page and the HTML full text, read through the WebFetch summarizer; I did not read the PDF myself.
papers.method: A formal framework separating two prediction targets: missingness-unconditional (MU) P(Y|X_o) and missingness-conditional (MC) P(Y|X_o, M_X). It compares pattern submodels, complete-case submodels, MI with and without indicators, MLE with marginalisation, MIA and deterministic imputation. Missingness is distinguished at the development, validation and deployment stages.
papers.shift_assumptions: Missingness at each of development, validation and deployment, with possible missingness shift between them. It gives conditions weaker than MAR for MU consistency (e.g. MARX-YO) and states that MC prediction is consistent under an arbitrary predictor-missingness mechanism, including MNAR, provided the mechanism is unchanged at deployment. Outcome missingness is also treated.
papers.source_access: Development data with natural missingness and labels.
papers.target_access: Validation and deployment data, whose missingness mechanism may differ. In the real application, labels come from leave-one-out cross-validation within a single registry.
papers.identification_result: The MC target (which uses mask information) is consistently learnable under any predictor-missingness mechanism, MNAR included, if development and deployment mechanisms match. Under shift it can be 'distorted', while the MU target is more robust. The paper recommends fixing the target probability before designing the model.
papers.experiments: Simulations over five DAG scenarios with synthetic masks and 0-70% missingness. Real data: Bordeaux trauma registry (N=678, ISS≥15) with NATURAL missingness (37.5% incomplete). There is no cross-site shift experiment.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Gives vocabulary N1 can reuse directly: mask-aware risk (MC) versus observed-only risk (MU), and the development/validation/deployment staging. N1's question is when the MC risk ranking survives an acquisition-policy shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the conceptual distinction behind N1's 'observed-only versus mask-aware' baselines and the warning that mask-exploiting models are fragile under shift. Not covered: target-risk estimation under shift, sensitivity analysis, model selection with uncertainty, and multimodal or natural-versus-artificial comparison.

papers.title: Sensitivity analysis for studies transporting prediction models
papers.authors: Jon A. Steingrimsson, Sarah E. Robertson, Issa J. Dahabreh
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML (via the WebFetch summarizer). The journal version is confirmed by search results (academic.oup.com/biometrics/article/80/4/ujae129; PubMed 39575627).
papers.method: Exponential-tilt sensitivity model f(y|x,S=target) ∝ exp(η q(y)) f(y|x,S=source), with an unidentifiable η. Target risk of a fixed model (Brier, MSE, loss-based) is computed as a function of η, using a conditional-loss plug-in and an influence-function-based augmented (doubly robust) estimator with large-sample theory.
papers.shift_assumptions: Covariate shift with a possibly violated conditional transportability assumption (Y ⟂ S | X), relaxed by the tilt. There is no missingness or mask structure.
papers.source_access: Labeled source (X, Y).
papers.target_access: Target X only, with no Y.
papers.identification_result: For each fixed η, target risk is point-identified; η=0 recovers standard transportability. The result is a sensitivity curve of target risk over η.
papers.experiments: CASS: observational participants (n=430) as source and trial participants (n=368) as target, with 10-year mortality. Target labels are not used; η ranges are informed by outcome prevalence.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the most direct methodological template for N1's sensitivity component. Replacing the S-conditioning by mask-pattern conditioning, a tilt P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m) ∝ exp(η_m y) P_S(Y|x_obs), applied to the risk DIFFERENCE of two models, is what an 'acquisition-aware model selection with sensitivity' would look like.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Substantial for the sensitivity and estimation machinery: tilt-based sensitivity of target risk with DR estimators and inference already exists for transported prediction models. N1 would add (i) mask- or acquisition-pattern-specific tilts, (ii) the pairwise risk difference and ranking-flip threshold (a 'tipping-point η') rather than a single model's risk, and (iii) a fully observed source with artificial masks. Whether that is a sufficient delta is a NO_GO risk N1 must assess honestly. The paper does not compare models or treat missingness.

papers.title: Beyond the Training Distribution: Evaluating Predictions Under Distribution Shift and Selection Bias
papers.authors: Annie Ulichney, Amanda Coston
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML (via the WebFetch summarizer).
papers.method: A double machine learning (cross-fitted, efficient-influence-function) estimator of the target risk E_T[ℓ(f(X),Y)] of a FIXED predictor under covariate shift plus selective labels, with Wald confidence intervals. It is compared against plug-in, covariate-shift-only and selective-labels-only estimators.
papers.shift_assumptions: Selection on observables (Y ⟂ D | X, R=1), covariate shift P_S(Y|X)=P_T(Y|X), positivity, and a bounded likelihood ratio. Robustness to unobserved-confounding and outcome-shift violations is only examined empirically; there is no formal sensitivity model.
papers.source_access: Source X, with Y observed only when the labeling decision D=1 (e.g. a lab test was ordered).
papers.target_access: Target X only.
papers.identification_result: Under those assumptions target risk is identified as E_T[μ(X)]. The DML estimator is √n-asymptotically normal and semiparametrically efficient. Bias grows under selection on unobservables and outcome shift.
papers.experiments: eICU, semi-synthetic: real covariates with synthetic outcomes and selection, plus three real target hospitals chosen for demographic shift. Real outcomes (BNP, troponin-I, CK, hypoxemia) are observed only when the lab was ordered, i.e. natural selective acquisition of LABELS. Only a single model is evaluated; there is no ranking.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Supplies the estimation and uncertainty machinery (DR/DML target-risk estimators with CIs) that N1's model-selection comparison should use or beat. Its lab-ordering setting is selective acquisition applied to labels rather than input modalities.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers DR/DML estimation of target risk with CIs under shift and selection. N1 cannot claim 'target risk estimation with uncertainty' as novel. Not covered: missing INPUT modalities or masks at prediction time, MNAR sensitivity, pairwise risk difference or model ranking, and artificial-versus-natural masking.

papers.title: Unsupervised domain adaptation with non-stochastic missing data
papers.authors: Matthieu Kirchmeyer, Patrick Gallinari, Alain Rakotomamonjy, Amin Mantrach
papers.venue_year: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 35:2714-2755, 2021. arXiv 2109.09505.
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract page; journal details come from search snippets. I did not read the full text, and details of how missingness was generated are not confirmed.
papers.method: Joint adaptation, imputation and classification: generative imputation of missing target components in a domain-invariant latent space, supervised indirectly by the complete source domain.
papers.shift_assumptions: General distribution shift between domains, plus 'systematically absent' (non-stochastic, block) components in the target. There is no formal MAR/MNAR framing.
papers.source_access: Labeled source with ALL components observed.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target in which some components are systematically missing.
papers.identification_result: None formal, as far as I could verify from the abstract.
papers.experiments: Digits, Amazon reviews and real digital-advertising datasets. I could not confirm whether missingness is synthetic, natural or both.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Structurally the closest data layout to N1: a fully observed labeled source and a target with blockwise-missing components. It is an early ML instance of 'complete source, incomplete target'.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the complete-source/incomplete-target UDA setting as a learning problem, and is a candidate 'imputation + adaptation' baseline. Not covered: selective or MNAR acquisition, evaluation or model selection, sensitivity, and uncertainty.

papers.title: Multimodal domain adaptation under label shift and blockwise missing modalities
papers.authors: Zebin Wang, Ziang Dou, Molei Liu, Tianxi Cai
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and HTML (via the WebFetch summarizer).
papers.method: Reference-anchored domain adaptation. A reference modality observed in all domains is used to estimate the target outcome distribution via likelihood ratios. Sources are then reweighted by label-shift weights, auxiliary modalities are mapped into a target-defined CCA representation via ridge maps, and an optional surrogate-label bridge is added.
papers.shift_assumptions: Label shift, with P(features|Y) invariant. Missingness is blockwise and structural by source design, since each source observes a fixed modality subset; it is not a unit-level MCAR, MAR or MNAR mechanism.
papers.source_access: Multiple labeled sources (with sparse gold labels plus surrogates), each with a different modality subset that always includes the reference.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target during fitting, with COMPLETE modalities in the primary analysis. Target labels are revealed only for final evaluation.
papers.identification_result: Target outcome distribution and conditional outcome are identified via the reference modality, with alignment up to a common rotation (Lemma 2), under label shift.
papers.experiments: Simulations, plus a Mass General Brigham renal cell carcinoma EHR cohort: 5,674 source patients (2000-2016) in 3 domains with modality subsets {1,2}, {1,2,3} and {1,4,5}, and 379 complete-modality target patients (2017-2022). Missingness is natural and structural. Uncertainty comes from 1,000 event-stratified bootstrap resamples; hyperparameters are pre-specified or selected on source only.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Multimodal, real-data, with target labels held out until final evaluation, which is a good design template for N1's 'fix cohort and cutoff first'. Missingness is by design (domain-level), not selective per-patient acquisition.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers multimodal adaptation with blockwise-missing modalities, bootstrap CIs, and leakage-safe tuning. Not covered: per-unit selective or MNAR acquisition, missingness shift at prediction time (its target is complete), model-selection risk differences and sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: MIRRAMS: Learning Robust Tabular Models under Unseen Missingness Shifts
papers.authors: Jihye Lee, Minseo Kang, Dongha Kim
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2507.08280 [stat.ML], v1 Jul 2025, v2 Aug 2025
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and the HTML of v2 (via the WebFetch summarizer).
papers.method: Mutual-information robustness conditions implemented by applying ADDITIONAL random masking to training data as a surrogate for the unseen test missingness. The loss combines cross-entropy on original data, cross-entropy on extra-masked data, and FixMatch-style consistency regularization.
papers.shift_assumptions: The test missingness mechanism is unknown and unseen; the method claims to need no MCAR/MAR/MNAR assumption. There is no identification theory, only an MI/KL surrogate argument.
papers.source_access: Training data with synthetic missingness, labels fully (or partly) observed.
papers.target_access: None at training time. Test labels are used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: None. Prop. 1 links cross-entropy minimization to the MI conditions.
papers.experiments: Ten complete tabular benchmarks (adult, bank, spambase, etc.) with SYNTHETIC MCAR, MAR and MNAR injection at rates of 0, 0.15 and 0.3 varied between train and test. No natural missingness.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the 'artificial dropout as robustness surrogate' approach whose external validity N1 questions. It is a natural 'dropout' baseline, and its evaluation is fully synthetic, so it never tests natural acquisition.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers dropout or masking augmentation for robustness to missingness shift. It does not address whether artificial-mask performance predicts natural-missingness risk or ranking, and has no sensitivity analysis or uncertainty.

papers.title: Still More Shades of Null: An Evaluation Suite for Responsible Missing Value Imputation
papers.authors: Falaah Arif Khan, Denys Herasymuk, Nazar Protsiv, Julia Stoyanovich
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2409.07510 (v1 Sep 2024, v6 Jul 2025). I could not confirm a venue.
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract and the HTML of v6 (via the WebFetch summarizer).
papers.method: An evaluation suite: 29,736 pipelines crossing imputers, downstream models, missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR, multi-mechanism) and 'missingness shift' (a different mechanism or rate at train and test), scored on accuracy, fairness and stability.
papers.shift_assumptions: Synthetic mechanisms are injected into clean data, with different mechanisms or rates at train and test.
papers.source_access: Clean data with injected nulls, plus labels.
papers.target_access: Test split with differently injected nulls; labels are used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: None; the study is empirical.
papers.experiments: Seven clean tabular datasets (Diabetes, German, Folk-Income, Law-School, Bank, Heart, Folk-Employment), all with SYNTHETIC missingness, a limitation the authors acknowledge. Findings: 'no consistent trend across MVI technique, missingness type and train test missingness rate'; fairness is highly sensitive to missingness shift.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Empirical evidence that method rankings are unstable under synthetic missingness shift, but it never compares artificial with natural missingness. This is exactly the gap in N1's step 8.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers 'rankings change under simulated missingness shift' at benchmark level. Not covered: natural missingness, acquisition semantics, S/M separation, sensitivity analysis and a model-selection procedure.

papers.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
papers.authors: Zihan Liang, Ziwen Pan, Ruoxuan Xiong
papers.venue_year: EMNLP 2025 (per the arXiv comment 'To appear in Proceedings of EMNLP 2025'). arXiv 2509.17228.
papers.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract page only. I did not read the full text.
papers.method: 'MMNAR-aware' fusion that conditions on modality-missingness patterns, contrastive reconstruction, and multitask prediction with bias correction for observation patterns.
papers.shift_assumptions: 'Modality missing-not-at-random' (MMNAR), where availability is driven by clinical decision-making. From the abstract I could not determine whether a formal shift or identification assumption is made.
papers.source_access: MIMIC-IV and eICU multimodal records (structured data, imaging, radiology reports, notes) with natural modality missingness, e.g. 24.5% of MIMIC-IV patients lack discharge summaries.
papers.target_access: From the abstract, it appears to be in-distribution train/test evaluation with labels.
papers.identification_result: Not determinable from the abstract.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-IV and eICU, natural modality missingness. The abstract reports gains of up to 13.8% AUC for readmission and 13.1% for ICU admission.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Coins and uses 'modality MNAR' for clinical acquisition, and is a strong 'mask-aware' baseline that exploits informative modality missingness. It is exactly the kind of model whose advantage could vanish or reverse under an acquisition-policy shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers mask-aware multimodal learning under informative modality missingness, which is a baseline for N1. Not covered: shift between source and target acquisition policies, target-risk estimation, sensitivity analysis and model selection.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
The exact title exists: "Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness" by Stokes, Do, Blecker, Chunara and Adhikari (NYU), arXiv 2504.00322, stat.ME, v1 of 1 Apr 2025, with no peer-reviewed venue found. I read the full text.

**Setup and main result.**
- Source is labeled, with its own natural or MNAR covariate missingness, so it is not fully observed. Target has covariates and masks but no labels.
- Assumed invariant: P(Y|Xo,Xu,R) and, in the base case, P(Xo,Xu). Only P(R|X) shifts.
- The MNAR class is self-censoring (Xi→Ri) with latent confounding. It is not nonparametrically identified, so identification is delegated to parametric MNAR imputers (Bayesian joint models, MICE, not-MIWAE, GINA).
- Main formal point: under MNAR, P(Y|x_obs,R) differs across domains even with an invariant full-data outcome model, so importance weighting on observed data is insufficient.
- Proposed procedure: impute each domain separately, then reweight with a domain classifier on (Xo, X̂u, R).
- Theorem 1 bounds the reducible target MSE by imputation error times P(R=0). It needs point imputation converging to the realized counterfactual Xu, which in my reading is a reduction rather than an identification result.
- No bounds, sensitivity model, confidence intervals, model selection, or S-versus-M distinction.

**Experiments.**
- About 120k synthetic self-masking simulations.
- eICU South vs Northeast with natural missingness, where the source/target direction is stated inconsistently in the paper.
- Target labels were used for evaluation and in the 'leak' imputers.
- The authors' own conclusion: no method beats mean imputation by a large margin.

**Comparison with Zhou, Balakrishnan and Lipton (AISTATS 2023, DAMS).**
- DAMS covers MCAR 'underreporting' without indicators, where absolute rates are not identifiable but relative rates and the optimal target linear predictor are.
- With observed indicators and MCAR or v-MAR, it reduces to covariate shift.
- Its own eICU discussion flags cohort selection bias and prevalence change as confounders of missingness shift, and names sensitivity analysis as future work.
- Stokes et al. extend this to MNAR by reducing to imputation.
- Neither paper addresses model ranking or selection, a fully observed source with artificial masks, or modality-level acquisition.

**Closely related work, 2021-2026.**
- Rockenschaub et al. 2024: the pattern-wise Bayes predictor is invariant only under ignorable (MAR-to-MAR) missingness shift. The paper explicitly says source performance may stop being a good selection criterion. Masks are synthetic only.
- Catoire et al. 2026: missingness-conditional vs missingness-unconditional prediction targets, and staging of missingness across development, validation and deployment.
- ICYM2I (ICLR 2026): IPW-corrected evaluation of multimodal models under MAR modality missingness, in the reverse direction (incomplete source to fully observed target). There are no MNAR guarantees, and the clinical cohort is itself selected on label acquisition.
- Steingrimsson, Robertson and Dahabreh (Biometrics 2024): an exponential-tilt sensitivity analysis with DR estimators for one model's target risk. This is the closest template for N1's sensitivity component.
- Ulichney and Coston 2026: DML target-risk estimation with CIs under covariate shift plus selective labels (lab ordering).
- Kirchmeyer et al. 2021: a complete labeled source with a target that has systematically missing components (UDA).
- Wang et al. 2026: multimodal DA with blockwise-missing modalities under label shift. The target is complete, and target labels are held out until final evaluation.
- MIRRAMS 2025 and Shades-of-Null 2024/25: synthetic-mask robustness and evaluation. Shades-of-Null reports that method rankings under missingness shift are inconsistent.
- Liang et al. (EMNLP 2025): 'modality MNAR' mask-aware multimodal learning.

**Existing pieces of the N1 candidate.**
- Non-transportability of P(Y|x_obs,M) under MNAR: Stokes App. A, Rockenschaub Thm 1.
- Reweighting on (x_obs, M) under MCAR/MAR: Zhou Prop. 1.
- IPW evaluation for modality missingness: ICYM2I.
- Tilt-based sensitivity of target risk with DR inference: Steingrimsson et al.
- DML target risk with CIs: Ulichney and Coston.
- Masking augmentation: MIRRAMS; Zhou's missingness filter.

N1's novelty therefore has to rest on the combination and the specific question, not on any single component.
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
1. **Model selection versus artificial dropout.** No paper asks N1's actual question: when does MCAR-style artificial modality dropout on a fully observed source cohort predict the RANKING, or the sign of the risk difference, of two fixed models on a target with naturally selective acquisition? Every related paper either learns an adapted predictor (Stokes, Zhou, Kirchmeyer, Wang, MIRRAMS) or evaluates a single model's target risk (Steingrimsson, Ulichney-Coston, ICYM2I).

2. **Sensitivity of the pairwise risk difference.** No sensitivity model or partial-identification bound exists for the pairwise target risk difference under mask-pattern-specific MNAR, for example a tilt or odds ratio on P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m) relative to the source, reported as a 'tipping-point' sensitivity value at which the ranking flips. Stokes et al. have no sensitivity analysis at all. Steingrimsson et al. tilt P(Y|X, population) for a single model with no mask structure. ICYM2I only shows empirically that MNAR biases its estimates.

3. **Uncertainty for the ranking decision.** No CI or bootstrap is attached to a ranking decision under missingness shift. Stokes uses 5 seeds; Rockenschaub and Shades-of-Null report no inferential CIs for rank changes.

4. **Population selection S versus observation mask M.** No paper formally separates them. Zhou et al. explicitly name cohort selection bias and prevalence change as unresolved confounders on eICU. ICYM2I's cohort is selected on label acquisition (having a TTE). Stokes applies APACHE and other exclusions without analyzing them. None tests whether apparent rank changes are explained by sample selection or class balance, which is N1 step 8.

5. **Record absence versus 'test not performed'.** Every paper treats a missing entry as simply NA.

6. **Artificial versus natural on the same real cohort.** No study compares artificial masking and natural missingness on the same real cohort with labels, checking rank concordance. Rockenschaub, MIRRAMS and Shades-of-Null use synthetic masks only. Stokes and Zhou use natural eICU missingness but never compare it to artificial masking of a complete subcohort.

7. **Modality-level selective acquisition.** Stokes and Zhou work at feature level in tabular EHR. ICYM2I and Liang et al. are modality-level but not about shift from a fully observed source to a naturally missing target.

**Caveats for N1's go/no-go.**
- The minimal counterexample, that artificial dropout cannot determine target risk under MNAR, is essentially implied by Stokes App. A and Rockenschaub Thm 1. N1's counterexample must add a concrete RANK REVERSAL between two models and the minimal extra assumption that restores comparability. Candidate assumptions: MAR given the observed modalities, which by Zhou Prop. 1 and Rockenschaub Thm 1 makes pattern-wise predictors invariant; or a bounded tilt.
- Any reweighting or IPW estimator on (x_obs, M) is prior art (Zhou Prop. 1, ICYM2I) and must not be called new.
- In the Stokes and Zhou eICU studies, target labels were available, so non-identifiability arguments do not apply to those empirical settings.
- If N1's delta over Steingrimsson et al. plus ICYM2I reduces to 'apply their tilt per mask pattern to a difference of two risks', that is a thin contribution and a NO_GO risk. The substantive novelty would have to come from the S/M separation, the real-data artificial-versus-natural rank-concordance test, and a tipping-point analysis.

sweeps.cluster: Evaluating multimodal models under missing modalities: is artificial/synthetic modality dropout representative of natural (selectively acquired) missingness, and do model rankings agree?

papers.title: DrFuse: Learning Disentangled Representation for Clinical Multi-Modal Fusion with Missing Modality and Modal Inconsistency
papers.authors: Wenfang Yao, Kejing Yin, William K. Cheung, Jia Liu, Jing Qin
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv PDF); Table 2 numbers and the 'domain shift' sentence read directly
papers.method: Disentangles shared and modality-specific features, with disease-aware attention fusion. When training on the matched (paired) subset, it randomly removes the CXR from 30% of samples per mini-batch as augmentation (artificial dropout). Baselines are fed zeros when the CXR is missing, or MedFuse's learned vector.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-IV + MIMIC-CXR, 25 phenotypes, first 48h of ICU stay. 59,344 ICU stays, of which 10,630 have a CXR (last AP image in the window). Two cohorts: full dataset (natural missingness) and matched subset (complete cases). A 2x2 design trains on matched or full and tests on matched or full. PRAUC with bootstrap CIs. All target labels are public.
papers.shift_assumptions: None formalized. Missingness is treated as an input problem. The authors informally attribute the matched-vs-full gap to 'severe domain shift', because 'patients who could not undergo X-ray scans may have more complex health conditions'.
