papers.source_access: Matched subset: EHR + CXR + labels (or the full dataset with its natural masks and labels).
papers.target_access: The full test set with natural masks and all labels (public).
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The strongest direct evidence of ranking disagreement between complete-case and natural-missing test populations for fixed trained models. Trained on matched and tested on matched, the ranking is DrFuse .450 > MedFuse .427 > MedFuse-II .418 > DAFT .417 > MMTM .416 > EHR-only Transformer .408. Tested on full, it becomes DrFuse .384 > Transformer .374 > MMTM .359 > DAFT .348 > MedFuse .329 = MedFuse-II .329, so the EHR-only model rises from last to second and MedFuse falls to last. The EHR-only Transformer's own drop (.408 to .374) does not involve the CXR mask at all, so it isolates a pure population-selection (S) effect. N1 can reuse this as a diagnostic that separates S from M.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Shows empirically that complete-case evaluation can mis-rank models on the natural-missing deployment population. It does not separate S from M formally, does not test whether reweighting or class balance explains the reversal, does not evaluate artificial test-time dropout on the matched set against the full set in the same table, and does no model selection, sensitivity analysis or uncertainty analysis on risk differences beyond per-model CIs.

papers.title: When Does Multimodal Learning Help in Healthcare? A Benchmark on EHR and Chest X-Ray Fusion (CareBench)
papers.authors: Kejing Yin, Haizhou Xu, Wenfang Yao, Chen Liu, Zijie Chen, Yui Haang Cheung, William K. Cheung, Jing Qin
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv PDF); cohort section, RQ3 text, and Tables 1 and 3 read directly
papers.method: Benchmark of 15+ unimodal and fusion methods: Transformer, LSTM, ResNet, LateFusion, MedFuse, MMTM, DAFT, UTDE, ShaSpec, Flex-MoE, DrFuse, SMIL, HEALNet, M3Care, UMSE, AUG, InfoReg. Methods not designed for missing inputs get zero-imputation for an absent CXR.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-IV v2.2 + MIMIC-CXR. Base cohort: 26,947 ICU stays of at least 48h (non-elective); about 75% have no CXR (natural missingness). Matched subset: 7,149 stays with a CXR from 24h before to 48h after ICU admission. Tasks are phenotyping, mortality and LoS. A controlled CXR-missingness sweep from 0% to 80% runs on the matched subset for the top 6 methods (Fig. 2); the text does not state the mechanism, presumably random. All labels are public.
papers.shift_assumptions: None formalized. Missingness is called 'realistic', but no MCAR/MAR/MNAR analysis is given. Missing-value indicators are added within the EHR because 'missingness itself can be informative'.
papers.source_access: Matched subset: EHR + CXR + labels.
papers.target_access: Base cohort: EHR + CXR where acquired + labels (public).
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The closest existing benchmark that reports both regimes for the same method set: complete-case, a synthetic missing-ratio sweep, and the natural-missing base cohort. The tables already show rank changes. For mortality AUPRC, DrFuse is 1st on the matched set (.481) but about 9th on the base cohort (.500), while InfoReg and MedFuse lead there (.511 and .508). The EHR-only Transformer is a strong baseline on the base cohort (.504) but weak on the matched set (.447). Absolute mortality AUROC is much higher on the base cohort (e.g., Transformer .867 vs .821), which points to a population (S) shift. Caveat: base-cohort models appear to be trained on the base cohort, so training data and test population change together. I did not verify this.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Provides data for, but does not perform, a rank-agreement analysis between the synthetic-dropout sweep and natural missingness. It has no S-vs-M decomposition, no reweighting or class-balance explanation test, no model-selection procedure, no sensitivity analysis and no treatment of acquisition semantics. A 'no CXR in window' stay is treated as missing.

papers.title: MedFuse: Multi-modal fusion with clinical time-series data and chest X-ray images
papers.authors: Nasir Hayat, Krzysztof J. Geras, Farah E. Shamout
papers.verification: fetched full text (PMLR PDF); Sec. 4.1.2, Tables 2-3 and Appendix A.4/A.6 read directly
papers.method: LSTM-based fusion that treats modality features as a sequence and uses a learnable vector for a missing CXR. Compared against early/joint fusion, MMTM, DAFT and Unified.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-IV + MIMIC-CXR, in-hospital mortality and 25 phenotypes. (EHR+CXR)PAIRED vs (EHR+CXR)PARTIAL test sets, where only 18.8% (phenotyping) and 26.2% (mortality) of partial test samples are paired. Appendix A.4 randomly drops the CXR from 0% to 100% of paired test samples. Appendix A.6 instead adds 0% to 100% of the naturally unimodal samples to the paired test set. Bootstrap CIs. Labels are public.
papers.shift_assumptions: None formalized.
papers.source_access: Paired and partial training sets with labels.
papers.target_access: Paired and partial test sets with labels (public).
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A clean single-model instance where artificial dropout and natural missingness point in opposite directions. Randomly dropping the CXR from paired test samples lowers AUROC for both tasks (A.4). Adding naturally CXR-absent patients raises in-hospital mortality AUROC and leaves phenotyping roughly flat (A.6). Every method's mortality AUROC is higher on the partial test set than on the paired one (e.g., Early .818 to .860). This shows that the natural-missing population differs in composition (S), which artificial dropout on the paired cohort cannot reproduce. Label prevalence differs between the paired test set and the partial training set (their Table 4).
papers.overlap_with_candidate: It supplies both evaluation modes (artificial dropout on the paired cohort and natural partial pairing) but never compares them, never ranks methods under artificial dropout, and does not explain the discrepancy. N1's contribution of explaining this formally and correcting selection for it is left open.

papers.title: ICYM2I: The illusion of multimodal informativeness under missingness
papers.authors: Young Sang Choi, Vincent Jeanselme, Pierre Elias, Shalmali Joshi
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv v3 PDF, header 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'); Sec. 3-4 and App. G read directly
papers.method: 'Double' IPW: an IPW-weighted training loss (Lemma 1) plus IPW-corrected evaluation metrics (AUC and Brier, citing Li et al.), and an IPW-corrected partial information decomposition. Missingness propensity p(m1, m2, m_y | C) is estimated by logistic regression.
papers.experiments: Synthetic bitwise AND/OR/XOR with 50% MAR missingness on X2. Semi-synthetic UR-FUNNY and Hateful Memes with induced MAR missingness at 30-70%. Real data: structural heart disease detection at Columbia with ECG always present and CXR present for 12.79%, which is natural missingness. The propensity for CXR uses ECG embedding, age and sex. Ground truth is only available in the (semi-)synthetic settings.
papers.shift_assumptions: MAR given covariates C, with positivity. 'Assumption A': demonstrating a modality's value makes it collected in the target, so the target is fully observed (Omega_target ~ Omega). S and M are lumped into one joint missingness indicator (M1·M2·M_Y). MNAR is only probed empirically in Appendix D, and the authors state there is no guarantee under MNAR.
papers.source_access: Curated/observed data with missingness in modalities and labels; covariates C are available for all units, to fit propensities.
papers.target_access: No target data; the target is the hypothetical fully observed population Omega.
papers.identification_result: Under MAR plus positivity, performance and PID on Omega are identified from Omega_obs by IPW. The paper shows naive complete-case estimates are biased: X1's AUROC is overestimated for OR and underestimated for AND, and the unique information of CXR is reduced from about 5% to 1.8%.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The closest formal work on missingness-induced shift in multimodal evaluation. It explicitly notes that prior robustness work assumes a fully observed source with missingness at the target (Omega_source_obs ~ Omega != Omega_target_obs), which is N1's direction, and does not treat that case itself. It shows that complete-case curation (a form of S) biases modality-value and model comparisons.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers IPW-corrected evaluation, i.e., correcting metrics for complete-case selection under MAR, and flags ranking/informativeness illusions. N1 therefore cannot present IPW-reweighted evaluation as new. It does not cover: the reverse direction (fully observed source, naturally masked target); separating cohort selection S from per-unit mask M; pairwise risk-difference model selection; MNAR sensitivity bounds (e.g., odds-ratio or marginal-sensitivity models) on P_T(Y | x_obs, M); or an artificial-vs-natural ranking comparison.

papers.title: Knockout: A simple way to handle missing inputs
papers.authors: Minh Nguyen, Batuhan K. Karaman, Heejong Kim, Alan Q. Wang, Fengbei Liu, Mert R. Sabuncu
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv PDF), Sec. 2.2 and 2.4 read directly; TMLR venue from ML Anthology/PMC search results
papers.method: Random 'knockout' of inputs or modalities during training, replacing them with out-of-support placeholder values. This is a formalized modality dropout.
papers.experiments: Simulations with complete, MCAR and MNAR training data; Alzheimer's forecasting; privileged information; tumor segmentation; tree genus, prostate cancer and food classification. Mostly synthetic masking; real missingness enters as training-data missingness.
papers.shift_assumptions: The induced mask must satisfy M ⊥ (X, Y). Then the model learns p(Y | X_{-M}) under the training distribution (eqs. 3-4). For naturally missing training inputs N, MCAR can reuse the same placeholder; MAR/MNAR need a separate placeholder, 'Unless stated otherwise, Knockout always uses a different placeholder for MAR and MNAR variables'.
papers.source_access: Training data (complete or with natural masks N) plus labels.
papers.target_access: Test inputs with missing entries; no target-shift analysis.
papers.identification_result: Shows that dropout with M ⊥ (X, Y) and out-of-support placeholders recovers every source marginal predictor p_S(Y | x_obs) at once.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Gives the precise estimand that artificial dropout evaluates: the source marginal p_S(Y | x_obs) and risk under an independent mask. N1's minimal counterexample follows directly. When acquisition is selective, P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) != P_S(Y | x_obs) and P_T(x_obs | M=m) != P_S(x_obs), so the dropout risk and the deployment risk can order two models differently.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the 'what does dropout estimate' part: a mask independent of (X, Y), and a separate placeholder for naturally missing values, which is a mask-aware baseline. It does not analyze target risk under selective acquisition, model ranking or evaluation.

papers.title: Deep Multimodal Learning with Missing Modality: A Survey
papers.authors: Renjie Wu, Hu Wang, Hsiang-Ting Chen, Gustavo Carneiro
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv v3 PDF), dataset/evaluation discussion read directly; grep confirmed no MCAR/MAR/MNAR terms
papers.method: Survey of missing-modality learning methods and applications.
papers.experiments: Meta-analysis of evaluation protocols in the surveyed works.
papers.shift_assumptions: Not discussed. The survey does not mention MCAR/MAR/MNAR.
papers.source_access: n/a
papers.target_access: n/a
papers.identification_result: n/a
papers.relevance_to_N1: Quantifies how the field evaluates. It states 'the majority of the publicly available datasets ... are complete in terms of modalities, and naturally occurring datasets with missing modalities are rare'. Tasks are therefore evaluated over all modality combinations with synthetic missing rates: 62% of reviewed works use random missing rates and 38% controlled rates. Benchmarking and evaluation is listed as an open issue.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Documents the prevalence of synthetic-dropout evaluation, which motivates N1. It has no formalization, no natural-vs-synthetic comparison and no discussion of missingness mechanisms.

papers.title: Are Multimodal Transformers Robust to Missing Modality?
papers.authors: Mengmeng Ma, Jian Ren, Long Zhao, Davide Testuggine, Xi Peng
papers.verification: fetched arXiv abstract; CVPR 2022 confirmed via CVF open-access listing (search result). Full-text experimental details from prior knowledge are not re-verified here.
papers.method: Studies how the fusion strategy affects robustness to missing modality, and proposes automatic search over fusion strategies plus multi-task optimization.
papers.experiments: MM-IMDb, UPMC Food-101 and Hateful Memes with synthetic test-time removal of a modality (text) at varying rates. Complete datasets; no natural missingness.
papers.shift_assumptions: Implicitly MCAR: a random subset loses the modality at test time.
papers.source_access: Complete image-text pairs with labels.
papers.target_access: The same distribution with a random mask.
papers.identification_result: None. Its empirical finding: 'the optimal fusion strategy is dataset dependent ... there does not exist a universal strategy'.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The canonical synthetic robustness benchmark. It already shows that model and fusion rankings depend on the test-time missing rate and the dataset, i.e., the evaluation mask distribution, even under MCAR.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Shows ranking sensitivity to the synthetic mask distribution. It does not consider natural or selective acquisition, population selection or target risk.

papers.title: MuteBench: Modality Unavailability Tolerance Evaluation for Incomplete Multimodal Fusion
papers.authors: Wugeng Zheng, Ziwen Kan, Tianlong Chen, Chen Chen, Song Wang
papers.verification: fetched arXiv HTML via summarizing fetch; the 'inconsistent method rankings' quote came from the summarizer and was not re-checked verbatim
papers.method: Clinical fusion benchmark of 6 fusion models (e.g., CLIMB, MIRA, ShaSpec, FuseMoE) plus curriculum dropout and diffusion imputation.
papers.experiments: 9 clinical datasets from 7 domains (over 125k samples). Synthetic whole-channel dropping (p = 0.2, 0.5) and within-modality contiguous gaps. Masks are deterministic per (seed, sample) and applied to train, val and test alike. No natural-missingness comparison.
papers.shift_assumptions: Synthetic, independent-per-channel (MCAR-like); the mechanism is not discussed.
papers.source_access: Complete data with labels.
papers.target_access: The same distribution with synthetic masks.
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Reports that the two synthetic failure modes 'produce inconsistent method rankings', and that curriculum dropout protects only up to the maximum dropout rate used in training. This is evidence that dropout-based rankings are fragile even among synthetic mask distributions.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Shows rank sensitivity to the synthetic mask type and rate. It has no natural missingness, no selection and no target-risk reasoning.

papers.title: Integrated multimodal artificial intelligence framework for healthcare applications (HAIM)
papers.authors: Luis R. Soenksen, Yu Ma, Cynthia Zeng, Leonard Boussioux, Kimberly Villalobos Carballo, Liangyuan Na, et al.
papers.verification: fetched full text (arXiv PDF); cohort filter and modality-combination design read directly
papers.method: Fixed embeddings per modality (tabular, time series, notes, CXR), concatenated, with XGBoost. 14,324 models are trained over all modality combinations.
papers.experiments: HAIM-MIMIC-MM: 34,537 samples from 7,279 hospitalizations, 'filtered to only include patients that have at least one chest X-ray'. Tasks: chest pathologies, LoS and 48h mortality. Modality value is judged by subset models; missing-input sensitivity is in Supp. Fig. 4.
papers.shift_assumptions: None. The cohort itself is conditioned on CXR acquisition.
papers.source_access: CXR-selected cohort with all modalities where present, plus labels.
papers.target_access: The same CXR-selected cohort (random split).
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A prominent example where population selection S (patients with at least one CXR) is baked into the cohort, and modality contributions are assessed by modality-subset or ablation evaluation within that selected population. This is exactly the setting in which N1 asks whether the resulting rankings transfer to the full eligible population.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on the method side. It serves as a motivating case of complete-case/selected-cohort evaluation.

papers.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness (CRL-MMNAR)
papers.authors: Zihan Liang, Ziwen Pan, Ruoxuan Xiong
papers.verification: fetched arXiv HTML via summarizing fetch; EMNLP 2025 confirmed via ACL Anthology search result
papers.method: MMNAR-aware fusion that conditions on the missingness pattern, plus contrastive reconstruction and a pattern-specific residual 'rectifier' estimated from held-out labeled folds.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-IV (20,000 single-ICU-stay adults, not restricted by modality: 75.5% have discharge summaries, 85% radiology reports) and eICU. Natural missingness only. Random masking is used only as a training-time augmentation. Labels are available.
papers.shift_assumptions: Latent health state h drives both the modality contents and the clinician-assigned observation pattern; the pattern may act like a treatment. No formal restriction or identification.
papers.source_access: Natural masks, inputs and labels.
papers.target_access: The same population; no train/deploy shift.
papers.identification_result: None. No identifiability theorem.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Treats acquisition as clinician-driven (MNAR) and informative, and uses pattern-specific label residuals. This is related to N1's mask-aware baselines, and it motivates why P(Y | x_obs, M) differs from the dropout marginal.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers mask-aware modeling of clinician-driven missingness. It has no source/target shift, no synthetic-vs-natural comparison, no model-selection or ranking analysis and no sensitivity bounds.

papers.title: A Study of Dropout-Induced Modality Bias on Robustness to Missing Video Frames for Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
papers.authors: Yusheng Dai, Hang Chen, Jun Du, Ruoyu Wang, Shihao Chen, Jiefeng Ma, Haotian Wang, Chin-Hui Lee
papers.verification: search snippet only (arXiv listing plus CVF open-access; the CVF PDF returned 403)
papers.method: Analyzes modality dropout and proposes MDA-KD (distribution-approximation knowledge distillation).
papers.experiments: AVSR with synthetically missing video frames.
papers.shift_assumptions: Synthetic missing frames.
papers.source_access: Complete AV data with labels.
papers.target_access: Synthetic missing-frame test sets.
papers.identification_result: None. Empirically, dropout improves robustness to missing video but hurts complete-input performance, due to over-reliance on audio.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Shows that the dropout rate trades off complete-input against missing-input performance. Which of two models looks better therefore depends on the assumed test-time mask distribution, a mechanism behind rank flips.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Only the observation that rankings depend on the test mask distribution. It has no natural acquisition and no selection.

papers.title: ModDrop: Adaptive Multi-Modal Gesture Recognition
papers.authors: Natalia Neverova, Christian Wolf, Graham W. Taylor, Florian Nebout
papers.verification: fetched arXiv abstract; TPAMI venue confirmed via ACM DL / search result
papers.method: Modality dropout: random dropping of whole modality channels during gradual fusion training.
papers.experiments: ChaLearn 2014 gesture recognition (1st of 17 teams). Robustness to missing or corrupted channels is tested by synthetically removing channels.
papers.shift_assumptions: Implicitly MCAR channel loss.
papers.source_access: Complete multimodal data with labels.
papers.target_access: The same distribution with synthetic channel loss.
papers.identification_result: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The origin of the modality-dropout training and evaluation paradigm that N1 questions.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None beyond defining the dropout baseline.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
(1) Evaluation with artificial dropout is the norm. Wu et al.'s survey (arXiv 2409.07825) finds most public multimodal datasets are complete, so 62% of the works it reviews use random missing rates. The same holds for ModDrop, SMIL, ShaSpec, missing-aware prompting (Lee et al., CVPR 2023, arXiv 2303.03369) and Ma et al. (CVPR 2022). Even among synthetic masks, rankings are unstable: Ma et al. find the best fusion strategy depends on dataset and missing rate, MuteBench finds the two synthetic failure modes give inconsistent rankings, and Dai et al. show dropout trades complete-input performance for missing-input performance.

(2) Knockout (TMLR 2025) states formally what dropout estimates. With a mask independent of (X, Y), the model learns the source marginal p_S(Y | x_obs). Under selective acquisition, P_T(Y | x_obs, M) differs from that, which is the core of N1's minimal counterexample.

(3) Clinical EHR+CXR work on MIMIC already contains the raw evidence that complete-case rankings do not carry over to naturally missing populations:
- DrFuse (AAAI 2024) Table 2: models trained on the matched subset and tested on the full dataset reorder. The EHR-only Transformer rises from last to second and MedFuse falls from second to last. The authors mention 'severe domain shift' and that patients without CXR may be sicker.
- MedFuse (MLHC 2022): randomly dropping the CXR from paired test samples lowers AUROC (App. A.4), but adding naturally CXR-absent patients raises mortality AUROC (App. A.6). Artificial and natural missingness move in opposite directions.
- CareBench (arXiv 2602.23614, 2026): reports a complete-case matched cohort, a 0-80% controlled missingness sweep and the natural 75%-missing base cohort for the same methods. The mortality AUPRC ranking changes: DrFuse is first on the matched set but mid-pack on the base cohort, and the EHR-only Transformer becomes competitive.
None of these papers computes rank agreement, separates population selection S from the mask M, or tests whether reweighting or class balance explains the change.

(4) The only formal evaluation-correction work in this cluster is ICYM2I (ICLR 2026). It uses IPW under MAR to correct complete-case (curated) estimates of performance and modality informativeness. Its target is the fully observed population, the reverse of N1's direction. It combines S and M into one indicator and handles MNAR only through an appendix robustness check. It explicitly names the fully-observed-source / naturally-missing-target direction as assumed by prior robustness work, and does not address it.

(5) CRL-MMNAR (EMNLP 2025) and a prospective UCSD study (arXiv 2605.26255, Lu & Nemati 2026) acknowledge that clinician-driven acquisition is non-random and 'introduc[es] potential selection bias'. Neither quantifies how that affects model rankings.

All MIMIC-based studies here have fully public target labels. Their ranking comparisons are therefore empirically checkable, and N1 should not make non-identifiability claims for those settings.
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
1. No paper measures rank agreement (e.g., Kendall tau or a pairwise sign test with CIs) for the same trained models under two evaluations: artificial dropout on the complete-case cohort vs natural missingness in the full eligible population. MedFuse, DrFuse and CareBench have the ingredients, but in DrFuse and CareBench the change of test population is confounded with a change of training data.
2. No paper formally separates cohort selection S (complete-case inclusion, an acquisition-window rule, 'at least one CXR' filters as in HAIM, CareBench's matched subset and DrFuse's matched subset) from the per-unit observation mask M. ICYM2I combines them into one indicator; DrFuse and MedFuse only speculate. A simple diagnostic is available but unused: the drop of a CXR-free (EHR-only) model between the matched and full sets isolates the S effect, as in DrFuse (.408 to .374).
3. No paper checks whether observed rank flips are explained by simple sample selection, label-prevalence or class-balance reweighting (N1 step 8) before invoking the missingness mechanism.
4. No paper covers N1's direction formally: a fully observed source with complete-case or artificial dropout, and a target where modalities are selectively acquired. That means no minimal counterexample showing that dropout risk cannot determine the sign of the target risk difference, and no statement of which added assumptions make it comparable, e.g., MAR given x_obs and pattern-level transportability of P(Y | x_obs, M). Knockout gives the estimand and ICYM2I the reverse-direction MAR correction.
5. No paper offers acquisition-aware model selection on the pairwise risk difference with MNAR sensitivity analysis (odds-ratio or marginal-sensitivity bounds on P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) relative to the source) and bootstrap uncertainty. ICYM2I is point-identified under MAR only. Plain IPW metric correction is already in ICYM2I (citing Li et al.) and cannot be claimed as new.
6. No paper distinguishes 'record absent' from 'test not performed': a CXR outside the time window, from another department, or missing a DICOM counts as missing. The prospective UCSD study forward-fills and borrows CXRs from other departments within 72h, which shows the ambiguity.
7. No paper compares all of the following under the same information and budget: observed-only, mask-aware (e.g., Knockout's separate placeholder, CRL-MMNAR), dropout, imputation, IPW reweighting, and a missingness-shift domain-adaptation baseline. The closest DA baselines (Zhou et al., 'Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift', cited by ICYM2I, and 'Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness') belong to a separate cluster and were not verified here.
8. For N1's NO_GO check: the empirical phenomenon (rank changes between complete-case and natural-missing evaluation) is already visible in published tables (DrFuse, CareBench, MedFuse). The IPW evaluation correction under MAR is already published (ICYM2I). N1's novelty must therefore rest on: the S/M decomposition; a formal non-determination result for dropout evaluation with the minimal extra assumptions; tests that rule out simple selection or class-balance explanations; and sensitivity-bounded pairwise selection. A new loss would not count.

sweeps.cluster: Clinical prediction modelling with informative/selective missingness and its transportability across settings (missing-indicator instability, dev-vs-deployment handling, missingness shift in EHR, and supervised-learning-with-missing-values theory)

papers.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts
papers.authors: Patrick Rockenschaub, Zhicong Xian, Alireza Zamanian, Marta Piperno, Octavia-Andreea Ciora, Elisabeth Pachl, Narges Ahmidi
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint 2406.16484, June 2024 (no peer-reviewed venue found via Crossref)
papers.verification: Fetched the full-text PDF from arXiv and read the theory (Def. 1-2, Theorem 1, Corollary 1, Sec. 4.2 and 6) and the experiments sections.
papers.method: Theory plus empirical comparison of impute-then-regress pipelines (ICE, ICE+mask, MICE, MICE+Y, MIWAE, each followed by an MLP), NeuMiss, and a proposed architecture (NeuMISE), benchmarked against analytic Bayes and oracle-imputation predictors. Models are trained in a source environment and evaluated in a shifted target environment.
papers.shift_assumptions: Assumes p(X,Y)=q(X,Y): no covariate or label shift, and only the missingness mechanism shifts. Missingness shift (Def. 1) means p(M=m|X) differs from q(M=m|X). An ignorable shift (Def. 2) is one where missingness depends only on X_obs in BOTH environments. The main text assumes p(M|X,Y)=p(M|X); Sec. 6 relaxes this to Y-dependent missingness. Mechanisms simulated: MCAR, non-monotone MAR, Gaussian self-masking MNAR, and MAR-Y.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y) with 50% missingness.
papers.target_access: (X_obs, M, Y) at 25% or 0% (complete-data) missingness. Target labels are used only to evaluate MSE. There is no target-based adaptation or model selection.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1 restates Zhou et al. 2023: the pattern-wise Bayes predictors E[Y|X_obs,M=m] are equal in source and target when the shift is ignorable in both environments. They may differ under an MNAR shift. Corollary 1: if target missingness depends on Y and changes, the shift cannot be ignorable. Moving to a complete-data target is treated as a special case (Sec. 4.2): E[Y|X] is recoverable if source missingness is ignorable. The paper gives no bounds and no sensitivity analysis.
papers.experiments: All missingness is synthetic. Data: simulated Gaussian covariates (d=50, N=100k), plus semi-synthetic LBIDD (real 1995 US infant birth/death covariates with a simulated outcome). Target labels are used for evaluation. Empirically, methods differ in robustness. MICE looked worse in the source but was more robust when missingness was highly informative; ICE+mask was the least robust on LBIDD.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the most direct precedent. It states explicitly that 'prediction performance in the source data may no longer be a good selection criterion' under missingness shift, and it formalises when the Bayes predictor is invariant. It also shows empirically that the ranking of methods in the source differs from their robustness in the target, which is the core phenomenon N1 targets.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: (i) the identification statement that ignorable missingness shift with fixed p(X,Y) leaves pattern-wise Bayes predictors unchanged, which is essentially the 'when artificial masking is enough' condition; (ii) the observation that model selection by source performance can fail under shift; (iii) Y-dependent acquisition as the non-ignorable case. Does NOT cover: a fully observed source with ARTIFICIAL dropout used as an evaluation proxy (their direction is incomplete source to less-incomplete or complete target); separating population selection S from mask M; ranking or risk differences for two fixed non-Bayes models; sensitivity bounds on P_T(Y|x_obs,M); uncertainty (only 10 reruns); natural acquisition shifts; modality-level blocks.

papers.title: On the consistency of supervised learning with missing values
papers.authors: Julie Josse, Jacob M. Chen, Nicolas Prost, Erwan Scornet, Gaël Varoquaux
papers.verification: Fetched the full text of arXiv v5 (PDF) and read Remark 1, Assumptions 1-4, Theorems 2-3 and the Discussion. Venue, volume, pages and DOI 10.1007/s00362-024-01550-4 confirmed via Crossref.
papers.method: Theory of Bayes-consistency for (a) test-time conditional multiple imputation plugged into the complete-data Bayes predictor f*, (b) constant or mean imputation applied at both train and test time followed by a universally consistent learner, and (c) missing-value handling inside trees (MIA recommended). Also gives counterexamples in which single imputation fails and missingness indicators are required.
papers.shift_assumptions: Train and test are assumed to come from the same distribution. Remark 1 says explicitly that differing missingness patterns constitute a distribution shift needing dedicated methods, with the example that operational recommendations can make practitioners measure variables systematically. Theorem 2 requires Assumption 2 'MAR-Y': Y independent of M given X_obs(M), which MAR satisfies under the additive-noise model. Theorem 3 requires MAR on a single variable X1 given fully observed X2..Xd.
papers.source_access: Sec. 4.1: the complete-data Bayes predictor f*(X)=E[Y|X] is assumed known or learned from complete data (e.g. complete cases under MCAR). Sec. 4.2: (X_obs, M, Y) in training.
papers.target_access: Test inputs (X_obs, M). Labels are not needed for the theory.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 2: under MAR-Y, f_MI(x_obs)=E_{X_mis|X_obs}[f*(X)] equals the Bayes predictor for incomplete data. So when the target satisfies MAR-Y, the optimal target predictor is determined by the complete-data regression plus the conditional distribution X_mis|X_obs. Theorem 3: constant imputation used at train AND test time is consistent (MAR, one missing variable). Example 3: when missingness depends on Y, imputation alone cannot recover the target and indicators are needed.
papers.experiments: Simulations only (synthetic data with synthetic MCAR/MAR/MNAR masks). No real-data shift experiment.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Theorem 2 is the formal bridge from a fully observed source to a naturally incomplete target, which is exactly N1's direction. It identifies MAR-Y (equivalently Catoire's NIMO) as the condition under which a complete-data model with test-time integration is target-optimal. Remark 1 already names the policy-change scenario of N1 as an out-of-scope distribution shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the identification condition (Y independent of M given X_obs, plus transfer of X_mis|X_obs) under which complete-data learning with mask handling is Bayes-optimal on a masked target. Does NOT cover: ranking of two arbitrary models; population selection (the complete-data source being a selected cohort); P(X,Y) differing between source and target; sensitivity or partial identification when MAR-Y fails; uncertainty; artificial-dropout evaluation protocols.

papers.title: Compatibility of Missing Data Handling Methods across the Stages of Producing Clinical Prediction Models
papers.authors: Antonia Tsvetanova, Matthew Sperrin, David A. Jenkins, Niels Peek, Iain Buchan, Stephanie Hyland, Marcus Taylor, Angela Wood, Richard D. Riley, Glen P. Martin
papers.verification: Fetched the full-text PDF from arXiv and read the setup (Sec. 2), the simulation design (DAGs a-f), the results on mechanism change, the NCORR empirical section, and the Discussion.
papers.method: A simulation plus an empirical study of 'compatibility'. The idea is that the development method should optimise deployment performance, and the validation method should give unbiased estimates of deployment performance. Methods compared across development, validation and deployment: complete-case analysis, mean imputation, regression imputation, multiple imputation with and without Y, and pattern sub-models. Deployment estimands include E-all (complete-data deployment), E-RI and E-MI. Metrics are 'model degradation' and 'validation bias' (validation estimate minus deployment performance).
papers.shift_assumptions: The missingness mechanism is allowed to DIFFER between development and validation. There are six DAGs for R1: none, MCAR, MAR on X2, dependence on X1 and X2, dependence on Y and X2, and dependence on X1, X2 and Y. All combinations are crossed, with 10-50% missingness. The joint (X,Y) distribution is identical across stages. Only one predictor (X1) can be missing.
papers.source_access: Development data (X_obs, M, Y) with Y fully observed.
papers.target_access: The validation set has Y fully observed and predictors possibly missing. In simulation, deployment performance is computed against the known truth.
papers.identification_result: No formal identification. Empirically: when deployment requires complete data, development and validation should use fully observed data or MI-with-Y. Under DAG (f) (MNAR involving X1 and Y), every approach gave degradation and biased validation for E-all. Validation bias depended mainly on how missing data were handled in VALIDATION, not in development. Similar patterns held when the mechanism changed between development and validation. Refitting imputation models in the validation set helped only partly.
papers.experiments: Synthetic simulation (N_dev=N_val=100,000, synthetic masks). Real data: the NCORR thoracic-surgery registry (lung resection 2012-2018, n about 6,600, 204 deaths within 90 days, natural missingness), with 100 bootstrap development sets. Fully observed data were unavailable there, so deployment performance was approximated. Target labels were used for evaluation.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the closest clinical-methodology analogue of N1's question: whether a given validation protocol yields unbiased estimates of deployment risk, including when the missingness mechanism changes between stages. Its central lesson, 'validate the way you will deploy', is the clinical version of 'artificial masking must match deployment acquisition'.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: a quantitative definition of the mismatch between validation-estimated and deployment performance ('validation bias'); crossing of development and validation mechanisms, including Y-dependent MNAR; a real registry example. Does NOT cover: fully observed source with artificial dropout; multi-modality block missingness; separating S from M; label-free target selection (their validation always has Y); two-model risk differences with sensitivity bounds; uncertainty beyond bootstrap summaries.

papers.title: Prediction with Missing Data: Target Probabilities and Missingness Mechanisms
papers.authors: Pierre Catoire, Robin Genuer, Cécile Proust-Lima
papers.verification: Fetched the full-text PDF from arXiv and read the abstract, Sec. 3.2 (NIMO/NICO definitions), Sec. 3.5 (missingness shift) and the limitations.
papers.method: A formal framework separating two prediction targets: MU = Pr(Y|X_o), which ignores the observation pattern, and MC = Pr(Y|X_o, M_X). It gives a nomenclature of mechanisms (NIMO, NICO, MARX-YO, MARX-YM) and maps methods to the target they consistently estimate: pattern sub-models, complete-case sub-models and MI with indicators estimate MC; MI and MLE estimate MU under MARX-YO. Recommendations are split by development, validation and deployment.
papers.shift_assumptions: NIMO: Y independent of M_X given X_o(m) for all patterns with positive probability; under NIMO, MU equals MC. NICO: Y independent of the complete-observation event {M_X=0} given X; this is the relevant condition when deployment is on complete cases. MARX-YO: M independent of X_m given (X_o, Y). MARX-YM: M independent of (X_m, Y) given X_o. 'Missingness shift' (Sec. 3.5) is discussed only qualitatively as a trade-off: MC gains information but is exposed to shift, while MU is unaffected. The authors state explicitly that the effect of shift was NOT investigated.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y).
papers.target_access: Evaluation uses held-out (X_obs, M, Y) under the same distribution: leave-one-out CV on real data and independent test sets in simulation.
papers.identification_result: Both targets can be predicted consistently under conditions weaker than MAR. MC is achievable under any mechanism, for example by complete-case sub-models for complete-data deployment. MU requires MARX-YO, or NICO for complete-case deployment. MU and MC diverge whenever NIMO fails.
papers.experiments: Simulations with a single missing predictor (synthetic masks). Real data: n=678 trauma patients in the Bordeaux ED, predicting ISS>=15 with natural missingness, i.i.d. LOO-CV, target labels used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: It provides the vocabulary N1 needs. NIMO is the condition under which a model trained or evaluated with random (non-informative) dropout on complete data targets the same quantity as the deployment MC target. NICO is the condition under which a fully observed (complete-case-selected) cohort carries no extra outcome information, which is the formal hook for N1's 'population selection S vs mask M' distinction.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: the conditions under which the observation pattern is or is not informative for Y (NIMO/NICO), and the recommendation to fix the target estimand before choosing development and validation procedures. Does NOT cover: missingness shift quantitatively; comparing or ranking models across shifted acquisition; sensitivity bounds; a dropout-evaluation proxy; modalities.

papers.title: Imputation and missing indicators for handling missing data in the development and deployment of clinical prediction models: A simulation study
papers.authors: Rose Sisk, Matthew Sperrin, Niels Peek, Maarten van Smeden, Glen P. Martin
papers.verification: Fetched the abstract via Europe PMC (published version) and the full-text arXiv PDF (read the methods, the performance assumptions in Sec. 3.6, results 4.1.3 and the Discussion).
papers.method: A simulation comparing regression imputation and multiple imputation, with or without Y in the imputation model and with or without a missing indicator (plus an X1:R1 interaction), in logistic CPMs. There are two deployment scenarios: missingness allowed at deployment (imputed) or prohibited (complete data required).
papers.shift_assumptions: The paper explicitly assumes the missingness mechanism stays constant across the pipeline. Mechanisms, one predictor missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR-X (depends on X1) and MNAR-Y (depends on Y). The only 'shift' is the deployment regime: complete data versus imputed missingness. The authors list mechanism change as future work.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y) in development.
papers.target_access: Validation/deployment (X_obs, M, Y) with Y used for evaluation. With complete-data deployment, the target is fully observed.
papers.identification_result: No formal identification. Findings: with complete data at deployment, use Y in MI but omit it in RI. With missingness allowed at deployment, omit Y from imputation at every stage. Missing indicators help under MAR/MNAR-X and under MNAR-Y when missingness is allowed, but under MNAR-Y with complete-data deployment they cause miscalibration (CITL > 0) and severe overfitting for RI. So a model that is best when missingness persists can be worst when the target is fully observed.
papers.experiments: Synthetic simulation with 2 covariates and 1 missing (synthetic masks), plus an application to critical-care data (natural missingness). Target labels were used for evaluation.
papers.relevance_to_N1: It shows concretely that the preferred handling strategy (a proxy for model ranking) depends on the deployment observation regime. In particular, outcome-dependent acquisition flips the value of missing indicators between the 'missing allowed' and 'complete at deployment' regimes. This is a within-paper ranking change driven only by the target mask regime.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: that rankings of handling strategies depend on the deployment observation regime, with MNAR-Y as the dangerous case for mask-aware models. Does NOT cover: changes of the mechanism itself; a fully observed source with artificial dropout; S vs M; sensitivity analysis or bounds; risk-difference uncertainty; multi-variable or modality missingness.

papers.title: Informative missingness in electronic health record systems: the curse of knowing
papers.authors: Rolf H. H. Groenwold
papers.verification: Fetched the full text on PMC (abstract verbatim and the scenario table). The numbers below were extracted by an automated fetch and should be re-checked against the article's table before quoting.
papers.method: An illustrative simulation of cardiovascular-risk prediction in which a lab predictor (cholesterol-like) is not measured when clinicians judge risk to be low, so missingness is informative. Four handling approaches are compared: zero imputation, mean imputation, complete-case analysis and multiple imputation. The first two exploit informative missingness in the manner of the separate-category or missing-indicator idea. Each model is then applied in several deployment scenarios.
papers.shift_assumptions: Development has informative, clinician-driven missingness. The deployment scenarios are: (1) the same mechanism; (2) the predictor is measured in everyone; (3) random 50% missingness (uninformative); (4) never measured. The motivating mechanism is a feedback loop: once a model is deployed and the predictive value of 'not measured' is known, clinicians change measurement behaviour.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y) in development.
papers.target_access: (X_obs, M, Y) in simulated deployment data, with labels used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: No formal identification. Rankings reverse across deployment scenarios. In scenario 1, zero or mean imputation performs best (c about 0.70 versus MI about 0.62). In scenario 3, zero or mean imputation drops to c about 0.54 while MI and CCA reach about 0.66. No method is optimal across scenarios. Performance depends on the transportability of the missing-data mechanism.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data only, with synthetic informative and uninformative masks. Target labels were used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is essentially a published minimal example of N1's step 4/8 phenomenon. The model that wins under the development acquisition policy loses when acquisition becomes random or universal. It also names the mechanism N1 cares about: acquisition policy changes BECAUSE of the model or its knowledge.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: an existence proof, in a simple simulation, that the ranking of models or handling strategies changes when the acquisition mechanism changes after deployment. Does NOT cover: conditions under which ranking is preserved, a dropout-evaluation proxy, bounds or sensitivity, S vs M, natural data, or multimodal settings.

papers.title: A cautionary note on the use of the missing indicator method for handling missing data in prediction research
papers.authors: Maarten van Smeden, Rolf H. H. Groenwold, Karel G. M. Moons
papers.verification: Metadata and keywords (including 'Transportability' and 'Missingness mechanisms') were fetched from the UMC Utrecht research portal, and bibliographic data was confirmed via Europe PMC. The full text was NOT accessible: the JCE page and Utrecht DSpace returned 403, PubMed returned a reCAPTCHA, and Europe PMC has no abstract for this commentary. The content is characterised from citing papers that were fetched: Sisk et al. 2023 (Discussion) and Catoire et al. 2026 (Sec. 3.5).
papers.method: Methodological commentary; no new method.
papers.shift_assumptions: As characterised by citing papers: including a missing indicator adds the assumption that the missingness mechanism is stable across development, validation and deployment. The propensity to measure predictors varies across care providers, settings and time as guidelines change. Methods that do not exploit missingness are unaffected by such shift.
papers.source_access: Not applicable (commentary).
papers.target_access: Not applicable (commentary).
papers.identification_result: None formal. The argument is qualitative: indicator-based predictions are not transportable when the measurement or acquisition mechanism differs.
papers.experiments: None reported, as far as could be verified (full text not accessed).
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the canonical citation for 'mask-aware models encode the acquisition policy and break when it changes'. It is the motivating claim N1 must go beyond, and it explains why mask-aware versus observed-only baselines must be compared under an explicit acquisition-shift model.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: the qualitative warning that mask-aware (indicator) models depend on a stable acquisition mechanism. Does NOT cover any formal condition, bound, evaluation protocol or experiment.

papers.title: Missing data should be handled differently for prediction than for description or causal explanation
papers.authors: Matthew Sperrin, Glen P. Martin, Rose Sisk, Niels Peek
papers.verification: Fetched the full abstract via the Europe PMC REST API and the Manchester research portal. Volume and pages confirmed via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.03.028).
papers.method: Methodological commentary arguing that, for prediction with routinely collected data, methods that use information in the missingness pattern should be explored. The inference-oriented MAR and MI canon does not directly apply.
papers.shift_assumptions: The paper highlights that 'the missing data method used in model development may not match the method used when a model is deployed', which can give over-optimistic performance assessments. It also notes that deployment of the model itself can change data collection, as cited by Rockenschaub et al.
papers.source_access: Not applicable (commentary).
papers.target_access: Not applicable (commentary).
papers.identification_result: None formal. Its recommendation: where missing-data methods differ between development and deployment, the implications must be explicitly evaluated. The trade-off between a causally principled model and one that maximises available information depends on intended use.
papers.experiments: None.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the origin of the 'evaluate as deployed' principle and the explicit flag that development-time evaluation can be over-optimistic when deployment handling or missingness differs. That is N1's claim in the clinical literature, stated without formal conditions.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: the problem statement that development-time evaluation may not reflect deployment performance under different missingness handling or mechanisms. Does NOT cover: formal identification, a dropout proxy, sensitivity, or model selection.

papers.title: Sharing pattern submodels for prediction with missing values
papers.authors: Lena Stempfle, Ashkan Panahi, Fredrik D. Johansson
papers.verification: Fetched the full-text PDF from arXiv and read the abstract, Sec. 4 (linear-Gaussian DGP, Condition 1), the experiments and related work.
papers.method: Sharing pattern submodels (SPSM): one submodel per missingness pattern, with parameters shared across patterns through sparsity-inducing regularisation (proved consistent). It builds on the pattern submodels of Mercaldo & Blume, Biostatistics 21(2):236-252, 2020, which are fit per pattern using only that pattern's data.
papers.shift_assumptions: Train and test have the same (X, M, Y) distribution, with missingness present at both train and test time. It allows MNAR: the DGP Y = θᵀX + α_M + ε, where M may depend arbitrarily on X and pattern-specific intercepts capture the dependence of Y on M. It gives conditions for sharing to be optimal even when missingness and outcome depend on unobserved variables.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y).
papers.target_access: Test (X_obs, M, Y), i.i.d. with training; labels used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: Bayes-optimal pattern model E[Y|X_obs, M=m] = θ_obsᵀ X_obs + ξ_m, where ξ_m is the bias of zero imputation. It characterises when optimal submodels share coefficients. Our inference (NOT a claim made in the paper): because pattern submodels condition on M=m, they remain optimal under shifts of the pattern marginal P(M) as long as P(Y|X_obs, M=m) is invariant per pattern. They are not robust if the meaning of a pattern changes.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data; ADNI (natural missingness); SUPPORT (natural missingness, with MNAR artificially induced by adding 25 units to the outcome for subjects missing arterial pO2, following Mercaldo & Blume). i.i.d. train/test; no deployment shift.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Pattern submodels are the natural 'mask-aware' baseline for N1. They make the invariance assumption explicit per pattern: P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m) = P_S(Y|x_obs, M=m). That is exactly the quantity N1's sensitivity analysis would perturb. Note that a fully observed source has no data for non-complete patterns, so pattern submodels cannot be fit there without artificial dropout.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: a strong mask-aware baseline that is consistent under MNAR in i.i.d. settings. Does NOT cover: acquisition shift, a fully observed source, dropout evaluation, selection under shift, or sensitivity analysis.

papers.title: What's a good imputation to predict with missing values?
papers.authors: Marine Le Morvan, Julie Josse, Erwan Scornet, Gaël Varoquaux
papers.venue_year: NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv 2106.00311). Companion paper: 'NeuMiss networks: differentiable programming for supervised learning with missing values', Le Morvan, Josse, Moreau, Scornet, Varoquaux, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv 2007.01627).
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page and the full-text PDF (confirmed the i.i.d. (X,M,Y) setup and the MCAR / Gaussian self-masking experiments). The NeuMiss 2020 abstract was fetched from arXiv 2007.01627.
papers.method: Theory showing that impute-then-regress with a sufficiently powerful learner is Bayes-optimal for almost all imputation functions. Learning imputation and regression jointly is better in finite samples (NeuMiss+). NeuMiss (2020) derives the optimal predictor under MAR and Gaussian self-masking and builds a network with mask-driven nonlinearities.
papers.shift_assumptions: The dataset is i.i.d. realisations of (X, M, Y). Results hold for any mechanism, including MNAR, but train and test share the mechanism. Experiments use MCAR and Gaussian self-masking (MNAR).
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y).
papers.target_access: Test (X_obs, M, Y) from the same distribution, used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: The Bayes predictor E[Y|X_obs, M] is reachable by impute-then-regress for almost all imputations, and perfect conditional imputation is unnecessary asymptotically. Under MNAR, adding the mask to mean or MICE imputation is critical. No shift results.
papers.experiments: Simulated data with synthetic MCAR and self-masking masks. Target labels used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This supplies the imputation and NeuMiss baselines N1 must include. It also explains why many handling methods look equivalent in-distribution: they all target the same Bayes predictor. Differences in ranking under acquisition shift therefore come from HOW each method factorises E[Y|X_obs,M], which Rockenschaub et al. later exploited.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: in-distribution optimality of impute-then-regress and of mask-aware learners. Does NOT cover: any train/test mechanism change, dropout proxies, or selection under shift.

papers.title: Biases in electronic health record data due to processes within the healthcare system: retrospective observational study
papers.authors: Denis Agniel, Isaac S. Kohane, Griffin M. Weber
papers.verification: Fetched the full abstract (structured) via PMC and Europe PMC.
papers.method: A retrospective observational analysis comparing, for 272 lab-test types, the predictive accuracy for 3-year survival of healthcare-process features (whether a test was ordered, time of day, day of week, ordering frequency) against the test result values.
papers.shift_assumptions: No shift is modelled. The data come from one year (2005-2006) at two Boston hospitals. The paper documents that acquisition (ordering) is itself outcome-informative.
papers.source_access: EHR records with process features and results for 669,452 patients, and survival labels.
papers.target_access: Not applicable (no transfer analysis).
papers.identification_result: None formal. The presence of a lab order, irrespective of its result, was significantly associated with survival odds for 233 of 272 tests (86%). Ordering-timing features predicted survival better than the result values for 118 of 174 tests (68%).
papers.experiments: Real EHR data with natural acquisition. Labels (3-year survival) used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is large-scale empirical evidence that, in real clinical data, acquisition M is strongly outcome-informative (NIMO fails). It also means a complete-case or fully-acquired cohort (population selection S) is outcome-selected. Artificial random dropout on such a cohort therefore discards exactly the signal that natural acquisition carries.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: empirical motivation that selective acquisition is informative in EHRs. Does NOT cover: transfer, ranking, identification, or methods. Its implication for policy change across sites or time is an inference, not something tested in the paper.

papers.title: The Missing Indicator Method: From Low to High Dimensions
papers.authors: Mike Van Ness, Tomas M. Bosschieter, Roberto Halpin-Gregorio, Madeleine Udell
papers.verification: Fetched the full-text PDF from arXiv (abstract, theory on MCAR and self-masking, experiments). Pages confirmed via Crossref.
papers.method: Theoretical and empirical study of the missing indicator method (MIM). MIM does not hurt linear models asymptotically under uninformative (MCAR) missingness, helps under informative missingness (self-masking analysis), and can overfit in high dimensions. The paper proposes Selective MIM (SMIM), which adds indicators only for features with informative missingness.
papers.shift_assumptions: The train/test missingness mechanism is the same (i.i.d.). The analysis covers MCAR and self-masking MNAR, and the paper notes that testing MAR versus MNAR is impossible.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y).
papers.target_access: Test (X_obs, M, Y) from the same distribution, used for evaluation.
papers.identification_result: Under MCAR with uninformative R, the indicators' optimal coefficients are zero asymptotically in linear models. Under independent self-masking, the indicator coefficients are nonzero in a characterised form. No shift results.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data with synthetic self-masking masks; OpenML datasets with synthetic masks; MIMIC-III clinical tasks with NATURAL missingness. All i.i.d.; target labels used.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This gives the mask-aware (indicator) baseline and SMIM, a selective-indicator variant N1 could compare. Its MIMIC-III results show indicators help under natural EHR acquisition in-distribution, which is precisely the gain that van Smeden et al. and Groenwold warn may not transport.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: in-distribution value and risks of indicators, including natural-missingness EHR evidence. Does NOT cover: acquisition shift, dropout proxies, ranking stability, or sensitivity analysis.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
These 12 papers come from two literatures. They agree on the phenomenon and disagree only on emphasis.

(1) Clinical prediction-model (CPM) methodology: Sperrin 2020, van Smeden 2020, Groenwold 2020, Sisk 2023 (SMMR), Tsvetanova 2025, plus the empirical EHR paper Agniel 2018.
- In routine data, acquisition is informative. Agniel: the presence of a lab order predicts 3-year survival for 86% of 272 tests. Exploiting it (indicators, missing categories, zero or mean imputation with flexible learners, pattern submodels) improves in-distribution performance.
- That gain silently assumes a stable acquisition mechanism (van Smeden 2020; Sisk JAMIA 2021).
- When the mechanism changes, rankings of handling strategies can reverse. Causes include clinicians learning the model ('curse of knowing'), guideline or cost changes, and deployment requiring complete data.
- Groenwold 2020 is effectively a published minimal example: zero or mean imputation is best under the development mechanism (c about 0.70 vs 0.62) and worst under random deployment missingness (about 0.54 vs 0.66).
- Sisk 2023: missing indicators help or hurt depending on whether deployment data are complete, with MNAR-Y as the dangerous case.
- Tsvetanova 2025 crosses development and validation mechanisms. It defines 'validation bias' and finds that it is driven by how VALIDATION handles missingness, not how development did.
- The field's prescription: choose the deployment regime first, then validate exactly as you will deploy. Use MI-with-Y for complete-data deployment; use the same imputation at every stage when missingness is allowed. Revalidate regularly.
- In every one of these papers the validation or target set has outcome labels. The problem there is choosing an evaluation protocol, not identification, so non-identifiability claims do not apply.

(2) Learning theory for prediction with missing values: Josse et al. 2024, Le Morvan 2020/2021, Van Ness 2023, Mercaldo & Blume 2020, Stempfle 2023, Catoire 2026.
- The target is E[Y|X_obs, M]. Many strategies (impute-then-regress with a strong learner, MIA trees, NeuMiss, pattern submodels, MIM) reach it under ANY mechanism, including MNAR.
- They all assume i.i.d. (X, M, Y) between train and test. Josse's Remark 1 flags policy-driven measurement change as an out-of-scope distribution shift.

Three results bridge to N1 and together already state the 'when is artificial masking enough' identification condition:
- Josse Theorem 2: a complete-data Bayes predictor plus test-time conditional multiple imputation is target-optimal under MAR-Y (Y independent of M given X_obs(M)).
- Catoire 2026: under NIMO, the observation-ignoring and observation-conditional targets coincide; under NICO, complete-case status is uninformative given X.
- Rockenschaub 2024 (restating Zhou, Balakrishnan & Lipton 2023): with p(X,Y) fixed, pattern-wise Bayes predictors are invariant under ignorable missingness shift. They also state that source performance may no longer be a valid selection criterion, and they observe empirical ranking changes (MICE worse in source but more robust).

Additional verified pointers, not in the list:
- Hoogland et al., Stat Med 39:3591-3607 (2020): validation should use missing-data methods that transfer to a single new patient.
- Sisk et al., JAMIA 28:155-166 (2021): review of informative presence, noting it may not generalise across settings.
- Nestor et al., MLHC 2019: natural EHR shift at the 2008 MIMIC record-keeping change; aggregating to clinical concepts improved robustness.
- Jeanselme et al., DeepJoint, NeurIPS 2022 TS4H workshop: 'clinical presence shift', weekday vs weekend admissions in MIMIC-III.
- Lin, Groenwold et al., Ann Intern Med 178:1451-1463 (2025): EHR missingness recommendations for validation and implementation.
- Stempfle et al., ICML 2025: models that learn to avoid missing features at test time.
- Zhou et al. 2023, 'Domain adaptation under missingness shift', belongs to the adjacent domain-adaptation cluster.

Novelty verdict: the identification half of N1 ('artificial dropout on complete data predicts the target iff p(X,Y) is shared, the target satisfies MAR-Y/NIMO, and the dropout mask distribution is matched or reweighted to P_T(M|X_obs)') is largely implied by Josse Theorem 2, Catoire (NIMO/NICO) and Zhou/Rockenschaub Theorem 1. It should not be presented as new. The phenomenon of ranking reversal under acquisition change is also documented, in simulation (Groenwold 2020; Rockenschaub 2024; Tsvetanova 2025).
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
1. No paper evaluates the protocol at the centre of N1: ARTIFICIAL random or designed dropout applied to a FULLY-OBSERVED cohort, used as a proxy for risk on a NATURALLY-missing deployment population. The closest works study the reverse direction: an incomplete source moving to a complete or less-missing target (Rockenschaub Sec. 4.2 and 7.2; Sisk and Tsvetanova 'complete data at deployment'). Josse Theorem 2 covers source complete to target MAR-Y, but only for the Bayes predictor, not for evaluating given models.

2. No paper separates population selection S (who ends up fully observed or in the cohort) from the per-unit observation mask M. Complete-case analysis is treated as a handling method, not as selection of the evaluation population. Catoire's NICO is the nearest formal condition but is never linked to dropout evaluation. Agniel's evidence implies that fully-acquired cohorts are outcome-selected, but nobody quantifies what that does to dropout-based rankings.

3. All formal results concern Bayes predictors, i.e. invariance of E[Y|X_obs,M]. None addresses the RISK DIFFERENCE or RANKING of two fixed, imperfect models under acquisition shift, or model selection in finite samples.

4. None provides sensitivity analysis or partial identification. Examples would be odds-ratio or marginal-sensitivity-style bounds on P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m) relative to the source, or a tipping-point analysis for when a ranking flips. The clinical literature stops at 'evaluate as deployed' and 'revalidate regularly'. Rockenschaub leaves non-ignorable shift unresolved, saying only that 'explicit specification of the missingness mechanism' may help.

5. No uncertainty quantification for between-model risk differences under shift. Tsvetanova reports bootstrap summaries of performance only; Rockenschaub reports 10 reruns.

6. Label-access regimes are never contrasted. Every clinical paper has labelled validation or target data, which makes the question moot there. None addresses selection when target labels are unavailable or delayed, or a prospective acquisition-policy change.

7. The settings are univariate or feature-level and mostly use synthetic masks: Groenwold, Sisk, Tsvetanova and Catoire use one missing predictor, Rockenschaub uses synthetic masks on synthetic or semi-synthetic data, and Van Ness uses OpenML with synthetic masks.
   - Natural-missingness evaluations are i.i.d. and involve no acquisition-policy shift: MIMIC-III (Van Ness), NCORR (Tsvetanova), Bordeaux ED (Catoire), ADNI and SUPPORT (Stempfle).
   - Natural shifts appear only in Nestor 2019 and DeepJoint 2022, with no identification analysis.
   - Modality-level block acquisition (imaging, genomics, notes) and multimodal deep models are absent.

8. No paper tests whether an observed ranking reversal is explained by simple sample selection or class-balance or prevalence differences before attributing it to the missingness mechanism. No paper distinguishes 'record absent' (linkage or documentation) from 'test not performed'.

9. Consequently, N1's defensible novelty is narrow. It lies in:
   - acquisition-aware selection between two models with explicit S-vs-M assumptions;
   - sensitivity bounds and uncertainty on the target risk difference under non-ignorable (Y-dependent) acquisition;
   - validation on real multimodal data with natural, selectively acquired modalities and a fixed eligible population.

   Plain importance weighting, or reweighting the dropout mask to P_T(M|X_obs), is already implied (Zhou et al. 2023; Rockenschaub Appendix A.5 shows Zhou's method reduces to inverse-probability weighting) and would not by itself constitute a contribution.

sweeps.cluster: Model selection / performance estimation on an unlabeled (or few-label) target, and partial identification / sensitivity analysis of predictive performance (incl. DRO-style evaluation under acquisition / missingness shift)

papers.title: Predictive Performance Comparison of Decision Policies Under Confounding
papers.authors: Luke Guerdan, Amanda Coston, Kenneth Holstein, Zhiwei Steven Wu
papers.venue_year: ICML 2024 (PMLR 235:16673-16705); workshop precursor 'Policy Comparison Under Unmeasured Confounding' (NeurIPS 2023 workshop)
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract and arXiv HTML full text (read through a summarizer); PMLR page and page range taken from a search snippet (proceedings.mlr.press/v235/guerdan24a.html)
papers.method: 'delta-regret intervals': partial-identification bounds on the DIFFERENCE in predictive performance (TPR/FPR, PPV/NPV, expected cost/utility) between a confounded status-quo policy pi0(X,U) and a proposed policy pi(X). Performance is split into v-statistic terms. Terms on the region where the two policies agree cancel, so the joint regret interval is provably tighter (Thm 4.3) than subtracting separately computed bounds. It plugs in bounding functions for E[Y(1)|D=0,X] from several identification strategies. Estimation uses cross-fitted plug-in and doubly robust estimators, with bootstrap CIs.
papers.identification_result: The regret (risk difference) is only partially identified. Its sharpness depends on the pointwise bounding function chosen: Manski no-assumption bounds, the MSM (odds ratio of selection bounded by Lambda), a Rosenbaum Gamma model, an IV, or proximal variables. Improvement over the 'baseline' interval (difference of per-policy bounds) grows with the probability mass of the agreement region.
papers.shift_assumptions: No domain shift: one population. The missing piece is the OUTCOME/label for units the status quo did not select (selective labels), so missingness is on labels and confounded by U. The sensitivity model bounds how much the unobserved outcome regression for D=0 can differ from the regression for D=1.
papers.source_access: X for all units, historical decision D, outcome Y only when D=1 (plus an instrument or proxies when those strategies are used).
papers.target_access: Same population. The proposed policy's decisions are computable for everyone; the outcomes of non-selected units are never observed.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data generated under MSM/IV (checks coverage), plus a semi-synthetic healthcare-enrollment comparison based on a synthetic version of the Obermeyer et al. (2019) data (~48k records): physician+algorithm vs algorithm-only on NPV and expected cost across subgroups. Ground truth comes from the simulation, not real target labels.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Closest methodological precedent for 'acquisition-aware model selection'. It DOES bound a risk difference between two predictors jointly, with a sensitivity parameter and CIs. It does NOT handle missing FEATURES/modalities: its missingness is on labels/potential outcomes, and it has no source-to-target domain structure or S/M distinction.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Heavy. (i) Bounding R(f1)-R(f2) directly rather than differencing per-model bounds. (ii) Cancellation where the models agree. (iii) An MSM/odds-ratio sensitivity parameter. (iv) DR estimation with bootstrap uncertainty. A generic 'risk-difference interval under an MSM' is therefore NOT new. N1 can only claim novelty in how feature-acquisition shift maps onto the bounding function: a sensitivity model on P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m) relative to a nominal built from the fully observed source, with S separated from M, and a breakdown value for the ranking.

papers.title: Evaluating Model Robustness and Stability to Dataset Shift
papers.authors: Adarsh Subbaswamy, Roy Adams, Suchi Saria
papers.verification: Fetched the full PDF from PMLR and extracted the text locally. Read the methods (Eq. 1-5), the sepsis experiment, the Hospital B validation and the model-comparison use case. Also arXiv 2010.15100 abstract.
papers.method: DRO-style evaluation of worst-case risk under a user-specified shift in a CONDITIONAL distribution P(W|Z), with the 'immutable' variables Z held fixed. The worst-case risk is the expected loss on the worst (1-alpha) subsample under the constraint E[h(W,Z)|Z]=1-alpha, which gives a CVaR form of E[loss|W,Z]. Estimation uses a cross-fitted debiased root-N estimator with asymptotic normality and 95% CIs.
papers.identification_result: The worst-case risk over the specified reweighting set is point-identified and root-N estimable from ONE labeled evaluation set. The uncertainty set is support-restricted: it can only reweight test-ordering patterns that already occur in the evaluation data.
papers.shift_assumptions: Explicitly models a shift in clinician LAB-TEST ORDERING, P(test order | demographics, disease status), while holding P(demographics, disease status) fixed. This separates practice/acquisition shift (the M-mechanism) from population shift (S). The shift magnitude is the subsample fraction alpha, not an odds-ratio parameter.
papers.source_access: Labeled evaluation data (X including lab tests present only when ordered, test-order indicators, Y).
papers.target_access: No target data needed for the analysis. For validation they used a second hospital with labels (Hospital B: ordering rate 23% vs 11% at Hospital A, similar demographics and prevalence).
papers.experiments: Real EHR sepsis diagnosis: Hospital A, 278,947 ED encounters, 2.1% prevalence, 17 vital/lab/demographic features, held-out n=10,000. The test-ordering missingness is NATURAL. Target labels were used to validate: observed accuracy at Hospital B fell inside the CI of the estimated worst case. They compared a 'classical' RF with a 'robust' (surgery-estimator) RF and with qSOFA.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The most directly relevant evaluation paper for selective modality acquisition. It evaluates and COMPARES two models under shifts in test ordering (feature acquisition), holds the population fixed, uses natural missingness and checks against a real second site. It does NOT give a joint bound on a risk difference: each model is scored on its OWN worst-case subsample. It also needs a labeled evaluation set that already contains natural ordering variation, rather than a fully observed source with artificial dropout. It is an existing 'acquisition-shift DRO evaluation' baseline for N1.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers: formalising an acquisition-policy shift as a shift in P(M | population variables, Y) with the population fixed (the S vs M separation in spirit), worst-case evaluation with CIs, and comparing two models' stability to ordering changes. Not covered: a common adversary for a two-model risk difference, an odds-ratio-type sensitivity parameter on P_T(Y|x_obs,M), transport from a complete-case source to a naturally-missing target, and any account of when MCAR dropout evaluation predicts the ranking.

papers.title: Robust Design and Evaluation of Predictive Algorithms under Unobserved Confounding (earlier title: Counterfactual Risk Assessments under Unmeasured Confounding)
papers.authors: Ashesh Rambachan, Amanda Coston, Edward H. Kennedy
papers.venue_year: arXiv 2212.09844, 2022; v6 Nov 2025 (econ.EM). No published venue listed on arXiv.
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract page and arXiv HTML full text (read through a summarizer)
papers.method: Mean-outcome sensitivity model. The confounding function delta(x)=P(Y*=1|D=0,x)-P(Y*=1|D=1,x) is bounded; for example, the unobserved rate is bracketed by multiplicative factors of the observed rate mu1(x). Proxy outcomes and IVs are alternative bounding strategies. Sharp bounds are derived on performance estimands (conditional likelihood, MSE, TPR/FPR, positive-class performance). Estimation uses debiased/DML estimators that are root-n and jointly asymptotically normal, with CIs for the identified set.
papers.identification_result: Performance of a SINGLE fixed algorithm is partially identified, and the identified set is sharp given the bounding assumptions. The authors do not develop a direct two-model comparison; differencing the two identified sets gives the looser 'baseline' interval that Guerdan et al. improve on.
papers.shift_assumptions: Selective labels, with selection D possibly confounded by unobservables. There is no feature missingness and no separate target domain.
papers.source_access: X for all units, D, Y only when D=1.
papers.target_access: Same population; the outcomes of unselected units are never observed.
papers.experiments: Real consumer-lending data from an Australian bank (Commonwealth Bank of Australia). Selective labels are NATURAL. They build confounding-robust credit scores and audit performance and disparities across income groups; there are no ground-truth labels for unselected applicants.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Supplies the sensitivity-model template (a bounded outcome-regression gap between observed and unobserved regimes) and the DML inference machinery that N1's bounds on P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m) would reuse. It bounds single-model performance, not a risk difference, and it concerns missing labels, not missing features.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the 'assumption + sensitivity + uncertainty' part for single-model performance under selective observation. It does not cover two-model ranking, missing modalities, domain transport, or S vs M.

papers.title: Confounding-Robust Policy Improvement
papers.authors: Nathan Kallus, Angela Zhou
papers.verification: Fetched NeurIPS abstract page. The uncertainty set being Tan's (2006) marginal sensitivity model with propensity-odds-ratio Gamma is from knowledge of the paper and consistent with the abstract ('uncertainty set around nominal propensity weights'); the full text was not re-read.
papers.method: Minimises the worst-case REGRET of a candidate policy against a baseline/status-quo policy over an uncertainty set of inverse-propensity weights. The adversarial subproblem is solved efficiently, and the paper gives generalisation guarantees.
papers.identification_result: If the uncertainty set is well specified, the robust policy is guaranteed to do no worse than the baseline and improves only where the data support it. The object bounded is the value DIFFERENCE between two policies, taken over a shared adversary.
papers.shift_assumptions: Unobserved confounding of treatment assignment, bounded by an MSM-type odds-ratio set. No feature missingness and no domain shift.
papers.source_access: Observational (X, T, Y(T)).
papers.target_access: Same population; counterfactual outcomes are unobserved.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data and a large clinical trial (per the abstract). Details were not re-verified.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Canonical example of bounding a DIFFERENCE (regret vs a baseline) under an MSM with a common adversary. A 'deploy model 2 only if its worst-case regret vs model 1 is < 0' rule is essentially this idea applied to model selection. It concerns treatment/label missingness, not missing features.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the decision rule 'select the challenger only if the worst-case risk difference under Gamma favours it' and the use of a shared adversary. N1's contribution cannot be that decision rule itself.

papers.title: Learning from a Biased Sample
papers.authors: Roshni Sahoo, Lihua Lei, Stefan Wager
papers.venue_year: arXiv 2209.01754 (2022-2026); listed as Management Science (forthcoming); EAAMO 2023 version exists
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract page and arXiv HTML v4 (read through a summarizer)
papers.method: Conditional Gamma-biased sampling: P[S=1|X=x,Y=y]/P[S=1|X=x] is in [1/Gamma, Gamma]. For a fixed model the worst-case target risk has a CVaR-type closed form. Rockafellar-Uryasev (RU) regression turns the DRO problem into augmented convex risk minimisation, fitted by sieves or deep nets.
papers.identification_result: Target risk is partially identified. The sharp worst case over all target distributions compatible with the biased sample and Gamma is CVaR-like and computable. With Gamma=1 it reduces to covariate-shift reweighting.
papers.shift_assumptions: POPULATION SELECTION S: sample inclusion can depend arbitrarily on X and, within the factor Gamma, on Y or unobservables. There is no feature missingness.
papers.source_access: Labeled biased sample (X,Y) of selected units.
papers.target_access: Optionally the target covariate marginal Q_X; no target labels.
papers.experiments: MIMIC-III ICU length of stay with SYNTHETIC selection by resampling, and a NATURAL survey-nonresponse shift: Household Pulse Survey (~5% response) to BRFSS (44% response), PHQ-4 mental health. Target labels were used to evaluate target risk.
