papers.relevance_to_N1: The right tool for the S part of N1: the complete-case or fully-observed cohort is itself a selected sample of the eligible population. It gives worst-case risk for a single model under a Gamma selection model. It does not give a joint two-model difference and does not treat masks M.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers sensitivity analysis of target risk under population selection with an odds-ratio-type parameter. Not covered: the mask mechanism M, modality dropout, or a two-model risk difference. Combining a Gamma_S for selection with a separate Lambda_M for acquisition is not present.

papers.title: Beyond the Training Distribution: Evaluating Predictions Under Distribution Shift and Selection Bias
papers.authors: Annie Ulichney, Amanda Coston
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract page and arXiv HTML (read through a summarizer)
papers.method: Double machine learning / influence-function (bias-corrected) estimator of the target risk psi=E_T[l(f(X),Y)] of a fixed black-box model. It combines covariate-shift density ratios with selective-label propensities, and gives Wald CIs.
papers.identification_result: Target risk is POINT-identified under: selection on observables (Y independent of D given X in source), covariate shift P_S(Y|X)=P_T(Y|X), positivity, and a bounded likelihood ratio. There are no bounds; violations are handled only by stress-test simulations.
papers.shift_assumptions: Covariate shift plus MAR selective labels. Missingness is on labels, not features.
papers.source_access: X for all source units, D, and Y only if D=1.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target X only.
papers.experiments: eICU: hospital 208 as source, hospitals 443/199/283 as targets. Semi-synthetic runs use an oracle outcome model for ground truth. In real runs, labels exist only when clinicians ordered the relevant lab, so there is no target ground truth. Baselines: CS-only (Morrison et al. 2024) and SL-only (Coston et al. 2020). Stress tests covered confounding, outcome shift, positivity and likelihood-ratio instability.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The nearest recent 'target-risk estimation from labeled source + unlabeled target with selection' method. It is a natural point-identified (MAR) baseline for N1's performance estimator. It does not bound a risk difference and does not handle missing features or modalities: lab ordering determines LABEL availability, not input availability.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers point estimation plus CI of target risk under covariate shift combined with selection, using DR/DML. Not covered: sensitivity bounds, two-model comparison, and feature-level acquisition masks.

papers.title: Nonparametric Analysis of Randomized Experiments with Missing Covariate and Outcome Data
papers.authors: Joel L. Horowitz, Charles F. Manski
papers.venue_year: Journal of the American Statistical Association 95(449):77-84, 2000 (with discussion by T. E. Raghunathan and rejoinder); Univ. of Iowa WP 97-16 (1997)
papers.verification: Fetched the working-paper abstract on EconPapers (RePEc:uia:iowaec:97-16). JASA volume/pages come from a search snippet.
papers.method: Sharp nonparametric (Manski-type) bounds on population parameters, such as conditional outcome distributions and treatment effects, when both COVARIATES and outcomes are partly missing. Additional bounds hold under MCAR covariates.
papers.identification_result: Without distributional assumptions the parameters are not identified but are sharply bounded. The bounds 'exhaust all the information' in the data. Under MCAR covariates the bounds narrow.
papers.shift_assumptions: No assumption on the missing-data mechanism in the main result; MCAR covariates in a secondary result. Single population.
papers.source_access: A single sample with partially missing covariates and outcomes.
papers.target_access: n/a (one population)
papers.experiments: Real hypertension clinical-trial data with NATURAL missingness. The bounds were narrow enough for substantive conclusions.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The classical partial-identification result for missing FEATURES, and the no-assumption end of N1's sensitivity spectrum. It shows that P(Y | full X) is only bounded when covariates are missing without assumptions. It does not concern predictor risk or model ranking, and it has no source/target structure.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers worst-case bounds with missing covariates, the Lambda-infinite limit of any N1 sensitivity model. Not covered: predictive-model risk differences, acquisition modelling, and uncertainty for model selection.

papers.title: Covariate Shift Adaptation by Importance Weighted Cross Validation
papers.authors: Masashi Sugiyama, Matthias Krauledat, Klaus-Robert Mueller
papers.verification: Fetched JMLR abstract page
papers.method: IWCV: cross-validation loss on the source, weighted by the density ratio p_T(x)/p_S(x). It is used for model and hyperparameter selection.
papers.identification_result: Unbiased for target risk under covariate shift (P(Y|X) invariant, overlap). No partial identification.
papers.shift_assumptions: Covariate shift only.
papers.source_access: Labeled source (X,Y).
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target X.
papers.experiments: Toy regression/classification and a real brain-computer-interface task with session non-stationarity.
papers.relevance_to_N1: The 'reweighting' baseline. Applied to (x_obs, M) it is exactly what Zhou et al. (DAMS) reduce missingness shift to when masks are observed. For N1 it fails structurally in two ways. (a) A fully observed source has no units with M=m, so there is no overlap in mask space. (b) After artificial MCAR dropout, overlap exists but P_S(Y|x_obs,M=m)=P_S(Y|x_obs), while informative acquisition makes P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m) differ; this is a conditional shift that weighting cannot fix. It is a single-model point estimate and does not bound a difference.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Plain importance weighting, which by the project rules must not be called new. It is the obvious baseline for 'dropout + reweighting'.

papers.title: Towards Accurate Model Selection in Deep Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (Deep Embedded Validation, DEV)
papers.authors: Kaichao You, Ximei Wang, Mingsheng Long, Michael I. Jordan
papers.verification: Fetched PMLR abstract page. The details (a domain discriminator on adapted features gives density ratios, IW source validation loss, control variate) come from knowledge of the paper and the Musgrave et al. description; the full text was not re-read.
papers.method: Importance-weighted validation risk in the learned feature space, with a control variate for variance reduction.
papers.identification_result: Unbiased target-risk estimate with bounded variance, assuming covariate shift in the embedded feature space.
papers.shift_assumptions: Covariate shift in feature space (P(Y|z) invariant).
papers.source_access: Labeled source.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target. Target labels were used only to score selection in the experiments.
papers.experiments: Standard deep UDA benchmarks (image classification). Shifts are natural domain shifts, not missingness. Target labels were used for evaluation only.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A standard unsupervised model-selection baseline. It inherits IWCV's failure under informative acquisition, because the conditional P(Y|x_obs,M) shifts. It does not bound a risk difference or handle missing modalities.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None beyond being a baseline in the 'same information / budget' comparison.

papers.title: Three New Validators and a Large-Scale Benchmark Ranking for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (v1 title: Benchmarking Validation Methods for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation)
papers.authors: Kevin Musgrave, Serge Belongie, Ser-Nam Lim
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract page and arXiv HTML (read through a summarizer). The companion paper Ericsson, Li, Hospedales 'Better Practices for Domain Adaptation' (AutoML 2023, PMLR 224) was also fetched at https://proceedings.mlr.press/v224/ericsson23a.html
papers.method: Benchmark of unsupervised validators over ~1M checkpoints: source accuracy, reverse validation, entropy, DEV, proxy risk, EMS, SND, and new BNM/ClassAMI/DEVN. Validators are scored by weighted Spearman correlation with true target accuracy.
papers.identification_result: Empirical only. Validator rank correlation with target accuracy is inconsistent. Simple source-validation accuracy was best on average for 6 of 10 UDA algorithms and on Office31/OfficeHome. DEV weights can blow up; DEVN fixes this with max-normalisation.
papers.shift_assumptions: Implicit, validator-specific assumptions; natural image domain shifts.
papers.source_access: Labeled source.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target for the validators. Target labels were used ONLY to score the validators.
papers.experiments: Vision UDA benchmarks (Office31, OfficeHome and others). No feature/modality missingness. Ericsson et al. similarly show that using target test labels for HPO inflates reported DA gains.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Protocol template for step 6: compare selectors under equal information, with target labels held out only for scoring, and measure ranking fidelity by (weighted) rank correlation. It is also direct evidence that unlabeled validators often fail to beat 'source accuracy', which is the analogue of 'complete-data or artificial-dropout accuracy' in N1. It neither bounds a risk difference nor covers missingness.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the empirical-evaluation methodology for selectors (rank correlation with the true target ranking). N1's 'does artificial dropout ranking predict natural-missingness ranking' is the same kind of question in a new shift class that it does not study.

papers.title: Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift with Black Box Predictors (BBSE)
papers.authors: Zachary C. Lipton, Yu-Xiang Wang, Alexander J. Smola
papers.verification: Fetched PMLR abstract page. The companion classic, Saerens, Latinne, Decaestecker 'Adjusting the outputs of a classifier to new a priori probabilities: a simple procedure' (Neural Computation 14(1):21-41, 2002, https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article/14/1/21/6577), is verified by search snippet only.
papers.method: Estimates target class priors via the black-box confusion matrix (moment matching), then importance-weights by q(y)/p(y). Includes a shift-detection test. Saerens et al. is the EM-based prior re-estimation and posterior adjustment.
papers.identification_result: The target label marginal is identified (consistent, with error bounds) under label shift (p(x|y) invariant) and an invertible confusion matrix. Target risk then follows by reweighting.
papers.shift_assumptions: Label shift only.
papers.source_access: Labeled source.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target inputs.
papers.experiments: MNIST/CIFAR-10 with SYNTHETIC label shift. Target labels were used for evaluation.
papers.relevance_to_N1: Implements the 'class-balance adjustment' check in step 8. If the ranking change between the complete-case cohort and the deployment population is explained by prevalence change alone, BBSE/Saerens-reweighted source risk should reproduce the target ranking. Under informative acquisition p(x_obs, m | y) itself shifts, so label shift is violated. Single-model point estimate; no difference bound; no missing features.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None for the candidate method. It is a required null-explanation baseline alongside S-reweighting.

papers.title: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Predict Out-of-Distribution Performance (ATC)
papers.authors: Saurabh Garg, Sivaraman Balakrishnan, Zachary C. Lipton, Behnam Neyshabur, Hanie Sedghi
papers.verification: Fetched arXiv abstract page. Related empirical work: Miller et al., 'Accuracy on the Line', ICML 2021 (https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/miller21b.html), verified by search snippet only.
papers.method: Average Thresholded Confidence: learn a confidence threshold on the source, then predict target accuracy as the fraction of unlabeled target points above the threshold.
papers.identification_result: The paper proves that identifying target accuracy from labeled source plus unlabeled target is as hard as identifying the optimal target predictor. Any estimator therefore relies on (implicit) assumptions about the shift. ATC's empirical accuracy is 2-4x better than prior methods.
papers.shift_assumptions: Implicit calibration/threshold-transfer assumption; no explicit shift class.
papers.source_access: Labeled source validation data.
papers.target_access: Unlabeled target.
papers.experiments: WILDS, ImageNet, BREEDS, CIFAR, MNIST, with synthetic corruptions and natural shifts. Target labels were used for evaluation only.
papers.relevance_to_N1: (a) A label-free performance-estimation baseline for step 6. (b) Its non-identifiability result is the generic version of N1's minimal counterexample: from source (X full, Y) plus target (x_obs, M), target risk, and hence ranking, is not identified without an assumption on P_T(Y|x_obs,M). It applies only when target labels are withheld at selection time. It does not bound differences or treat missing features.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Covers the generic claim that 'target performance is non-identified without shift assumptions'. N1 must go further, to the specific acquisition structure and the ranking (sign of the risk difference), not just risk levels.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
This cluster splits into three families. Most details below come from fetched primary pages; any exceptions are noted.

(A) Label-free target-performance estimation and model selection
- Papers: IWCV (Sugiyama 2007), DEV (You 2019), BBSE (Lipton 2018) with Saerens-EM (2002; snippet-verified only), ATC (Garg 2022), accuracy-on-the-line (Miller 2021; snippet only), and the validator benchmarks of Musgrave et al. 2022 and Ericsson et al. (AutoML 2023, PMLR 224).
- Each gives a POINT estimate of ONE model's target risk under an invariance assumption: covariate shift, label shift, or an implicit calibration transfer.
- ATC proves that target accuracy is not identified without such an assumption.
- Musgrave finds that unlabeled validators often do not beat plain source-validation accuracy.
- None bounds a two-model risk difference or treats missing features.
- Mapped to N1:
  - IWCV/DEV on (x_obs, M) are the 'dropout + reweighting' baseline. Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton (AISTATS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02093; snippet-verified) show that missingness shift with observed masks reduces to covariate shift.
  - That reduction fails exactly in N1's case. A complete source has no overlap in mask space. After artificial MCAR dropout, P_S(Y|x_obs,M=m)=P_S(Y|x_obs), whereas informative acquisition changes P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m). This is a conditional shift that weighting cannot correct.
  - BBSE/Saerens provide the 'class-balance explains it' null check required in step 8.

(B) Partial identification and sensitivity analysis of predictive performance under selective observation
- Rambachan-Coston-Kennedy (single-model sharp bounds, mean-outcome sensitivity model, DML CIs).
- Coston-Rambachan-Chouldechova, ICML 2021 (https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/coston21a.html; abstract fetched): Rashomon set under MAR selective labels. That it computes the disparity range by reduction to weighted classification is from memory, not re-verified.
- Kallus-Zhou 2018: minimax regret vs a baseline under an MSM (Tan 2006, JASA 101:1619-1637; snippet only).
- Dorn and Guo, JASA 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04543; fetched): sharp MSM bounds via quantile balancing; the Zhao-Small-Bhattacharya bounds are too wide.
- Sahoo-Lei-Wager: a Gamma model for sample SELECTION with CVaR worst-case risk.
- Guerdan et al., ICML 2024: joint 'delta-regret' intervals for the performance DIFFERENCE between two policies under MSM/IV/proximal assumptions, with DR estimation and bootstrap CIs. They are provably tighter than differencing per-model bounds because the agreement region cancels.
- Also relevant:
  - Kallus-Zhou NeurIPS 2019 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01552; fetched): partially identified ROC under monotone treatment response.
  - Liu-Molinari-Velez 2026 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14977; fetched): sharp bounds and DML inference for fairness-accuracy frontiers with selective labels.
  - Rotnitzky-Faraggi-Schisterman, JASA 2006 (snippet): doubly robust AUC under verification bias, with a nonignorability sensitivity parameter.
- Consequence for N1: a risk-difference interval under an odds-ratio sensitivity model with uncertainty quantification is ESTABLISHED, by Guerdan et al. and by Kallus-Zhou for policies. However, every paper here puts the missingness on LABELS or potential outcomes (selective labels, verification, confounded treatment). None puts it on input features or modalities, and none has a fully observed source and a naturally masked target.
- Horowitz-Manski 2000 is the only verified partial-identification result for missing COVARIATES. It covers parameters, not predictor risk or rankings.

(C) DRO or robust evaluation under acquisition and missingness shift
- Subbaswamy-Adams-Saria, AISTATS 2021, is the closest evaluation paper. It shifts P(lab-test order | demographics, disease) while holding the population fixed, which is effectively M separated from S. It gives root-n CIs for worst-case risk and compares a classical and a robust sepsis model under natural test ordering. Validation used a second hospital with labels and a different ordering rate (23% vs 11%).
- Its limits:
  - The adversary is support-restricted reweighting of an already naturally-missing, LABELED evaluation set.
  - Models are compared on their respective worst-case subsamples, not through a joint difference bound.
  - There is no transport from a complete source with artificial dropout.
- Related work:
  - Thams-Oberst-Sontag, NeurIPS 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.15947; fetched abstract): parametric robustness sets.
  - Cai-Namkoong-Yadlowsky (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02011; fetched abstract): DISDE decomposition into X-shift vs Y|X-shift. It is a useful tool for step 8, attributing a ranking change to selection vs conditional shift.
  - Chen-Zaharia-Zou, NeurIPS 2022, sparse joint shift (snippet).
  - Rockenschaub et al. 2024 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16484; fetched): the Bayes predictor is invariant under ignorable missingness shift, and method rankings flip across shift types, but only with SYNTHETIC masks and simulated outcomes.
  - Stokes et al. 2025, 'Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00322; snippet): reduces MNAR shift to imputation.
  - Ulichney-Coston 2026: DML target risk under covariate shift plus selective labels on eICU.
  - Catoire-Genuer-Proust-Lima 2026 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17599; fetched abstract): distinguishes P(Y|X_obs,M) from P(Y|X) and missingness at development, validation and deployment.
  - Sisk et al., SMMR 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.12295; fetched): missing indicators can harm when missingness depends on the outcome; simulation only.

NO_GO risk: if N1's method is 'Guerdan-style joint regret interval + MSM + bootstrap' relabelled for modalities, the method contribution is thin. Defensible novelty would have to come from four things:
1. An explicit identification analysis of when artificial MCAR dropout on a complete, S-selected cohort identifies the target ranking.
2. A sensitivity model placed on P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m), anchored to the source nominal, with separate parameters for S (Sahoo-type Gamma_S) and M (Lambda_M).
3. A ranking breakdown value (the smallest Lambda that flips the sign of R_T(f1)-R_T(f2)).
4. An empirical test on NATURAL missingness with held-out target labels.
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
1. No verified paper bounds the TWO-MODEL target risk difference when the shift is in FEATURE/MODALITY acquisition. Guerdan and Kallus-Zhou bound differences but only for label or treatment missingness. RCK and Sahoo-Lei-Wager bound single-model risk. Subbaswamy handles acquisition shift but uses per-model worst cases on a labeled, already-missing evaluation set.
2. No paper models a fully observed source, which is itself selected (S), against a deployment population with natural masks (M) with distinct sensitivity parameters for S and M. Sahoo-Lei-Wager covers S only. Subbaswamy covers M with the population fixed. DAMS and IWCV assume observed masks plus covariate shift, which fails for a complete source because of no mask overlap and a conditional shift in P(Y|x_obs,M).
3. No formal condition was found for when MCAR artificial dropout evaluation predicts the deployment ranking. The natural condition is P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m)=P_S(Y|x_obs) together with reweightable P_T(x_obs,m). No minimal counterexample in which the sign of R_T(f1)-R_T(f2) is non-identified was found, and no ranking breakdown value (the smallest sensitivity parameter that flips the selection) exists in this cluster. ATC's non-identifiability result is generic and concerns risk levels, not rankings.
4. No empirical study compares artificial-masking vs natural-missingness model rankings on real multimodal or clinical data with held-out target labels while first ruling out pure sample-selection or class-balance explanations with BBSE/Saerens, S-reweighting and a DISDE-style decomposition. Rockenschaub 2024 uses synthetic masks and outcomes; the validator benchmarks use vision domain shift.
5. The distinction between record absence and test-not-performed, and the case where target labels are fully public (where non-identifiability claims do not apply and only the empirical ranking-agreement question remains), are not addressed in any of these works.
6. No verified work provides uncertainty for the risk-DIFFERENCE sign under a feature-acquisition sensitivity model combined with a DR/DML estimator. The machinery exists (Guerdan's DR delta-regret, Dorn-Guo sharp MSM, RCK DML) but has not been instantiated for P_T(Y|x_obs,M).

sweeps.cluster: Evaluation of active feature acquisition (AFA) / test-ordering policies from retrospective data with naturally missing features, framed as missing-data or off-policy evaluation, plus the missing-data identification results these evaluations rely on (m-graphs, full-law completeness, no self-censoring, shadow variables, refreshment samples, causal discovery with missing data)

papers.title: Evaluation of Active Feature Acquisition Methods for Time-varying Feature Settings
papers.authors: Henrik von Kleist, Alireza Zamanian, Ilya Shpitser, Narges Ahmidi
papers.venue_year: Journal of Machine Learning Research 26(60):1-84, 2025 (arXiv:2312.01530, v1 Dec 2023, v4 Apr 2025)
papers.verification: Fetched the JMLR abstract page and the arXiv abs page (version history, journal ref). Downloaded the arXiv v4 PDF and read the problem definition, assumptions, Sec. 2.7, Sec. 5 and the experiments section.
papers.method: Defines AFAPE, active feature acquisition performance evaluation: estimating the expected acquisition cost plus misclassification cost of a fixed target acquisition policy pi_alpha and a fixed classifier f_cl from retrospective data logged under the natural policy pi_beta. Three views are covered. (1) Offline RL / dynamic treatment regimes, under NUC. (2) Missing data + online RL, under NDE: J = sum over (X(1),Y) of E[C | X(1),Y] p(X(1),Y); the inner expectation is Monte Carlo simulation of the known policy and classifier on full-data draws, and the outer term is a missing-data problem. (3) The new semi-offline RL view, under NDE+NUC, which gives DM, IPW and DRL (doubly robust) estimators.
papers.identification_result: Missing-data view: J is identified whenever p(X(1),Y) is identified (any identified MNAR m-graph qualifies), given complete-case positivity pi_beta(R=1|X(1))>0. Offline and semi-offline RL views: identified under NUC, meaning acquisitions depend only on recorded features. The semi-offline view needs only the weaker positivity condition that logged data contain supersets of the acquisitions the target policy wants. If NUC fails, the offline and semi-offline targets are not identified. The paper offers no bounds or partial identification; it suggests running several views and estimators together as an informal sensitivity analysis.
papers.shift_assumptions: The same population at development and deployment (no population/selection shift). Only the acquisition policy changes. NDE: acquisitions do not change feature values. NUC for the RL views. The target policy pi_alpha is known, because it is the agent being evaluated. No measurement error, no interference, no non-compliance. Unobserved confounding between U or X and Y is allowed.
papers.source_access: Retrospective data (X_obs, acquisition indicators or actions, Y). Y is ALWAYS observed.
papers.target_access: Nothing is observed from the deployment population. The deployment acquisition policy and the classifier are known functions that can be simulated.
papers.experiments: Synthetic datasets only, with artificially induced missingness (MAR/MNAR, including an NUC violation and an NDE violation). Ground truth comes from running the agent on fully observed data. No natural missingness.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is the closest formal precedent. Sec. 2.7 states that when the feature-acquisition policy differs between hospital 1 and hospital 2 and the hospital-2 policy is known, one can 'treat the acquisition policy at hospital 2 as the AFA policy' and apply their estimators. That is N1's development-to-deployment mask shift. The decomposition J = E_{p(X(1),Y)}[E(C | X(1),Y)] also answers N1's core question in the favourable case. Artificial dropout on a fully observed source estimates deployment risk exactly when three things hold: the dropout distribution equals the deployment acquisition law pi_T(M | X(1), Y); the source full-data law p_S(X(1),Y) equals the target's, i.e. there is no S-selection; and NDE holds. N1's source (fully observed, R=1 everywhere) is the trivially positive special case of their retrospective dataset.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: High. The following is already covered: the target risk of any fixed predictor under a specified deployment acquisition policy is identified and estimated with IPW/DM/DR estimators and positivity conditions. The risk difference J(f1) - J(f2) is a linear contrast of these same functionals, so a DR or bootstrap contrast estimate is not a new method. Not covered: (a) any separation of population selection S from mask M, since they assume one population; (b) a deployment policy that is unknown and must be learned from unlabeled target (X_obs, M); (c) acquisition driven by Y or by unrecorded clinician information in the target, and bounds or sensitivity on the SIGN of the risk difference, i.e. rank stability; (d) validation on natural missingness; (e) modality/block acquisition; (f) record absence versus test not performed. A related precedent they cite, Robins, Orellana and Rotnitzky 2008 (Stat Med 27:4678-4721, known from a search snippet only), transports regimes between health-care systems 'when the systems differ in the frequency and reasons for both laboratory tests and physician visits'.

papers.title: Evaluation of Active Feature Acquisition Methods for Static Feature Settings
papers.authors: Henrik von Kleist, Alireza Zamanian, Ilya Shpitser, Narges Ahmidi
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abs page. Downloaded the full PDF and read Secs. 1-7, Appendix D and the conclusions.
papers.method: Extends AFAPE to static features where the acquisition order is unknown: only the final acquired set R is logged. Missing-data + online RL view: IPW-Miss, which reweights complete cases only, and G-formula/multiple imputation. Semi-offline RL view under the special MAR assumption R ⊥ X(1) | X_o (X_o always observed): the agent's acquisitions are simulated on each logged record, and acquisitions of logged-missing features are 'blocked' and bias-corrected (DM, IPW, DRL). A hybrid missing-data + semi-offline estimator covers MNAR when R ⊥ X(1) | X_adj(1) and X_adj can itself be missing.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1: J is identified if p(X(1),Y) is identified, and they note that a large class of MNAR m-graphs is identified (citing Bhattacharya et al. 2020 and Nabi et al. 2020). This needs the strong positivity pi_beta(R=1 | X(1)=x)>0 for all x. Theorem 3: under special MAR the semi-offline view identifies J with the weaker positivity pi_beta(r ≥ r' | x_o)>0. Theorem 9: the hybrid identification needs missing-data positivity for X_adj plus semi-offline positivity. Appendix D gives a worked m-graph identification of p(R|X(1)) when R3 depends on a sometimes-missing X2. There is no partial identification; sensitivity analysis is deferred to their pattern-graph work (Zamanian, Ahmidi, Drton, Stat Med 2023).
papers.shift_assumptions: Same population. The deployment policy is known. Y does not affect R (they say this is 'easily extended'). No unobserved X(1)-R confounding. Retrospective missingness is MAR, or MNAR with an identified adjustment set.
papers.source_access: Retrospective (X_obs, R, Y) with Y always observed. The acquisition order is not recorded.
papers.target_access: None observed. The known AFA policy and classifier are simulated.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data plus the real Heloc and Income tabular datasets, both fully observed, with SYNTHETICALLY induced MAR and MNAR missingness. Ground truth J is computed by running the policy on the fully observed data. Classifiers are impute-then-regress models (mean imputation + random forest).
papers.relevance_to_N1: It shows that 'artificial masking of fully observed data' is exactly their ground-truth construction, and that the correct dropout distribution is the deployment acquisition law, not uniform dropout. It supplies the positivity language N1 needs: a dropout evaluation says nothing about patterns the deployment policy never produces, and in reverse, target patterns need source support. Its 'blocking' bias is the formal analogue of evaluating on naturally missing records while treating record absence as not-acquired.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: High for estimation machinery: IPW, DM and DR estimators of a fixed classifier's risk under a different acquisition policy, with positivity analysis, are already here, so N1 cannot present reweighting or DR evaluation as novel. It does not cover model comparison or ranking, uncertainty for the difference, sensitivity for outcome-dependent or U-dependent acquisition, population selection, an unlabeled target, or natural-missingness validation.

papers.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts
papers.authors: Patrick Rockenschaub, Zhicong Xian, Alireza Zamanian, Marta Piperno, Octavia-Andreea Ciora, Elisabeth Pachl, Narges Ahmidi
papers.venue_year: arXiv:2406.16484, June 2024, preprint (no journal version found)
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abs page and the arXiv HTML full text. Details come from the fetch tool's summary of the HTML, not a line-by-line read.
papers.method: Studies how predictors behave when the missingness mechanism shifts from p(M|·) at training to q(M|·) at deployment. Compares impute-then-regress (ICE, MICE, MIWAE, autoencoders), pattern/mask-aware models (ICE+mask) and missingness-native networks (NeuMiss, NeuMISE) against oracle Bayes predictors.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1: with p(X,Y)=q(X,Y), the pattern-wise Bayes predictors are invariant across environments in general only if the missingness shift is ignorable, i.e. depends on observed values only. Under non-ignorable shifts, p(X_mis | X_obs, M) changes, so the target Bayes predictor can change and no method recovers it reliably. No identification or estimation of target risk and no sensitivity bounds are given.
papers.shift_assumptions: Pure missingness shift: the complete-data law p(X,Y) is invariant, with no covariate, label or population shift. Mechanisms studied: MCAR, MAR, MNAR self-masking, and outcome-dependent MAR-Y.
papers.source_access: (X_obs, M, Y) under the source mechanism.
papers.target_access: Evaluation data under the shifted mechanism. Because the missingness is simulated on complete data, full ground truth including labels is available to the authors. No target-unlabeled selection protocol.
papers.experiments: Simulated Gaussian data and LBIDD, the real linked birth/infant-death data (~3.9M records, 50 covariates). All missingness is SYNTHETIC (for example 50% in source shifting to 25% or 0% in target).
papers.relevance_to_N1: It is by the same group as AFAPE and explicitly motivates that source validation performance 'may no longer be a good selection criterion' under missingness shift, which is N1's model-selection question. It gives the key structural fact for N1's counterexample: under an ignorable (MAR) shift with invariant p(X,Y), the pattern-wise Bayes predictors transfer. Ranking changes for finite models can then come only from changed pattern weights and changed p(X_obs | M) mixtures, which is a simple reweighting or selection explanation. Genuinely new ranking reversals need a non-ignorable (self-masking or Y-dependent) shift.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: Medium-high on the motivation and on the observed-only vs mask-aware vs imputation baseline comparison, which is essentially N1's item 6 done with synthetic masks. It does not cover target-risk estimation, a risk-difference or ranking criterion, sensitivity analysis, population selection S, unlabeled target data, or natural missingness.

papers.title: Analysis of Missingness Scenarios for Observational Health Data
papers.authors: Alireza Zamanian, Henrik von Kleist, Octavia-Andreea Ciora, Marta Piperno, Gino Lancho, Narges Ahmidi
papers.verification: Fetched the PMC full text; content was extracted through two summarizer prompts with verbatim quotes. The MDPI page returned 403.
papers.method: Lists ten domain-grounded missingness scenarios in EHR data and maps each to m-graph structure, estimand formulation, identification, estimation and sensitivity analysis through a series of 'Inquiries'. The scenarios are: patient non-visit, health-status-driven missed follow-up, events during hospitalisation, refusal, physician 'diagnostic irrelevance', outside-protocol measurements, resource shortage, unrecorded observations, omission by inclusion/exclusion criteria, and invalid-entry omission.
papers.identification_result: Conceptual, with no new theorems. It distinguishes the estimands E_{pi_init}, E_{pi_new} and E_{pi_full}. For prediction it defines the deployment estimand E_{pi_new}[(y - f(x*, r_X; w))^2], the 'MSE loss under new missingness scenarios at deployment'. Inquiry 2 asks whether a scenario undergoes a parametric shift at deployment with an invariant m-graph, for example when a cheaper test changes ordering. Scenario 8 (observed by the clinician but unrecorded) makes latent causes of missingness, which is an NUC violation. Sensitivity uses exponential tilting with an odds-ratio parameter δ = log[O(R|healthy)/O(R|sick)], with ranges elicited from guidelines, protocols and physicians.
papers.shift_assumptions: A scenario-dependent mix of MCAR, MAR and MNAR. The deployment policy pi_new is treated as a parametric shift of the development mechanism.
papers.source_access: Observational EHR data (X_obs, R, Y), in general with missingness.
papers.target_access: Hypothetical deployment policy pi_new; nothing about target data is used.
papers.experiments: Simulation only (synthetic cardiovascular data under three scenario combinations). MIMIC-IV is used only for illustrative examples.
papers.relevance_to_N1: It provides the conceptual vocabulary N1 insists on. Scenario 9 (inclusion/exclusion curation) is exactly the population selection S, distinct from the acquisition mask M. Scenario 8 (unrecorded observations) is 'record absent' as opposed to 'test not performed', and a source of NUC violation. The deployment-loss estimand under a new missingness policy is stated explicitly. Its outcome-dependent acquisition odds ratio δ is essentially the sensitivity parameter N1 proposes for P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) relative to the source.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: High on framing: S vs M, deployment loss under a new acquisition policy, and an OR/tilting sensitivity parameter with expert-elicited ranges. It does not cover formal identification of the risk difference between two predictors, a selection rule, inference or uncertainty, or real natural-missingness validation. N1 must cite it and cannot claim the S/M distinction or OR-tilting sensitivity for deployment loss as conceptual novelty.

papers.title: Full Law Identification in Graphical Models of Missing Data: Completeness Results
papers.authors: Razieh Nabi, Rohit Bhattacharya, Ilya Shpitser
papers.verification: Fetched and read the full PDF: Theorems 1-4, Lemmas 1-3 and the target-law remark.
papers.method: Nonparametric identification theory for missing-data DAGs and ADMGs, using an odds-ratio parameterization of p(R | X(1), O).
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1/2 (sound and complete): the full law p(R, X(1), O) of a missing-data DAG is identified if and only if there is no self-censoring edge X_i(1) → R_i and no colluder X_j(1) → R_i ← R_j, given positivity p(R | X(1), O) > δ > 0. Lemma 1: such models are submodels of the ICIN / no-self-censoring model. Theorems 3/4: with unmeasured confounders (ADMGs), the full law is identified if and only if there are no 'colluding paths' between X_i(1) and R_i. Lemma 3: a single colluding path makes the full law non-identified. The target law p(X(1)) can still be identified when the full law is not.
papers.shift_assumptions: A single population. The missingness mechanism is encoded by a DAG/ADMG, with positivity.
papers.source_access: Generic observed-data law p(X, R, O). Not a transfer setting.
papers.target_access: N/A (single-population identification theory).
papers.experiments: Theory paper with illustrative scenarios; no empirical deployment study.
papers.relevance_to_N1: It gives the sharp graphical boundary for N1's minimal counterexample. When target labels are unavailable, deployment risk depends on p_T(X(1), Y, M). If modality acquisition has a self-censoring edge (the modality value drives its own acquisition) or a colluding path, for example unrecorded clinician information U ↔ X_i together with U → R_i, which is Zamanian scenario 8, then the target full law, and hence the target risk of a mask-aware or imputation model, is not identified from target (X_obs, M). Two target laws with the same observed law can then give opposite rankings. A test cannot causally depend on its own not-yet-measured value, so pure self-censoring is less plausible for ordering decisions. The realistic threat is colluding paths through unrecorded information. If target Y is fully observed, the risk of any deployable predictor f(X_obs, M) is a functional of the observed target law and is identified, so these non-identification results do NOT apply to that case.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on method. It is the identification backbone that N1 should use instead of re-deriving it, together with the 'no self-censoring / no colluders' conditions under which point-identified acquisition-aware comparison is possible and beyond which sensitivity analysis is needed. It does not address comparing predictors, transfer between populations, or a fully observed auxiliary source.

papers.title: Graphical Models for Processing Missing Data
papers.authors: Karthika Mohan, Judea Pearl
papers.venue_year: Journal of the American Statistical Association 116(534):1023-1037, 2021
papers.verification: Fetched and read the full author version (UCLA tech report R-473, marked 'Forthcoming, JASA', Oct 2020): Theorems 1-4, Corollaries 1-2, Example 8. JASA volume and pages come from a search snippet (DOI 10.1080/01621459.2021.1874961).
papers.method: A review and synthesis of m-graphs, recoverability (identification of a query from p(V*, V_o, R)) and testability for MCAR, MAR and MNAR.
papers.identification_result: Theorem 1: a query is recoverable if it has an admissible ordered factorization in which each factor is conditionally independent of the relevant R's. Corollary 2: P(X|Y) is recoverable from complete cases if X ⊥ R | Y. Theorem 2: with no R-R edges, the joint P(V) is recoverable if and only if no X is adjacent to R_X or linked to it by an all-collider path. Theorem 3: P(X|Y) is not recoverable if X is adjacent to R_X or linked by a collider path through Y. Example 8: a self-masked binary I becomes recoverable using a fully observed Y with Y ⊥ R_I | I, by matrix inversion (shadow-variable logic). Theorem 4: claims of the form X ⊥ R_X | Z, W, R_Z are untestable. It notes that external studies can be used, and that Heckman-type corrections or sensitivity analysis are the fall-backs.
papers.shift_assumptions: Single population. Arbitrary m-graphs (MCAR, MAR, MNAR, self-masking) with 'R are not causes' typical.
papers.source_access: Observed-data law p(V*, V_o, R).
papers.target_access: N/A.
papers.experiments: Illustrative examples; no empirical deployment study.
papers.relevance_to_N1: It supplies the tools for N1's step 4 (a minimal counterexample): Theorem 3 gives the minimal non-recoverable structure (modality → own mask), and Theorem 4 explains why the key acquisition assumptions cannot be tested from target data alone. Example 8 shows that a fully observed proxy (such as another always-available modality, or Y when target labels exist) can restore identification. Its mention of external studies connects to N1's fully observed source acting as auxiliary information, which is valid only if the source is not S-selected relative to the target.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on model selection. It is background identification theory that N1's assumptions section should cite. It does not treat prediction risk under a changed mask process or two-population designs.

papers.title: On varieties of doubly robust estimators under missingness not at random with a shadow variable (with the companion 'Identification and semiparametric efficiency theory of nonignorable missing data with a shadow variable')
papers.authors: Wang Miao, Eric J. Tchetgen Tchetgen (Biometrika 2016); Wang Miao, Lan Liu, Yilin Li, Eric J. Tchetgen Tchetgen, Zhi Geng (companion; arXiv 1509.02556, ACM/IMS J. Data Science 2024)
papers.venue_year: Biometrika 103(2):475-482, 2016; companion paper ACM/IMS Journal of Data Science 1(2), 2024 (arXiv:1509.02556, 2015-2019)
papers.verification: Fetched the Oxford Academic abstract page for the 2016 paper and the arXiv abs page for 1509.02556. The JDS 2024 venue is from a search snippet only (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3592389).
papers.method: Identification and estimation for an MNAR outcome using a shadow variable Z: Z is associated with the missing variable but independent of missingness given the (possibly missing) variable and the fully observed covariates. The estimators are IPW-type, regression/imputation-type, and doubly robust, with goodness-of-fit tests for the working models.
papers.identification_result: Under the shadow-variable condition and completeness-type conditions, the odds-ratio function linking p(Y | X, R=0) to p(Y | X, R=1), and hence the full data law, is identified. The companion paper stresses that the conditions 'only involve the observed data and thus can be justified empirically'.
papers.shift_assumptions: Single population. The outcome, or more generally a variable, is MNAR, possibly self-masked. A fully observed shadow variable Z with Z ⊥ R | (Y, X).
papers.source_access: (X, Z, R, R·Y): covariates and shadow variable always observed, target variable observed when R=1.
papers.target_access: N/A (single population).
papers.experiments: Simulation plus an applied example in the 2016 paper (details not verified beyond the abstract).
papers.relevance_to_N1: It gives an assumption N1 could add to make the risk difference identified even under self-masked or outcome-dependent acquisition. In an unlabeled target, an always-acquired modality or a downstream record correlated with the missing modality but not directly affecting its acquisition can act as a shadow variable for P_T(X_mis | X_obs, M). The odds-ratio function is the natural sensitivity parameter when no valid shadow variable exists, which matches N1's plan for OR-style bounds on P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) relative to the source.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on model selection. It gives an identification route plus DR estimation of means, which N1 would reuse for risk functionals. It does not cover two-population transfer, predictor comparison, or acquisition policies.

papers.title: Itemwise conditionally independent nonresponse modelling for incomplete multivariate data
papers.authors: Mauricio Sadinle, Jerome P. Reiter
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abstract page. Biometrika volume and pages come from a search snippet (academic.oup.com). The Nabi et al. 2020 full text confirms the ICIN definition and its equivalence to Shpitser's 2016 no-self-censoring model.
papers.method: Proposes the ICIN ('no self-censoring') nonresponse mechanism: for each item, X_j ⊥ R_j | X_{-j}, R_{-j}. It builds nonparametric saturated full-data model classes under this assumption and a sensitivity analysis for violations.
papers.identification_result: Under ICIN the full-data law of the multivariate data and the nonresponse indicators is nonparametrically identified. It is nonignorable, because R_j may depend on other items' missing values. Violations are handled by sensitivity parameters rather than identification.
papers.shift_assumptions: Single population. Nonmonotone MNAR restricted by no self-censoring.
papers.source_access: Generic incomplete multivariate data (X_obs, R).
papers.target_access: N/A.
papers.experiments: Applied survey data analyses, per the abstract (not verified in detail).
papers.relevance_to_N1: For modality acquisition, ICIN means that whether modality j is acquired may depend on other modalities' values and on which other tests were ordered, but not on modality j's own value given everything else. It is the weakest standard assumption that point-identifies the target full law from unlabeled target (X_obs, M). It is plausible for ordering decisions made before a result is known, and violated when unrecorded information correlated with X_j drives ordering. Its built-in sensitivity analysis is a template for N1's 'assumption + sensitivity' requirement.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on model selection. It is an identifying assumption and sensitivity device N1 can adopt. It does not cover prediction risk, deployment shift, or ranking.

papers.title: Combining Panel Data Sets with Attrition and Refreshment Samples
papers.authors: Keisuke Hirano, Guido W. Imbens, Geert Ridder, Donald B. Rubin
papers.verification: Fetched the NBER abstract page, which states that 'a class of non-ignorable missing data models can be identified without making strong distributional or functional form assumptions if refreshment samples are available'. The Econometrica venue and the 'additive non-ignorable' (AN) class naming are from a search snippet. The AN model's nesting of MAR and Hausman-Wise is from memory and NOT verified.
papers.method: Uses a refreshment sample, an independent fresh random draw from the same population giving the marginal distribution of the later-wave variable, to identify a nonignorable attrition mechanism in panel data.
papers.identification_result: With a refreshment sample from the SAME population, the AN class of MNAR attrition models is identified nonparametrically. The refreshment sample also makes MAR testable.
papers.shift_assumptions: Same population for the panel and refreshment samples. The attrition logit is additive in the early-wave and late-wave variables (AN).
papers.source_access: Panel with attrition: early wave complete, later wave missing for attriters.
papers.target_access: Refreshment sample: an independent draw giving the marginal of the later-wave variable.
papers.experiments: Econometric application; not verified in detail.
papers.relevance_to_N1: This is structurally N1's design: a complete sample (N1's fully observed source) plus an incomplete sample (N1's naturally masked target). If the source is a random sample of the target population with no S-selection, the source's P(X(1)) acts as a refreshment sample. It can then identify target acquisition mechanisms that depend on unobserved modality values without shadow variables, e.g. p_T(M=1 | x1, x2) = p_T(x2 | x1, M=1) p_T(M=1 | x1) / p_S(x2 | x1). This is exactly where N1's S vs M distinction bites: a complete-case development cohort is typically selected, which voids the refreshment-sample identification. That clarifies which extra assumption (the invariance of P(X(1),Y) across S) makes dropout-based comparison valid.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on prediction or model selection. It provides a data-fusion identification route and the precise invariance assumption N1 must state or test. Neither this paper nor the AFA literature applies refreshment-sample logic to predictor evaluation.

papers.title: Learning to Maximize Mutual Information for Dynamic Feature Selection
papers.authors: Ian Covert, Wei Qiu, Mingyu Lu, Nayoon Kim, Nathan White, Su-In Lee
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abs page (2301.00557). Downloaded the full PDF and grepped the training procedure and dataset appendix. The word 'missing' does not occur in the paper.
papers.method: Dynamic feature selection by amortized greedy conditional mutual information. A policy network and a predictor are trained jointly. The predictor is pre-trained on RANDOM feature subsets (artificial masking), and the mask can be passed as input.
papers.identification_result: None. It is a learning method and assumes oracle or complete access to features at training and evaluation.
papers.shift_assumptions: Implicitly MCAR/complete data. The feature subsets at test time are chosen by the policy on fully observed test records.
papers.source_access: Fully observed (X, Y). Artificial masks are generated during training.
papers.target_access: Held-out fully observed records. Evaluation reveals features according to the learned policy (artificial masking).
papers.experiments: Spam and MiniBooNE (UCI), NHANES diabetes (Kachuee preprocessing), MNIST, CIFAR-10, and three private Harborview emergency-medicine cohorts. In the 'bleeding' cohort they 'only included patients whose fibrinogen levels were measured', which is a population selection S driven by whether the label test was acquired. Natural missingness is never discussed.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A representative of the artificial-dropout paradigm N1 questions. Train and evaluate with synthetic masks on complete records, with no account of natural acquisition. The fibrinogen-measured cohort is a concrete published example of S (selection on test acquisition) being conflated with the observation process.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None on evaluation under natural missingness. It is a candidate model or baseline family (mask-aware predictor trained with random subsets) whose dropout-based ranking N1 would test against natural-missingness risk.

papers.title: Opportunistic Learning: Budgeted Cost-Sensitive Learning from Data Streams
papers.authors: Mohammad Kachuee, Orpaz Goldstein, Kimmo Kärkkäinen, Sajad Darabi, Majid Sarrafzadeh
papers.verification: Fetched the arXiv abs page. Downloaded the full PDF and grepped the implementation details (Sec. 3.2) and the dataset table.
papers.method: RL-based (deep Q-learning) cost-sensitive feature acquisition at prediction time. The reward is based on the change in MC-dropout model uncertainty per unit cost, and representations are shared between predictor and value networks.
papers.identification_result: None. Features are normalized and 'missing features' are imputed with zeros. NaN is used both for 'not available' and 'not yet acquired' features, so natural absence and non-acquisition are not distinguished.
papers.shift_assumptions: None stated about the retrospective missingness mechanism.
papers.source_access: (X with natural NaNs, Y), streamed.
papers.target_access: Test records (X with natural NaNs, Y). The agent acquires features on them; naturally missing features read as 0.
papers.experiments: MNIST, Yahoo Learning-to-Rank, and an NHANES diabetes dataset with real survey and lab missingness and expert feature costs. Evaluation uses held-out labels.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A canonical AFA baseline that shows the failure modes N1 targets. Naturally missing entries are treated like un-acquired or zero values, so 'record absent' is conflated with 'test not performed' and with a value of zero. Evaluation on naturally incomplete test data is the biased 'blocked' evaluation that von Kleist et al. later showed needs correction.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None. It is historical context and a possible baseline; it motivates why naive evaluation on naturally missing data is biased.

papers.title: Causal Discovery in the Presence of Missing Data
papers.authors: Ruibo Tu, Cheng Zhang, Paul Ackermann, Karthika Mohan, Hedvig Kjellström, Kun Zhang
papers.verification: Fetched the PMLR abstract page. Downloaded the full PDF and read the assumptions section (Sec. 2) and the dataset description.
papers.method: Missing-Value PC (MVPC): a PC algorithm with corrections, via density-ratio weighting or generative correction, to conditional-independence tests that are distorted by MAR or MNAR missingness encoded in m-graphs.
papers.identification_result: Asymptotically correct recovery of the causal skeleton and CPDAG under the PC assumptions (Markov, faithfulness, no confounding or selection) plus four more. Assumption 1: missingness indicators are not causes of substantive variables. Assumption 2: faithful observability. Assumption 3: no missingness indicator is a deterministic function of others. Assumption 4: no self-masking.
papers.shift_assumptions: Single population, with no latent confounding and no selection bias. MNAR is allowed except self-masking.
papers.source_access: Incomplete observational data (X_obs, R).
papers.target_access: N/A.
papers.experiments: Synthetic data with induced MCAR, MAR and MNAR, plus two real healthcare datasets (a US cognition study and an Achilles tendon rupture study) with natural missingness. Evaluation against domain knowledge; no ground truth for the real data.
papers.relevance_to_N1: A possible tool to probe the target m-graph from unlabeled target (X_obs, M), i.e. to check whether an acquisition indicator depends on other modalities, before choosing the identification route. It has limits for modality acquisition. Assumption 3 is violated when several features share one modality-level indicator unless indicators are defined per modality. Assumption 4 and 'no selection bias' exclude exactly the self-masking and S-selection cases where N1 needs sensitivity analysis, and Mohan and Pearl's Theorem 4 says those cases are untestable anyway.
papers.overlap_with_candidate: None. It is at most an auxiliary diagnostic for the mask mechanism; it says nothing about predictor risk or ranking.

sweeps.cluster_summary:
**AFAPE already covers the core estimation problem.** The AFA-evaluation line by von Kleist, Zamanian, Shpitser and Ahmidi (JMLR 2025 time-varying paper; arXiv 2023 static paper) already frames 'the deployment acquisition/missingness process differs from the one that generated the development data' as a missing-data plus off-policy evaluation problem.
- It gives identification conditions: NDE, NUC, and view-specific positivity. It also gives IPW, DM and DR (DRL) estimators for the expected misclassification cost of any fixed classifier under a specified acquisition policy.
- It explicitly notes (JMLR Sec. 2.7) that a hospital-to-hospital change in a KNOWN acquisition policy can be handled by treating the target policy as the evaluated policy.
- Their decomposition J = E_{p(X(1),Y)}[E(C | X(1),Y)] answers N1's headline question in the favourable case. Artificial dropout on a fully observed source predicts deployment risk exactly when all of the following hold:
  - the dropout distribution equals the deployment acquisition law pi_T(M | X(1), Y);
  - the source full-data law equals the target's (no S-selection);
  - NDE holds.
- Uniform random dropout matches only an MCAR target with matching rates.

**The same group supplies N1's conceptual vocabulary and main baseline.**
- Zamanian et al. 2024 (J Pers Med) already separates curation/inclusion selection (S, scenario 9) from acquisition missingness. It flags unrecorded-but-observed information (record absence, NUC violation, scenario 8). It writes the deployment loss E_{pi_new}[loss(f(x*, r))] and proposes an outcome-dependent odds-ratio tilting parameter δ with expert-elicited ranges.
- Rockenschaub et al. 2024 shows that pattern-wise Bayes predictors are invariant only under ignorable missingness shifts, and warns that source validation is a poor selection criterion under missingness shift. Its experiments use only synthetic masks.

**The missing-data identification literature fixes the boundary for N1's counterexample.**
- Nabi, Bhattacharya and Shpitser 2020: the full law is identified if and only if there are no self-censoring edges or colluders (no colluding paths with latent variables).
- Mohan and Pearl 2021: X adjacent to R_X makes the target non-recoverable, and X ⊥ R_X-type assumptions are untestable.
- Identification-restoring assumptions N1 could add: no self-censoring (ICIN; Sadinle and Reiter 2017), shadow variables (Miao and Tchetgen Tchetgen 2016; Miao et al. 2024), or a refreshment sample (Hirano et al. 2001).
- The refreshment sample is structurally N1's 'complete source plus incomplete target' design. It is valid only if the source is not S-selected.

**Important caveat for N1.** When target labels are fully observed, the target risk of any deployable predictor f(X_obs, M) is a functional of the observed target law and is identified. The non-identifiability results above then do not apply, and the only open question is explanatory: why dropout rankings differ. Candidate explanations are pattern-weight or selection mismatch versus a genuine shift in P(Y | x_obs, M).

**AFA method papers.** Kachuee 2019 and Covert 2023 represent the artificial-mask paradigm, or naive treatment of natural missingness (NaN → 0). Covert's fibrinogen-measured cohort is a published example of S driven by test acquisition.

**Related work noted but not in this cluster's list:**
- Robins, Orellana and Rotnitzky 2008 (Stat Med), transporting regimes across systems with different testing frequency and reasons (search snippet only).
- Zamanian, Ahmidi and Drton 2023 (Stat Med), pattern-graph sensitivity analysis (search snippet and a citation inside the AFAPE paper).
- Ulichney and Coston 2026 (arXiv 2606.14506), DML target-risk estimation under covariate shift plus selective labels with no missing covariates (abstract fetched).
- Rheude et al. (arXiv 2505.16791), cohort-level test-time modality acquisition (abstract fetched).
- Kobayashi et al. (arXiv 2510.12624), AFA from retrospective missingness under MAR (abstract fetched).
- A TUM PhD thesis by von Kleist ('Deciding What to Measure') exists according to search results, but the fetch timed out: UNVERIFIED.

**Novelty implication.** Estimating each model's target risk, or their difference, under a known or MAR deployment acquisition policy with IPW or DR on the same population is already covered by AFAPE. Presenting it as 'acquisition-aware model selection' would be NO_GO unless N1 adds the elements listed below.
sweeps.gaps_left_open:
What this cluster does NOT address, and where N1 could still contribute:

1. **Separating population selection S from the acquisition mask M in a two-population design.** Every AFAPE, missingness-shift and m-graph result assumes one population, with only the mask process changing. None treats a fully observed but S-selected development cohort (the complete-case cohort is itself a product of acquisition) alongside a naturally masked deployment population. None states when source invariance P_S(X(1),Y) = P_T(X(1),Y) can be used, as refreshment-sample identification does, or when it fails.
2. **An unknown, possibly outcome- or U-dependent target acquisition policy learned from unlabeled target (X_obs, M).** AFAPE assumes the evaluated policy is known. Zamanian 2024 treats pi_new as hypothetical.
3. **Inference about the SIGN of the risk difference between two predictors (ranking).** This means partial identification or sensitivity bounds, e.g. OR/tilting on P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) or on the acquisition odds, with a 'rank-flip threshold' and bootstrap uncertainty. Existing work gives point estimates of single-policy cost (AFAPE), or conceptual OR sensitivity for means or losses without any model-comparison criterion (Zamanian 2024; Sadinle-Reiter; Miao-Tchetgen).
4. **A minimal ranking-reversal counterexample tied to the Nabi/Mohan boundary.** The case is self-censoring or colluding paths via unrecorded clinician information with an unlabeled target. The counterexample must be explicitly separated from the labelled-target case, where target risk is identified and no non-identifiability claim applies.
5. **Diagnostics that decompose dropout-vs-natural ranking changes.** The components are (i) pattern-frequency and class-balance reweighting (a simple selection explanation) versus (ii) a genuine shift in P(Y | x_obs, M) or P(X_mis | x_obs, M). Rockenschaub's Theorem 1 implies that only (ii) produces non-trivial reversals for Bayes predictors.
6. **Validation on NATURAL missingness with verified acquisition semantics.** All AFAPE, Rockenschaub and Zamanian experiments use synthetic masks on complete data. Kachuee and Covert conflate natural absence with non-acquisition or zero. Record absence versus test not performed is only discussed conceptually (Zamanian scenario 8).
7. **Modality-level (block) acquisition.** Here several features share one indicator, which breaks Tu et al.'s Assumption 3. Modality-level positivity for dropout-to-deployment transfer is also untreated.

If N1 cannot deliver items 1-3 plus 6 on approved real data with verified acquisition meaning and labels, the remaining contribution collapses onto AFAPE plus Zamanian 2024. Per the user's rule, that is NO_GO, or BLOCKED_REALDATA if acquisition semantics or labels cannot be confirmed.

synthesis.dams_vs_damnar_prose:
Both anchor papers exist, and I read both in full; the key passages were re-checked against the extracted PDF text for this synthesis. They are two ends of one line of work. Neither studies N1's exact configuration: a fully observed, possibly selected source; a naturally masked target; and a choice between two fixed models.

**DAMS (Zhou, Balakrishnan & Lipton, AISTATS 2023)** is the positive result.
- With clean P(X,Y) invariant and masks MCAR/UCAR, relative missingness rates are identified (Remark 5). The labeled target law is then identified from the source (Thm 5.2).
- Algorithm 1 is literally target-calibrated artificial dropout of the source. When m^s ⪯ m^t, it produces data i.i.d. with the labeled target, which determines the target risk, and hence the ranking, of any model.
- With indicators observed and MCAR or v-MAR masks, missingness shift is ordinary covariate shift on (x~, ξ) (Prop. 1). Importance weighting on (x_obs, M) is therefore prior art, as are the AFAPE estimators of von Kleist et al.
- On real eICU data with natural underreporting, the adjustments lose to the unadapted source model. The authors explicitly blame cohort selection, label shift and prevalence rather than missingness shift. That is N1's S-versus-M confound, stated in 2023 and left unanalyzed.

**DAMNAR (Stokes et al., arXiv 2504.00322, no verified venue)** is the negative result plus a workaround.
- App. A shows that under MNAR, P(Y | x_obs, R) differs across domains even when P(Y | X) and P(X) are invariant, so observed-data IW fails.
- It then assumes the problem away with parametric MNAR imputers. Thm 1 bounds target error by imputation error; this needs imputation to converge to the realized counterfactual Xu, so it is a reduction rather than an identification result.
- It offers no bounds, sensitivity model, confidence intervals, ranking analysis or S/M separation.
- Its derivation quietly assumes R ⊥ Y | X while its simulations include R→Y edges, and its eICU source/target direction is stated both ways.
- Its eICU result also fails to beat mean imputation by much. The authors attribute this to concept shift, echoing DAMS.

**Label access in both papers.** Target labels were public and were used for evaluation; in DAMNAR they were also used inside the leak imputers and for concept-shift diagnostics. Their non-identifiability statements therefore apply only to the formal selection-time information set. N1 must keep the same scope and cannot claim non-identifiability on public-label benchmarks such as eICU, MIMIC or PhysioNet 2012.

**What this leaves for N1:**
- (1) The two-population design, in which the fully observed source is itself S-selected (e.g., complete-case). Neither paper allows P(X,Y) to differ.
- (2) Model selection on the sign of the target risk difference, rather than learning an adapted predictor.
- (3) Sensitivity and partial identification for non-ignorable or Y-dependent acquisition. DAMS names this as future work and DAMNAR avoids it via parametric imputation.
- (4) A real-data audit of artificial-versus-natural ranking agreement that controls for cohort selection and prevalence. Both eICU studies show the confound but never compare against artificial masking of the same cohort.

**Two further points.**
- Rockenschaub et al. 2024 Thm 1 and the AFAPE papers (von Kleist et al., JMLR 2025) already state the invariance boundary and supply IPW/DM/DR estimators under a known acquisition policy, so items (2) and (3) are the only method-level room left.
- Even there, Guerdan et al. (ICML 2024) and Steingrimsson et al. (Biometrics 2024) supply most of the machinery.

nearest_neighbours.what_it_already_does: Proves that target-calibrated artificial re-masking of a labeled source (Alg. 1) reproduces the labeled target law under invariant P(X,Y) and UCAR with m^s ⪯ m^t, so every model's target risk and the ranking are identified. With observed masks and MCAR/v-MAR, reduces missingness shift to covariate shift and hence IW (Prop. 1). Shows that on real eICU the adjustments fail, citing cohort selection and prevalence.

N1 must present calibrated dropout and IW as DAMS baselines, not as contributions.

nearest_neighbours.what_N1_adds_if_anything: A related but different estimand (value of acquisition vs ranking under a changed policy). Relevant as prior art for 'performance under the current measurement policy' language.

candidate_contributions_assessment.claim: Formal separation of population selection S from observation mask M when evaluating modality-dropout robustness, with a decomposition of the gap between artificial-dropout risk and deployment risk into (a) pattern-weight mismatch, (b) within-pattern population shift, and (c) MNAR acquisition selection.
candidate_contributions_assessment.prior_work_covering_it: The decomposition technique is Zhang, Singh, Ghassemi & Joshi (ICML 2023; Shapley attribution over factorized distributions) and DISDE (Cai, Namkoong & Yadlowsky, arXiv 2303.02011; X-shift vs Y∣X-shift vs unseen support). The S vs M conceptual split appears in Zamanian et al. 2024 (J Pers Med), where scenario 9 (inclusion/exclusion curation) is distinct from the acquisition scenarios and scenario 8 is unrecorded information. An M-only shift with the population held fixed is in Subbaswamy, Adams & Saria (AISTATS 2021). S-only sensitivity is in Sahoo, Lei & Wager. ICYM2I (ICLR 2026) lumps S and M into one indicator. DAMS names cohort selection as the confounder of its eICU failure. Catoire et al. 2026 give NICO as the formal condition for complete-case status being uninformative. DrFuse's EHR-only model drop (.408 to .374) is an informal S-only diagnostic. Knockout gives the dropout estimand p_S(Y ∣ x_obs).
candidate_contributions_assessment.reasoning: The three-term decomposition is a telescoping identity over the factorization P(M)·P(X_obs ∣ M)·P(Y ∣ X_obs, M). It is a direct instantiation of Zhang et al. / DISDE, with (a) and (b) estimable by reweighting from unlabeled target data and (c) needing labels or a sensitivity model, which is exactly DISDE's structure. The S/M distinction is stated conceptually by Zamanian et al. and operationally, for M alone, by Subbaswamy et al. What remains is writing the two-population design formally (fully observed but S-selected source; naturally masked target) and labelling which terms are identified from which data. This is useful framing, and every cluster flagged it as open, but it is not a standalone contribution. It adds value only if paired with the real-data audit (C4). Also note that term (b) under S-selection is a source-vs-target covariate shift already handled by IWCV/DAMS-style weighting.

candidate_contributions_assessment.claim: A minimal counterexample showing that artificial dropout cannot determine the target model RANKING under MNAR or label-dependent acquisition, even with pattern rates matched to the target and unlabeled target data available. Plus an assumption ladder that restores comparability: MCAR+invariance, MAR+invariance, covariate shift on the always-observed part, and MNAR with a bounded odds ratio.
candidate_contributions_assessment.prior_work_covering_it: Non-transportability of P(Y ∣ x_obs, M) under MNAR: DAMNAR App. A. Non-ignorability of Y-dependent shift: Rockenschaub et al. 2024 Thm 1 and Cor. 1. Graphical non-identification boundary: Nabi, Bhattacharya & Shpitser 2020, and Mohan & Pearl 2021 Thm 3, with Thm 4 on untestability. Generic non-identifiability of target accuracy from labeled source plus unlabeled target: Garg et al. ICLR 2022 (ATC). What dropout estimates: Knockout. Simulated ranking reversals under acquisition change: Groenwold 2020, Sisk et al. 2023, Rockenschaub 2024. Ladder rungs: DAMS Thm 5.2/Alg. 1 (UCAR, calibrated dropout exact); DAMS Prop. 1 (MCAR/v-MAR, i.e. covariate shift on (x_obs, M)); AFAPE missing-data view (any identified full law plus a known policy); Josse et al. Thm 2 (MAR-Y); Catoire NIMO/NICO; Sadinle & Reiter ICIN; Miao & Tchetgen Tchetgen shadow variables; Hirano et al. 2001 refreshment sample; Steingrimsson et al. 2024 and Zamanian 2024 bounded tilt/odds ratio.
candidate_contributions_assessment.reasoning: Once P_T(Y ∣ x_obs, M=m) is not identified (DAMNAR App. A, Rockenschaub Cor. 1), constructing two fixed predictors whose target ranking flips within the observationally equivalent set is a one-line corollary: for example, two constant predictors, or an observed-only vs a mask-aware model, can be ordered either way. So the sign-level statement adds little over the risk-level statements already published. The ladder is a synthesis of known results. The only non-trivial residue is: (i) stating the ladder for the specific two-population design, including an S-selected source; (ii) noting that the refreshment-sample rung (Hirano et al.), which would identify some MNAR mechanisms from a complete random source, is exactly what S-selection destroys (the candidate ladder currently omits this rung); and (iii) noting that under invariance plus MAR, target-calibrated dropout is exact (AFAPE, DAMS), so the counterexample needs Y-dependence, unrecorded information (colluding paths) or S-selection. The counterexample must also be scoped to label-free selection time. On public-label benchmarks (eICU, MIMIC, PhysioNet 2012) target risk is identified and the claim does not apply. Valuable as exposition; not a contribution.

candidate_contributions_assessment.claim: Acquisition-aware model selection: sharp partial-identification bounds on the target RISK DIFFERENCE between two predictors, under an odds-ratio sensitivity model on P_T(Y ∣ x_obs, M=m) relative to the source-identified P(Y ∣ x_obs). Optionally with a known or estimated target prevalence constraint (a linear program), bootstrap uncertainty, and a breakdown value Γ* at which the ranking becomes undetermined.
candidate_contributions_assessment.prior_work_covering_it: Guerdan, Coston, Holstein & Wu, ICML 2024: joint regret intervals for the performance DIFFERENCE of two policies under MSM, Rosenbaum Γ, IV or proximal assumptions, with the agreement region cancelling, DR estimators and bootstrap CIs. Kallus & Zhou, NeurIPS 2018: minimax regret against a baseline under an MSM-type set, which is the 'switch only if worst-case ΔR < 0' rule. Steingrimsson, Robertson & Dahabreh, Biometrics 2024: exponential-tilt sensitivity for transported prediction-model risk, with the parameter anchored to target outcome prevalence. Rambachan, Coston & Kennedy: sharp single-model bounds with DML inference. Dorn & Guo, JASA 2023: sharp MSM bounds via quantile balancing. Sahoo, Lei & Wager: Γ-selection CVaR bounds. Zamanian et al. 2024: an outcome-dependent acquisition odds ratio δ with elicited ranges. Rosenbaum-style sensitivity values / tipping points are the standard breakdown concept. Subbaswamy et al. 2021: worst-case risk under ordering shift.
candidate_contributions_assessment.reasoning: Every component already exists: joint (not differenced) bounds on a two-model performance difference, the MSM/odds-ratio parameterization, DR/DML estimation, bootstrap CIs and tipping points. Guerdan et al. do the risk-difference version; Steingrimsson et al. do the transported-risk tilt with a prevalence anchor. Mathematically, for binary Y and a pointwise loss, the risk difference is linear in p_T(x_obs, m), so the sharp bound under a pointwise odds-ratio box is endpoint evaluation. Adding a prevalence equality turns it into a fractional-knapsack LP, the same structure as Dorn & Guo's balancing constraint. Neither is technically new. The genuine residue is the instantiation: conditioning on (x_obs, M=m), a nominal built from a fully observed source, and separate S and M parameters (Γ_S à la Sahoo et al., Λ_M on acquisition). That instantiation is legitimate as applied methodology but thin as a method contribution. Per the user's rule, it must not be sold as a new method. Two caveats: 'sharp' must be proven for the chosen constraint set, and an estimated prevalence adds uncertainty that the bootstrap must propagate. If N1's method section reduces to 'Guerdan-style interval, Steingrimsson-style tilt, per mask pattern', the method side is NO_GO.

candidate_contributions_assessment.claim: An empirical test on real data with natural missingness of whether model rankings flip between artificial dropout and natural missingness, and whether any flips are explained by simple sample selection or class-balance adjustment.
candidate_contributions_assessment.prior_work_covering_it: Published tables already show the phenomenon without controls: DrFuse (AAAI 2024) Table 2, with complete-case vs full-cohort ranking reversals; MedFuse (MLHC 2022) App. A.4 vs A.6, where artificial and natural missingness move AUROC in opposite directions; CareBench (arXiv 2602.23614), which reports a synthetic 0-80% sweep plus the natural base cohort, with changed mortality-AUPRC rankings but training data confounded. Qian et al. 2024 show on PhysioNet 2012 that artificial-mask protocol changes imputation-method rankings (artificial only). Synthetic-only ranking instability: Rockenschaub et al. 2024, Shades-of-Null (arXiv 2409.07510), MuteBench (arXiv 2605.15235), Ma et al. CVPR 2022, Groenwold 2020. Natural-missingness shift studies without an artificial comparison: DAMS and DAMNAR on eICU, Subbaswamy et al. 2021. Tools for the null explanations: BBSE (Lipton et al. 2018) and Saerens et al. 2002 for prevalence; DISDE and Zhang et al. 2023 for attribution; ICYM2I-style IPW for complete-case selection.
candidate_contributions_assessment.reasoning: No verified paper runs the controlled comparison N1 proposes. That means: one fixed eligible population and prediction cutoff; the same trained models; artificial dropout on the complete-case subcohort vs natural acquisition in the full cohort; pairwise sign tests or Kendall-τ with CIs; and, before invoking any missingness mechanism, testing whether flips disappear after complete-case (S) reweighting and prevalence adjustment. That controlled attribution is the residual. The raw phenomenon is not new (DrFuse, MedFuse, CareBench, Groenwold). Limits: (i) it is an empirical/analysis contribution, not a method, and may yield a negative result, e.g. flips fully explained by S and prevalence, which should be reported as such. (ii) On public-label data (PhysioNet 2012, eICU, MIMIC) it is purely descriptive; no non-identifiability claims apply. (iii) Its validity depends on acquisition semantics. In PhysioNet 2012, for example, an absent variable means 'not recorded in the first 48 h', which cannot be distinguished from 'not performed'. Unless the acquisition meaning can be established from documentation, the item should be recorded as BLOCKED_REALDATA rather than silently treating absence as non-acquisition. (iv) The comparison must hold information and budget equal across baselines: observed-only, mask-aware, dropout-trained, imputation, IPW/DAMS reweighting, DAMNAR impute-then-reweight, and StableMiss/MIRRAMS.
