refutations.residual_gap:
No single verified paper makes C1 as stated. The pieces are all prior art, so what is left is a narrow instantiation, not a methodological contribution.

(1) Already covered:
- The conceptual separation of S from M: Haneuse & Daniels 2016, the Peskoe/Thaweethai sequential factorization, Zamanian scenario 9, survey unit vs item nonresponse.
- A graph that carries S and R/M as distinct mechanisms: Tikka et al., Saadati & Tian.
- The decomposition machinery: Zhang et al. ICML 2023 Shapley attribution over an arbitrary factorization; Feng et al. and DISDE for p(X) vs p(Y|X), both with debiased CIs.
- The pattern-mixture risk identity: Mercaldo & Blume.
Taking Zhang et al. with the factorization P(M)·P(X_obs|M)·P(Y|X_obs,M) mechanically gives the three terms: pattern-weight mismatch, within-pattern shift and MNAR conditional shift.

(2) Not found in any verified work:
- The artificial-dropout estimand R_drop(f) = E_{P(X,Y|S=1)} E_{m~q}[l(f(x_m),Y)]: a complete-case-selected source crossed with an independent synthetic mask law q. It is set against the natural deployment estimand on a fixed eligible population and cutoff.
- An exact decomposition of R_T − R_drop, and of the pairwise difference Δ_T(f1,f2) − Δ_drop(f1,f2), into those three terms, with a sign/ranking-preservation condition.
- Using this to audit real data: why a dropout-based ranking does or does not carry over.

(3) The only substantive new question is about identification of the S/M split. The within-pattern and conditional-outcome terms can be split further into a cohort-selection (S) part and an acquisition (M) part only against an anchor law, such as P(X_obs,Y) on the full eligible population. That anchor is not identified from a complete-case source without extra assumptions: S ⊥ Y | X, a refreshment sample (Hirano et al.), or public target labels. Existing attribution tools assume every factor is observed in both environments.

(4) Caveat: when target labels are public (eICU, MIMIC), every term can be estimated directly with existing IW or HDPD estimators, and C1 reduces to a descriptive attribution with a known method. It should be framed as the setup and diagnostic for N1, with DAMS Alg. 1 (pattern re-weighting) and IW (covariate shift) credited as existing remedies for the first two terms. It should not be claimed as a contribution in its own right.

prior_work.title: A hierarchical decomposition for explaining ML performance discrepancies (Feng, Singh, Xia, Subbaswamy, Gossmann), NeurIPS 2024
prior_work.verification: Downloaded the arXiv PDF and read Sec. 3 in the extracted text. The NeurIPS 2024 listing was confirmed by search results (proceedings.neurips.cc hash e83e27af..., neurips.cc poster 93686, and ML Anthology).
prior_work.how_it_covers: It factorizes each domain as p_D(W)·p_D(Z|W)·p_D(Y|W,Z) and gives the aggregate decomposition Λ = ΛW + ΛZ + ΛY. ΛW is the baseline shift in p(W), ΛZ is the conditional-covariate shift E_1[E_{·10}[ℓ|W] − E_{·00}[ℓ|W]], and ΛY is the conditional-outcome shift. It comes with debiased estimators and asymptotically valid CIs. Map D=0 to the artificial-dropout law π_drop(m)·P_S(x_obs)·P_S(y|x_obs), D=1 to the naturally masked target, W to the mask pattern M, and Z to X⊙M with placeholders. The three terms are then exactly C1's pattern-weight mismatch, within-pattern population shift and MNAR/acquisition (Y|x_obs,M) term. Because the decomposition is linear in ℓ, using ℓ_f1 − ℓ_f2 gives the ranking version directly. The paper itself says a large ΛZ 'can be due to differences in missingness rates, prevalence, or selection bias', so it names, and lumps together, the very S and M sources C1 wants to separate.

prior_work.title: 'Why did the Model Fail?': Attributing Model Performance Changes to Distribution Shifts (Zhang, Singh, Ghassemi, Joshi), ICML 2023; and Diagnosing Model Performance Under Distribution Shift / DISDE (Cai, Namkoong, Yadlowsky), arXiv 2303.02011
prior_work.verification: I fetched the Zhang et al. arXiv abstract page (it says ICML 2023). I downloaded the DISDE PDF and read the abstract and intro in the extracted text.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Zhang et al. attribute a performance change with Shapley values over any causal factorization of the joint distribution, estimated by importance weighting. A graph with separate S → X, X → M and (X,Y) → M factors is therefore an instance of their game. DISDE splits a performance drop into X-shift, Y|X-shift and unseen-support terms. With X := (M, X_obs) this covers C1's three terms, plus a support term that C1 omits (target patterns or x_obs values that dropout never generates).

prior_work.title: Analysis of Missingness Scenarios for Observational Health Data (Zamanian, von Kleist, Ciora, Piperno, Lancho, Ahmidi), J Pers Med 14(5):514, 2024
prior_work.verification: I re-fetched the PMC full text in this review. Quotes checked: Scenario 9, 'Samples are included or excluded depending on data and missingness characteristics...'; Scenario 8 on observed-but-unrecorded information; Eq. 4, the deployment loss E_π_new[(y − f(x*, r_X; w))²]; and Eq. 10, the outcome-dependent odds-ratio parameter δ.
prior_work.how_it_covers: It separates cohort inclusion/exclusion (a population-selection S acting on rows) from variable-level acquisition mechanisms (M). It flags record absence as distinct from not-performed. It writes the deployment risk under a new acquisition policy and adds an outcome-dependent odds-ratio sensitivity parameter. That covers the conceptual S-vs-M separation and the MNAR-acquisition term as a sensitivity object. It does not give a decomposition.

prior_work.title: Causal Effect Identification from Multiple Incomplete Data Sources: A General Search-based Approach (Tikka, Hyttinen, Karvanen), J Stat Softw 99(5), 2021
prior_work.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract page (JSS venue listed) and downloaded the PDF. The extracted text says 'Selection bias can be seen as a special case of missing data...'. It uses separate selection nodes S alongside per-variable response indicators R_Vi, and it handles 'combined transportability and selection bias'.
prior_work.how_it_covers: A formal graphical model with distinct unit-selection (S), item-response (R) and domain/transport nodes in one identification framework. The formal separation of S from M is therefore not new as a modelling device. It is applied to causal-effect identification, not to predictive risk.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness (Stokes, Do, Blecker, Chunara, Adhikari), arXiv 2504.00322, 2025
prior_work.verification: I downloaded the PDF and read the abstract and Sec. 2 in the extracted text. The abstract says the procedure 'can be extended to handle simultaneous MNAR missingness and covariate shifts'. Sec. 2 uses weights P_T(Xo,Xu,R)/P_S(Xo,Xu,R) after imputation.
prior_work.how_it_covers: It formally treats a population shift in P(X) and an MNAR missingness-mechanism shift at the same time, as separate components of the source-to-target change. That is an S-type plus M-type decomposition of the shift in the DA setting, though not of an evaluation gap.

prior_work.title: Discrete Choice Models for Nonmonotone Nonignorable Missing Data: Identification and Inference (Tchetgen Tchetgen, Wang, Sun), Statistica Sinica 28(4):2069-2088, 2018; building on Little (1993) CCMV
prior_work.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract (1607.02631) and the PMC full text. It quotes Sec. 3.2: taking the LDCM condition as primitive 'amounts to nonparametric identification under the complete-case missing value restriction of Little (1993)', i.e., the law of the unobserved variables given the observed ones in any pattern equals the complete-case law.
prior_work.how_it_covers: In the usual repository design, the 'fully observed source' is the complete-case subset of the same eligible population, so S = 1{M = all-observed}. C1's MNAR-acquisition term is then exactly the departure of P_T(Y | x_obs, M=m) from P_T(Y | x_obs, M=1). That term is zero under the Y-margin of Little's CCMV restriction, and its sensitivity analysis is standard pattern-mixture practice (identifying restrictions plus tilts; cf. Linero & Daniels, Stat Sci 2018, confirmed by search only). Artificial dropout on complete cases is thus implicitly a CCMV-type identifying restriction.

prior_work.title: Missing Data and Prediction: the pattern (mixture kernel) submodel (Mercaldo & Blume), arXiv 1704.08192; Biostatistics 21(2):236, 2020
prior_work.verification: I fetched the arXiv abstract: 'the expected loss of a forecasting algorithm is minimized when each pattern-specific loss is minimized', with comparison to complete-case submodels. The Biostatistics venue comes from search results; PubMed returned a captcha.
prior_work.how_it_covers: It establishes the pattern-mixture risk decomposition R = Σ_m P(M=m)·R_m and contrasts it with complete-case-trained models. This is the source of the 'pattern-weight × pattern-specific risk' first term.

prior_work.title: Methods to handle missing values and missing individuals (Bonander & Strömberg), Eur J Epidemiol, 2018; A General Framework for Considering Selection Bias in EHR-Based Studies: What Data are Observed and Why? (Haneuse & Daniels), eGEMs 4(1):1203, 2016
prior_work.verification: I fetched the PMC text of Bonander & Strömberg, which explicitly contrasts item missingness with non-participation (50.5% of the target population missing) and notes that the two need different handling. I fetched the Haneuse & Daniels eGEMs landing page (abstract only), which describes modularizing the observation mechanism into a sequence of patient and provider decisions.
prior_work.how_it_covers: The epidemiological distinction between unit and item missingness (selection vs. mask), and its modular sub-mechanism form for EHR data. This is prior art for the conceptual S/M separation.

prior_work.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts (Rockenschaub et al.), arXiv 2406.16484; Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton), AISTATS 2023
prior_work.verification: I downloaded both PDFs and read them in extracted text. Rockenschaub: abstract, and Def. 1/Thm 1, which hold p(X,Y) fixed ('Assuming no other shifts'). DAMS: the Discussion attributes the eICU failure to 'selection bias (very different cohort), label shift, or changes in prevalences'.
prior_work.how_it_covers: They cover the M-only part: when p(Y|x_obs,M) transports, and that performance-based selection on the source can fail under non-ignorable target missingness. DAMS explicitly names cohort selection as a confounder separate from missingness shift, but leaves it unformalized.

refutations.residual_gap:
Taken as a theoretical contribution, C1 is essentially covered. Its three-term decomposition is the Feng/Singh et al. (NeurIPS 2024) aggregate decomposition p(W)p(Z|W)p(Y|W,Z) with W := M and Z := X⊙M, estimators and CIs included. It is also an instance of Zhang et al. ICML 2023 and of DISDE. The S-vs-M separation already exists conceptually (Zamanian 2024 scenario 9; Bonander & Strömberg; Haneuse & Daniels) and formally (Tikka et al. S and R nodes; Stokes et al. simultaneous covariate and MNAR shift). I found no paper that writes this decomposition specifically for 'artificial dropout on a fully observed source vs naturally masked target', and none that states how S enters it. That residue is instantiation and identification bookkeeping, not a standalone contribution. A defensible remnant would have to show one of three things:
(a) Where S goes. The three terms do NOT separate S from M. S effects load into ΛZ, and into ΛY when S depends on Y. Separating them needs an extra reference sample (the eligible population's always-observed block) or an extra factor P(S|X,Y), which gives a four-term chain.
(b) The complete-case special case. When the complete source is the complete-case subset of the same eligible population (S = 1{M=1}), 'S vs M' collapses, and the MNAR term equals the departure from a Y-margin CCMV restriction (Little 1993 / Tchetgen Tchetgen et al. 2018). It should be presented that way, not as new.
(c) Per-term identification. Which terms are identified from unlabeled target (x_obs, M) plus a labeled source (pattern weights and within-pattern shift, under overlap, plus DISDE's unseen-support term, which C1 omits), and which need target labels or a sensitivity parameter (the Y|x_obs,M term). This parallels DAMS Prop. 1 and DISDE.
The applied part is not covered by this prior work: a real natural-vs-artificial ranking audit with a fixed eligible population and cutoff. It belongs to a different candidate.

prior_work.title: Why do probabilistic clinical models fail to transport between sites (Lasko, Strobl, Stead), npj Digital Medicine 7:53, 2024
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC abstract and full-text XML (PMC10907678) fetched. The passage defining the selection variables was read verbatim.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Gives a causal DAG of transport failure with separate selection variables. S_o is the decision of WHEN to record, i.e. the patient presenting for care: 'patient deciding to present for care... brought to the hospital by ambulance'. S_{O_i} is the decision of WHICH O_i to record. It calls their combination 'selection bias on selection bias' and names P(O_i | S_{O_i}=1) ≠ P(O_i | S_{O_i}=0) as informative missingness that shifts across sites through test-ordering practice. This already separates presence/population selection from the observation mask as distinct selection nodes in a clinical transport argument. It is qualitative only: there is no risk decomposition, no dropout estimand and no model ranking.

prior_work.title: Prediction of Survival Outcomes under Clinical Presence Shift: A Joint Neural Network Architecture (Jeanselme, Martin, Sperrin, Peek, Tom, Barrett), arXiv 2508.05472, 2025 (earlier DeepJoint, NeurIPS 2022 workshop, arXiv 2205.13481)
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract and HTML Sec. 4 fetched. Definitions quoted verbatim by the summarizer.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Formally defines 'clinical presence shift' as 'a change in the distribution q(E,O)' (O is the observed-variable indicator, E the inter-observation time), holding q(X) and q(Y | X,E,O) invariant. So the observation-process shift is defined separately from population shift. It states that this 'results in shifts in the observed covariate distribution q(X*) and the modelled q(Y | X*)', 'both a concept and covariate shift'. That is the pattern/within-pattern covariate component plus the observed-data conditional component of C1's decomposition, stated qualitatively. It includes a real MIMIC-III shift (weekend vs weekday admissions).

prior_work.title: A General Framework for Considering Selection Bias in EHR-Based Studies: What Data Are Observed and Why? (Haneuse, Daniels), eGEMs 4(1):1203, 2016
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC abstract and full-text XML fetched. The Table 2 sub-mechanism list and the factorization sentence were read verbatim.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Breaks the provenance of 'complete data' into sub-mechanisms: 1. enrollment status, 2. multiple facilities, 3. encounters, ... measurement. It factorizes P(S=1) = P(S1=1)·P(S2=1 | S1=1)·P(S3=1 | S1,S2) with a separate model for each sub-mechanism. This is the modular separation of population/enrollment selection from measurement availability. The target is association/CER estimation, not prediction risk or dropout evaluation.

prior_work.title: Analysis of Missingness Scenarios for Observational Health Data (Zamanian, von Kleist, et al.), J Pers Med 14(5):514, 2024
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC full-text XML re-fetched in this review. Scenario 8 and Scenario 9 text quoted verbatim.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Scenario 9, 'Data sample omission based on inclusion/exclusion criteria... depending on... measurement availability, values within a specific range, or patient cohort', is a separate pre-processing stage (S) from the acquisition scenarios (M). Scenario 8 covers unrecorded observations. It defines E_{π_new} for a changed availability policy. Note that the paper files S under 'missingness scenarios' and does not formally separate it from M. It gives no risk-gap decomposition.

prior_work.title: A hierarchical decomposition for explaining ML performance discrepancies (Feng, Singh, Xia, Subbaswamy, Gossmann), NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv 2402.14254)
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched. The NeurIPS 37 venue was confirmed via a Crossref record (DOI 10.52202/079017-4082).
prior_work.how_it_covers: A nonparametric aggregate decomposition of a performance gap into a feature-distribution shift and an outcome-given-features shift, plus variable-level detail, with debiased estimators and CIs. Take the covariates to be (X_obs, M). The aggregate X-shift term then contains C1's 'pattern-weight mismatch' and 'within-pattern population shift', and the Y | X term is C1's 'MNAR acquisition selection' term. The detailed decomposition can attribute to M. Together with DISDE (Cai et al.) and Zhang et al. (ICML 2023), which are already in the synthesis, this makes the decomposition technique prior art once target labels are available.

prior_work.title: Biases introduced by filtering electronic health records for patients with 'complete data' (Weber et al.), JAMIA 24(6):1134-1141, 2017; and Berkson's bias, selection bias, and missing data (Westreich), Epidemiology 23(1):159-164, 2012
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC abstracts fetched for both (PMID 29016972; PMC3237868).
prior_work.how_it_covers: Weber: empirically, filtering EHR cohorts on completeness selects older, more female, sicker populations, i.e. a complete-case source is itself S-selected. Westreich: formally shows that missing data is a selection (collider) problem, so complete-case analysis is selection on S = 1{complete}. Together they establish that a 'fully observed source' is a selection event induced by M. This undercuts any claim that S and M are separable when the source is the complete-case subset of the same eligible population.

prior_work.title: Missing data should be handled differently for prediction than for description or causal explanation (Sperrin, Martin, Sisk, Peek), J Clin Epidemiol 125:183-187, 2020; Imputation and missing indicators... development and deployment (Sisk, Sperrin, Peek, van Smeden, Martin), SMMR 2023 (arXiv 2206.12295); Handling missing predictor values when validating and applying a prediction model (Hoogland et al.), Stat Med 39:3591-3607, 2020
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC abstracts fetched for Sperrin 2020 and Hoogland 2020. arXiv abstract fetched for Sisk.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Clinical-epidemiology prior art for the premise. The missingness mechanism and handling at development/validation may not match deployment, 'leading to overoptimistic assessments'. Validation should use methods and mechanisms that transfer to practice. Sisk simulates development-vs-deployment mechanism mismatch, including outcome-dependent missingness. None of these papers separates S from M or decomposes the gap.

prior_work.title: The effect of selection bias on the performance of a deep learning-based intraoperative hypotension prediction model (Yang, Celi, Lee et al.), Br J Anaesth 2025
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC abstract fetched.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Real-data demonstration that curating the evaluation sample (an S-type selection) inflates PPV (0.937 vs 0.068) and changes the clinical meaning of a two-model comparison (DL vs MAP-only). This is prior evidence that S alone can drive an apparent model ranking or advantage. It involves no missingness mask.

refutations.residual_gap: No single verified paper makes C1's exact claim. The ingredients are nonetheless prior art, so novelty is thin and must be framed as an instantiation or accounting identity, not a method. What is already covered: (a) separating population or presence selection from the observation or acquisition mask, qualitatively in Lasko 2024 (S_o vs S_{O_i}), Haneuse & Daniels 2016 (factorized sub-mechanisms) and Zamanian 2024 (Scenario 9 vs acquisition scenarios); (b) formally defining an M-only shift with the population held fixed, in Jeanselme 2025 (q(E,O) shift with q(X) and q(Y | X,E,O) fixed), DAMS and Subbaswamy 2021; (c) the fact that such a shift induces both covariate and concept shift in the observed space (Jeanselme 2025); (d) decomposing a performance gap into marginal and conditional parts with CIs (Feng et al. NeurIPS 2024, DISDE, Zhang et al. ICML 2023). With target labels available, C1's three-term split (pattern weights, within-pattern X_obs shift, P(Y | x_obs, m) shift) is a direct application of (d) with covariates (X_obs, M), so it is not new. What remains possibly new: (1) the specific comparator estimand, i.e. the MCAR artificial-dropout risk computed on a fully observed source, versus natural-missingness deployment risk. (2) An explicit S factor that is NOT a function of M, such as different eligibility, cohort, site or time. If the source is the complete-case subset of the same eligible population, then S = 1{M = full}, and Weber 2017 and Westreich 2012 show the S/M 'separation' is vacuous and the within-pattern term is just complete-case selection. (3) Stating which terms can be identified from unlabeled target (x_obs, M): the pattern weights and within-pattern X_obs shift can, under positivity. The acquisition-selection term cannot, and needs a sensitivity parameter. (4) Carrying the decomposition to the sign of the two-model risk difference, where terms common to both models cancel. If N1's target labels are fully public (e.g., MIMIC or eICU), point (3) does not apply and the decomposition reduces to known methods. C1 should then be claimed only as a diagnostic instantiation. Caveat: my WebSearch budget ran out partway through, and later searches used Europe PMC and Crossref APIs plus direct fetches. A clinical-epidemiology paper giving exactly this three-term dropout-vs-deployment identity could still exist unfound, though targeted searches in JCE, Stat Med, SMMR, JAMIA and npj DM returned none.

prior_work.title: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Predict Out-of-Distribution Performance (Garg, Balakrishnan, Lipton, Neyshabur, Sedghi), ICLR 2022
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract page and HTML v3 fetched. Verbatim Prop. 1: 'Absent further assumptions, accuracy on the target is identifiable iff p_t(y|x) is uniquely identified given p_s(x,y) and p_t(x).' Corollary 1 (impossibility) and Example 1 were also read: the same p_s(x,y) and p_t(x) give different errors under covariate shift and under label shift.
prior_work.how_it_covers: This is the general theorem behind C2's counterexample. Take the augmented input x~ = (x_obs, m). Dropout on the labeled source supplies p_s(x~, y), and the unlabeled masked target supplies p_t(x~). Target risk, and therefore any risk difference or ranking, is identified iff p_t(y | x~) is identified. CE1's two worlds are an instance of Example 1. W1 (MCAR) keeps p_t(y|x~) = p_s(y|x~), a covariate-shift-type world. W2 (label-dependent acquisition) is a label-shift-type world with the same p_t(x~). Once p_t(y|x~) is not pinned down, a ranking flip follows in one line.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness (Stokes, Do, Blecker, Chunara, Adhikari), arXiv 2504.00322, 2025
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract and HTML fetched. Verbatim: 'even when P^T(Y|X_o,X_u,R) = P^S(Y|X_o,X_u,R), if P^T(R|X_o,X_u) ≠ P^S(R|X_o,X_u) then P^T(Y|X_o,X*_u,R) ≠ P^S(Y|X_o,X*_u,R).' The target has covariates only ('no outcome data'). Self-censoring is identified only under parametric assumptions.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Gives the negative ingredient for the exact information set: labeled source, unlabeled masked target, MNAR acquisition. The conditional that dropout evaluation implicitly transports, P(Y | x_obs, M), does not carry over even when the full-data outcome model is invariant. There is no ranking statement, but ranking non-identification follows directly.

prior_work.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts (Rockenschaub et al.), arXiv 2406.16484, 2024
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract and HTML fetched. Thm 1: pattern-wise Bayes predictors are invariant 'in general only if the missingness shift is ignorable.' Cor. 1: 'If q(M|X,Y) ≠ q(M|X) and q(M|X,Y) ≠ p(M|X,Y), then the missingness shift cannot be ignorable.' Abstract: 'Prediction performance in the source data may no longer be a good selection criterion.' Its experiments artificially mask fully observed LBIDD data.
prior_work.how_it_covers: States in words C2's conclusion: under Y-dependent (non-ignorable) target acquisition, source-based selection stops being valid. It also supplies the MCAR/MAR/MNAR ignorability rungs of the ladder.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton), AISTATS 2023
prior_work.verification: PDF downloaded and text extracted. Re-read in the extracted text: Prop. 1 (with masks observed, MCAR or v-MAR missingness shift satisfies covariate shift), Thm 5.2 and Alg. 1 (with relative rates estimated from unlabeled target data, re-masking the labeled source reproduces the labeled target law under UCAR, m^s ⪯ m^t), and Remark 4 (a counterexample showing missingness rates are not identified).
prior_work.how_it_covers: Supplies the lower rungs of C2's ladder. L1 (no S, target MCAR, rate-matched dropout is valid) is Thm 5.2 and Alg. 1, which estimates rates from the unlabeled target. L2 and L3 (masks observed, MAR on always-observed covariates, reduction to covariate shift and IW) is Prop. 1. The positive identification result that the ladder builds on is already here.

prior_work.title: Every Missingness not at Random Model Has a Missingness at Random Counterpart with Equal Fit (Molenberghs, Beunckens, Sotto, Kenward), JRSS-B 70(2):371-388, 2008
prior_work.verification: OUP article page fetched. Summary quote: 'each MNAR model fit to a set of observed data can be reproduced exactly by an MAR counterpart', and the two give different predictions for unobserved values.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Gives the general construction C2 uses: an MAR/MCAR world and an MNAR world with the same observed-data law but different conditionals of the unobserved quantities, here Y in the target. CE1's W1/W2 pair is a small instance.

prior_work.title: Censoring of outcomes and regressors due to survey nonresponse: Identification and estimation using weights and imputations (Horowitz, Manski), J Econometrics 84:37-58, 1998
prior_work.verification: RePEc abstract fetched: 'Except in special cases, identification is possible only if one makes untestable assumptions about the distribution of the missing data.' The paper covers missing regressors as well as outcomes, and gives bounds.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Classical statement that functionals are not identified, and are only bounded, when regressors are nonrandomly missing. The target risk of a fixed predictor is such a functional.

prior_work.title: Combining Panel Data Sets with Attrition and Refreshment Samples (Hirano, Imbens, Ridder, Rubin), Econometrica 69(6):1645-1659, 2001
prior_work.verification: NBER abstract fetched: 'a class of non-ignorable missing data models can be identified without making strong distributional or functional form assumptions if refreshment samples are available.' The venue and pages come from Wiley and Harvard listings in the search results.
prior_work.how_it_covers: A fully observed source drawn from the same population works as a refreshment sample. C2's minimality remark says that without label dependence r(x) is identified from P_T(M=1, X=x) = r(x) P(x). That is the single-variable case of this refreshment and additive-nonignorable identification, so the 'where identification returns' rung is prior art.

prior_work.title: Sequentially additive nonignorable missing data modelling using auxiliary marginal information (Sadinle, Reiter), Biometrika 106(4):889-911, 2019
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched verbatim. It lets nonresponse probabilities depend on the variable's own value, and identifies them using auxiliary marginal distributions. The Biometrika venue is confirmed by the OUP search result.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Self-masking MNAR on inputs is identified when marginals are known from another source, which is what a complete source provides. This covers the ladder rung where a complete source restores identification despite X-dependent MNAR, and it bounds C2's minimality claim.

prior_work.title: How to rank imputation methods? (Näf, Grzesiak, Scornet), arXiv 2507.11297, 2025
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract and HTML fetched. The abstract says artificially masking observations 'can be misleading if not done carefully and ... is generally not valid under MAR.' Sec. 2.2 and Example 1 give a counterexample where masking ranks a distorted imputation above the truth. Definition 3.2 (CIMAR_j) and Prop. 3.1 give an assumption that restores a proper ranking.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Same logical template as C2: a counterexample showing that an evaluation built on artificial masking gives the wrong ranking, plus the extra missingness assumption under which the masked evaluation ranks correctly. Here it is applied to imputation methods rather than deployed predictors.

prior_work.title: Predictive Performance Comparison of Decision Policies Under Confounding (Guerdan, Coston, Holstein, Wu), ICML 2024
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched in this check (regret intervals, 'regions of uncertainty that we can safely ignore in the policy comparison'). The claim that its bounds are tighter than differencing per-policy bounds was verified in the prior synthesis.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Shows that the performance DIFFERENCE between two predictors or policies is only partially identified under non-ignorable selection, with sharp joint intervals that are tighter where the two agree. This covers C2's top rungs, L4 and the ranking-breakdown value, and the observation that the ranking is insensitive where the two models agree on incomplete patterns (the report's g_AB term).

prior_work.title: Robust Design and Evaluation of Predictive Algorithms under Unobserved Confounding (Rambachan, Coston, Kennedy), arXiv 2212.09844
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched verbatim. It bounds how much outcomes may differ between selected and unselected units with the same observed characteristics, and applies this to MSE, TPR/FPR and likelihood performance measures.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Bounds the performance of predictive models when observation is selective and depends on unobservables. Its sensitivity rung is the one C2's ladder ends with.

prior_work.title: Non-Invariance in Nested Prediction Models under Selective Predictor Availability (Delord), arXiv 2609.02836, Sep 2026
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched verbatim. It decomposes non-invariance between patients selected for measurement and the target population. It shows that 'imputation based on the conditional distribution of the additional predictor in the selected population transfers the restricted-model non-invariance' to the imputed model. Real data: KFRE, where ACR is selectively measured.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Covers the S rung (C2's CE2). A complete-case development cohort selected on measurement does not match the deployment population, so matching mask rates alone is insufficient.

prior_work.title: Conservative Inference Rule for Uncertain Reasoning under Incompleteness (Zaffalon, Miranda), JAIR 34:757-821, 2009
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched verbatim. The incompleteness process may be partly unknown, and set-valued (imprecise) updating is applied to pattern classification.
prior_work.how_it_covers: An older formal treatment of the same point for classification: when the incompleteness process is unknown (not MAR), P(Y | observed inputs) is only set-identified. Model comparisons made through it are indeterminate unless assumptions are added.

prior_work.title: Graphical Models for Processing Missing Data (Mohan, Pearl), JASA 2021, arXiv 1801.03583; and Full Law Identification in Graphical Models of Missing Data (Nabi, Bhattacharya, Shpitser), ICML 2020
prior_work.verification: Mohan and Pearl: arXiv abstract fetched in this check (recoverability and testability under MNAR). Nabi et al.: full PDF read in the prior synthesis (identified iff no self-censoring and no colluders).
prior_work.how_it_covers: Give the sharp graphical boundary of when missing-data conditionals are recoverable. C2's L0 'no rule works' rung and its restoring conditions sit inside this known boundary.

refutations.residual_gap:
I found no single verified paper that states C2 in exactly its setting: a labeled, fully observed source that may be S-selected, rate-matched or calibrated artificial dropout, an unlabeled target with natural masks, and the question of the SIGN of R_T(f1) − R_T(f2). The substance is still covered.

(1) The counterexample is a one-line instance of Garg et al. Prop. 1 applied to the augmented input (x_obs, M). CE1's MCAR vs label-dependent pair is their covariate-shift vs label-shift Example 1, and the MNAR form is covered by Stokes App. A and Molenberghs et al. 2008. Ranking non-identification follows immediately.

(2) Every rung of the ladder is published:
- L1 and L2/L3: Zhou et al. Thm 5.2/Alg. 1 and Prop. 1.
- Refreshment and auxiliary-marginal identification: Hirano et al. 2001, Sadinle & Reiter 2019.
- S-selection of the complete-case cohort: Delord 2026, and standard IW.
- Ignorability conditions: Rockenschaub Thm 1/Cor. 1, Josse, Catoire.
- Sensitivity and difference bounds: Guerdan 2024, Rambachan-Coston-Kennedy, Steingrimsson 2024.
- The template 'masking-based evaluation ranks wrongly, plus an assumption that restores it': Näf-Grzesiak-Scornet 2025, for imputation.

What remains is packaging only: ordering these rungs around the dropout-vs-deployment ranking question, and stating that DAMS-style rate matching fails under MAR once the complete source is S-selected, which standard IW then repairs. That is fit for a lemma inside a paper whose contribution lies elsewhere, such as the controlled real-data artificial-vs-natural audit (C4). It is not a standalone contribution.

Caveat for the repository's CE1 minimality remark ('label dependence is required'): it holds only for one modality with no always-observed covariates. With two or more modalities and non-monotone patterns, acquisition that depends on X_mis but not on Y is already unidentified even with a complete, invariant source. Two binary modalities give 8 independent observed-data equations against 12 free mechanism parameters. The boundary of identification there is the additive-nonignorable class (Hirano; Sadinle-Reiter), not 'Y-dependence'. The minimality claim must be restated accordingly.

prior_work.title: Robust prediction under missingness shifts (Rockenschaub, Xian, Zamanian, Piperno, Ciora, Pachl, Ahmidi), arXiv 2406.16484, 2024
prior_work.verification: Cached full text re-read in this session: the abstract, Sec. 6.1-6.2 including Corollary 1, App. A.4 and App. C.1.
prior_work.how_it_covers: States the qualitative claim of C2. Source (held-out) performance 'may no longer be a good selection criterion' under a missingness shift. Pattern-wise Bayes predictors are invariant only under ignorable shifts (Thm 1). Corollary 1: if q(M|X,Y) != q(M|X) and q != p, the shift cannot be ignorable. App. C.1 gives the X-only rung: when M is independent of Y given X, complete-case estimation of f* is unbiased even under MNAR in X. This covers the 'Y-dependent acquisition breaks comparability' step and one ladder rung. It has no observational-equivalence argument and no ranking counterexample.

prior_work.title: Every Missingness not at Random Model Has a Missingness at Random Counterpart with Equal Fit (Molenberghs, Beunckens, Sotto, Kenward), JRSS-B 70(2):371-388, 2008
prior_work.verification: Crossref metadata (authors, volume, issue, pages) and the abstract fetched in this session.
prior_work.how_it_covers: The generic engine of CE1. Every MNAR model fitted to the observed data is reproduced exactly by an MAR counterpart that predicts the unobserved data differently. CE1's two worlds, W1 (MCAR) and W2 (label-dependent), have the same observed target law P_T(M, X*M) and therefore different P_T(Y | M=0). That is an instance of this result, applied to a risk functional.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness (Stokes, Do, Blecker, Chunara, Adhikari), arXiv 2504.00322, 2025
prior_work.verification: Cached full text re-read in this session: the abstract and App. A (non-transportability derivation), C and D.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Shows that P(Y | x_obs, R) depends on the domain-specific P_d(R|X) and P_d(Xu|Xo) even with an invariant full-data outcome model. MNAR shift is therefore not reducible to covariate shift or importance weighting. This is the 'dropout/source evaluation does not transport under MNAR' statement. It assumes Y is independent of R given X and an incomplete source, so it does not isolate Y-dependence, and it restores identification through assumed MNAR-identifiable imputers.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton), AISTATS 2023
prior_work.verification: Cached full text re-read in this session: Remarks 4-5 (missingness rates are not identifiable from corrupted data; relative rates are) and the Discussion (eICU failure, 'important to clarify assumptions').
prior_work.how_it_covers: Gives the lower rungs of the ladder and the 'rate-matched, target-calibrated dropout' device. Under MCAR/MAR with indicators, missingness shift reduces to covariate shift (Prop. 1). Under UCAR, target-calibrated re-masking of the labeled source identifies the target law and hence every model's risk (Alg. 1). The Discussion states that these adjustments can be worse than no adaptation when the assumptions fail on real data.

prior_work.title: Prediction with Incomplete Data under Agnostic Mask Distribution Shift (Zhu, Yuan, Jiang, Lin, Jin, Wang, Zhou), IJCAI 2023
prior_work.verification: Venue confirmed in this session through Crossref (DOI 10.24963/ijcai.2023/525). Cached full text re-read: Assumption 1 (invariant p(x,y)), Theorem 1 and its App. A proof.

This is the 'restoring comparability' rung, which implies that a mask-matched evaluation is valid under these assumptions.

prior_work.title: Informative missingness in electronic health record systems: the curse of knowing (Groenwold), Diagn Progn Res 4:8, 2020
prior_work.verification: Europe PMC full-text XML fetched in this session. The four deployment missingness scenarios, including random 50% missingness, are confirmed.

The phenomenon behind CE1 is therefore published, although with a known, different deployment mechanism rather than observationally equivalent worlds.

prior_work.title: Knockout: A simple way to handle missing inputs (Nguyen et al.), TMLR 2025
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched in this session. The formal claim that dropout with M independent of (X,Y) learns p_S(Y | x_obs) was read in the earlier sweep (Secs. 2.2 and 2.4).

refutations.residual_gap:
The substance of C2 is prior art when the listed papers are taken together. MNAR/MAR observational equivalence comes from Molenberghs 2008 and Mohan-Pearl. Non-transportability of P(Y | x_obs, M) under MNAR shift comes from Stokes 2025. Source or held-out performance failing as a selection criterion once acquisition depends on Y comes from Rockenschaub 2024, Cor. 1. A published ranking reversal is in Groenwold 2020. What dropout estimates is in Knockout. The comparability rungs (MCAR/MAR with indicators leading to importance weighting, UCAR leading to calibrated re-masking, M independent of Y given X, Y-only acquisition via label shift, refreshment-sample/AN counting, and algorithmic graph identification) are in DAMS, Zhu et al. IJCAI'23, Rockenschaub App. C.1, BBSE, Hirano 2001 and Tikka 2021. C2 therefore cannot be a headline contribution. What remains is corollary-level and fits as a proposition with citations:
(1) No verified paper gives the exact construction for N1's design. The construction has four conditions at once. The source is labeled and fully observed. Its complete-data law P(X,Y) is also held fixed in the target, which is a stronger constraint than Molenberghs' equal-fit counterpart, since that counterpart changes the full-data law. The target is unlabeled and observes only (M, X*M). Rate-matched dropout returns identical estimates in two worlds, yet R_T(A) - R_T(B) has opposite signs in them. I checked by hand that CE1's two worlds give the same P_T(M=1, X=x) = 1/4 for both x.
(2) The design-specific boundary is not stated explicitly in the prior work, though it follows from counting.
- With an unselected complete source and a single modality block, X-dependent acquisition, including self-masking, is identified from the unlabeled target through r(x) = P_T(x, M=1)/P(x). So Stokes-type MNAR is not the obstruction here. The obstruction is dependence of M on Y given X.
- Y-only acquisition is identified (label-shift argument).
- A logit-additive (Hirano AN) mechanism is not identified when target Y is never observed: with k levels of x and binary Y it has k+1 parameters against k equations. Hirano's panel setting is different: there AN is just-identified.
- With several modality blocks and non-monotone patterns, pattern-specific r_m(x) is not identified even without any Y-dependence.
- The refreshment route fails as soon as the source is an S-selected complete-case cohort (CE2), where S is a function of M.
(3) The estimand is the sign of a risk difference. It needs P_T(Y | x_obs, m) only where the two models disagree. That links C2 to Guerdan et al.-style joint regret bounds, but the linkage is framing, not a new identification result.
Search limits: the WebSearch budget was exhausted before this review started. I searched with arXiv full-site search, Crossref, Europe PMC, and full texts cached earlier in this session. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited. So an obscure 2025-2026 workshop paper stating exactly (1) cannot be ruled out, but none turned up in arXiv searches on missingness shift, modality dropout, MNAR domain adaptation, or label-dependent missingness.

prior_work.title: Informative missingness in electronic health record systems: the curse of knowing (Groenwold), Diagn Progn Res 4:8, 2020
prior_work.verification: Full text fetched in this session through the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint (PMC7371469). Table 1 values were read from the fetched text.
prior_work.how_it_covers: This paper already shows the phenomenon at a matched missingness rate. Development used informative missingness at about 50% (R depends on P and on an unobserved U). Scenario 1 keeps that same mechanism and Scenario 3 masks a random 50%, which is a rate-matched artificial dropout. The ranking reverses. Under the natural mechanism, zero or mean imputation gets c=0.699 and multiple imputation gets c=0.622. Under rate-matched random masking, zero or mean imputation gets 0.541 and MI gets 0.663. So a 'rate-matched dropout gives the wrong ranking' demonstration is not new. Groenwold does not do the following: argue non-identification from unlabeled target (x_obs, M), use a fully observed or S-selected source, or give an assumption ladder.

prior_work.title: Every Missingness not at Random Model Has a Missingness at Random Counterpart with Equal Fit (Molenberghs, Beunckens, Sotto, Kenward), JRSS-B 70(2), 2008
prior_work.verification: Crossref record and abstract fetched in this session.
prior_work.how_it_covers: The abstract shows that each MNAR model fitted to observed data can be reproduced exactly by an MAR counterpart. The pair has the same observed-data fit but different predictions of the unobserved values. C2's counterexample is an instance of this: two target laws agree on P_T(x_obs, M) and differ in P_T(Y | x_obs, M). Picking two models whose risks differ only on the affected patterns turns the non-identified level into a non-identified sign. The core non-identification step is therefore classical.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation Under MNAR Missingness (Stokes, Do, Blecker, Chunara, Adhikari), arXiv 2504.00322, 2025
prior_work.verification: Extracted full text re-checked in this session (Sec. 2.1 setting; the self-censoring non-identifiability passage).
prior_work.how_it_covers: Setting: the target has only observed covariates and no outcomes, and the missingness mechanism differs between source and target. The paper states that self-censoring MNAR structures are not non-parametrically identifiable, and assumes an invariant full-data outcome model. This covers the step 'an unlabeled target under MNAR does not identify the target conditional'. It does not cover ranking, a fully observed or S-selected source, or calibrated dropout.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton), AISTATS 2023
prior_work.verification: Extracted text re-checked in this session (Remark 4 counterexample; Discussion and future-work paragraph).

prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract fetched in this session.

refutations.residual_gap:
After a serious search, no verified paper states and proves C2 in its specific form. The form is: in the two-population design, a complete-case source that may be S-selected, with labels, plus an unlabeled, naturally masked target (x_obs, M), artificial dropout cannot determine the SIGN of R_T(f1) − R_T(f2). This holds even when the dropout is calibrated to the target's observed mask rate or to P_T(M | always-observed X), once acquisition depends on Y or on unrecorded information. No paper pairs this with a ladder ordered by what each assumption identifies for the sign rather than the level.

What is new is narrow and mostly corollary-level:
(1) The sign-level version, with an explicit two-model, two-pattern binary construction. It follows directly from Molenberghs et al. 2008 and Stokes et al. 2025 applied to a risk difference.
(2) A characterisation of when the ranking is identified although the individual risks are not. This happens when the models agree on the patterns where acquisition is MNAR, so the ambiguity cancels. This is the Guerdan et al. cancellation idea, not yet written down for missing inputs.
(3) Ordering the known rungs by what they buy for the sign, with separate S and M parameters. The rungs are MCAR, MAR on always-observed X or UCAR (DAMS, Josse), known or NUC policy (Boyer 2025, Keogh 2024, von Kleist), shadow or label-shift (Miao 2016, Miller 2023), refreshment or double sampling (Hirano 2001, Levis 2024), bounded OR tilt (Steingrimsson 2024, Zamanian 2024), and worst case (Horowitz–Manski). No rung is new.

The rate-matched reversal itself is already shown numerically in a clinical-epidemiology journal (Groenwold 2020: 0.699 vs 0.622 becomes 0.541 vs 0.663 at 50% random masking) and must be cited as such. So C2 is defensible only as a short unifying proposition that serves the audit and the selection rule. As a headline contribution it would be NO_GO.

Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted. Coverage came from Europe PMC (J Clin Epi, Stat Med, SMMR, Diagn Progn Res, JAMIA, npj Digit Med and BMJ are indexed there), arXiv full-text search and Crossref. Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar-style citation chasing was not possible.

prior_work.title: Predictive Performance Comparison of Decision Policies Under Confounding (Guerdan, Coston, Holstein, Wu), ICML 2024, PMLR 235
prior_work.verification: I fetched the abstract and the arXiv HTML full text in this session. Checked: the bounds are closed-form, computed by optimizing over user-specified bounding functions on the partially identified terms (Lemma 5.2). Thm 5.3 shows the uncertainty set is minimal ('no strict subset ... is consistent'), so the bounds are sharp. Fig. 5 reports '95% bootstrap confidence intervals around upper and lower regret bounds.' There is no breakdown or tipping-point analysis and no outcome-prevalence constraint. Labels are missing (selective labels) and inputs X are fully observed. Measures covered are accuracy, TPR/FPR, PPV/NPV and expected utility.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Covers the core of C3. It gives a joint partial-identification interval on the DIFFERENCE in predictive performance between two decision rules, and that interval is tighter than differencing per-model bounds because the region where the two rules agree cancels. It is built from generic user-specified bounding functions, including the MSM, which is an odds-ratio box, and it comes with bootstrap CIs. C3's 'sharp bounds on R_T(f1)−R_T(f2) under an OR box, plus bootstrap' is this construction with the bounding function placed on P_T(Y|x_obs,M=m) instead of on unselected outcomes. For binary Y and pointwise loss, the difference is linear in q=P_T(Y=1|·). So without a coupling constraint, the sharp bound is simply evaluation at the box endpoints, which is exactly Guerdan's closed-form mechanism.

prior_work.title: Sensitivity analysis for studies transporting prediction models (Steingrimsson, Robertson, Dahabreh), Biometrics 80(4) 2024
prior_work.verification: I fetched the arXiv PDF in this session and extracted the text locally. The quotes are verbatim. Eq. (3): 'Pr[Y = 1|X, S = 0] ∝ e^η Pr[Y = 1|X, S = 1]'. Eq. (4) gives the equivalent odds-of-selection form. Sec. 6: 'we can base this choice on background knowledge of the marginal probability of the outcome in the target population ... we may estimate η as the solution to' a prevalence estimating equation (13). CIs use a non-parametric bootstrap with 1,000 replicates, and the analysis is run over a prevalence range [µ/2, 2µ]. The discussion lists 'missing data (other than the outcome data in the target population)' as future work.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Covers C3's sensitivity parameterization and its prevalence anchoring. The model is an odds-ratio tilt of the target conditional outcome law relative to the source, P_T(Y|X) vs P_S(Y|X), for the transported risk of a fixed model, with the tilt tied to a known target prevalence and with bootstrap CIs. C3 has three differences: the OR is allowed to vary within [1/Γ,Γ] per (x_obs,m) instead of being constant (a box versus a point), the conditioning is on (x_obs, M=m) rather than X, and the target is a two-model difference. The paper names missing covariates as future work, so it does not cover the mask-pattern instantiation.

prior_work.title: Robust Design and Evaluation of Predictive Algorithms under Unobserved Confounding (Rambachan, Coston, Kennedy), arXiv 2212.09844 v6 (Nov 2025)
prior_work.verification: I fetched the abstract and the HTML full text in this session. Bounding assumption: 'Γ̲μ₁(x) ≤ P(Y*=1|D=0,X=x) ≤ Γ̄μ₁(x)', a multiplicative box on the unobserved conditional outcome probability relative to the observed nominal. C3's per-(x_obs,m) OR band around P_S(Y|x_obs), with LP-computed bounds, is the same template with a different nominal (the source instead of selected units).

refutations.residual_gap:
No verified paper states C3 in exactly its combined form. At the method level, though, every ingredient is verified prior art, and the combination is a mechanical instantiation:
(1) Joint sharp interval on a two-model performance DIFFERENCE, with agreement-region cancellation, bounding functions and bootstrap CIs: Guerdan et al. 2024, with Kallus & Zhou 2018 earlier for regret against a baseline.
(2) OR/exponential tilt of the target P(Y|·) relative to the source P(Y|·) for transported model risk, with the tilt anchored to a known target prevalence and bootstrap CIs: Steingrimsson et al. 2024.
(3) Multiplicative box on the unidentified P(Y=1|x) around an identified nominal, with LP-computed sharp bounds: Rambachan, Coston & Kennedy; Zhao, Small & Bhattacharya.
(4) Sharpening a box by a moment or marginal constraint: Dorn & Guo; Nie, Imbens & Wager; Kallus, Mao & Zhou.
(5) Breakdown Γ*: the standard sensitivity value (Zhao 2017) or Rosenbaum breakdown point.
(6) An outcome-dependent OR acquisition tilt inside the deployment loss E_πnew[loss]: Zamanian et al. 2024.
For binary Y and pointwise loss, R_T(f1)−R_T(f2) is linear in q(x_obs,m)=P_T(Y=1|x_obs,m). The sharp bound is therefore endpoint evaluation of the box, and with a prevalence equality it becomes a continuous fractional-knapsack LP. Both results are textbook consequences.

What remains, all of it application-level and incremental:
(a) Placing the sensitivity box on P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m) per mask pattern, with the nominal P_S(Y|x_obs) taken from a FULLY OBSERVED source by marginalizing X_mis. The missing quantities are input modalities, not labels, which is what Guerdan, Rambachan and Steingrimsson treat; Steingrimsson explicitly lists missing covariates as future work.
(b) The one verified gap is combining a single global prevalence equality with a JOINT two-model difference bound. Guerdan's bounds are pointwise, so they stop being sharp once a coupling constraint is added. I found no paper doing prevalence-constrained, sharp, pairwise-difference bounds, but it is a routine LP extension that follows Dorn & Guo and Nie, Imbens & Wager.
(c) Reporting Γ* for the SIGN of a model-ranking difference. Guerdan et al. do not report this, but it is standard post-processing.
(d) Separate sensitivity parameters for cohort selection S (Γ_S) and acquisition M (Λ_M), with a joint breakdown curve. C3 as stated does not include this, and it is the only direction that might rise above marginal.

Verdict: C3 is not a new method. It should be presented as a tool that instantiates Guerdan et al. and Steingrimsson et al. per mask pattern, which matches the repository's existing NO_GO/marginal classification in docs/REPORT.md.

Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) when this review began. Every item above was verified by direct WebFetch of known URLs, not by fresh keyword search. Very recent (2025–2026) preprints on 'sensitivity analysis under missingness shift' may therefore have been missed, but they could only strengthen the NO_GO.

prior_work.title: Predictive Performance Comparison of Decision Policies Under Confounding (Guerdan, Coston, Holstein, Wu), ICML 2024, PMLR 235
prior_work.verification: arXiv abstract page and arXiv HTML full text fetched in this session. Verified quotes: the MSM 'assumes there is some Λ≥1 such that the odds ratio ... lies within [Λ⁻¹,Λ]'; the δ-regret interval bounds 'the difference in the oracle regret ... m(v0*,v1,π) − m(v0*,v1,π0)' directly, not as a difference of per-policy bounds; the set is proven minimal; a doubly robust estimator is used; bootstrap CIs appear in Fig. 5; outcomes are binary Y∈{0,1}, with accuracy, TPR, FPR, PPV and similar metrics. No prevalence/LP constraint and no missing features were found.
prior_work.how_it_covers: This is the core of C3. It gives joint, sharp (minimal) partial-identification intervals for the DIFFERENCE in predictive performance of two predictors or policies under an odds-ratio MSM band on the unobserved conditional outcome probability. It adds DR estimation and bootstrap CIs, and says explicitly that the regions where the two predictors agree cancel, which is exactly why C3's joint interval is narrower than differencing per-model bounds. C3 only relabels the unobserved stratum: 'D=0 given X' becomes 'target, M=m given x_obs', with the nominal taken from source P(Y|x_obs).

refutations.residual_gap:
No single paper I verified applies the exact bundle to missing INPUT modalities. That bundle is: an OR band on the target P_T(Y|x_obs, M=m), separate for each mask pattern, around a nominal P_S(Y|x_obs) marginalized from a fully observed source by dropout; a joint two-model risk-difference interval; a target-prevalence equality constraint; bootstrap CIs; and a ranking breakdown Γ*. Guerdan et al. works with missing labels/potential outcomes under decisions, not missing input features, and has no prevalence constraint. Steingrimsson et al. has prevalence anchoring but only a single tilt, for one model and without masks. Zamanian et al. has an acquisition OR tilt but no two-model bounds or inference.

That remaining gap is an instantiation, not a method. With binary Y and pointwise losses the risk difference is linear in each p_T(x), so the sharp interval is just endpoint evaluation by the sign of l_A(y)−l_B(y), exactly Guerdan's agree/disagree cancellation. The prevalence-constrained version is the continuous-knapsack/quantile-threshold solution (Dorn & Guo; Nie, Imbens & Wager). The bootstrap is Zhao, Small & Bhattacharya / Dorn & Guo. The breakdown value is standard global-sensitivity practice (Steingrimsson; Rosenbaum-style).

The only elements with possible residual novelty are unverified as prior art either way:
(a) separate sensitivity parameters for cohort selection S (Γ_S, cf. Sahoo, Lei & Wager) and acquisition M (Λ_M), with a joint two-parameter ranking-breakdown frontier under identifiable calibration constraints. I could not check breakdown-frontier work such as Masten & Poirier because the search budget was exhausted.
(b) an empirical demonstration that such bounds decide more model pairs correctly than a dropout+bootstrap baseline given the same information.

The repository's own real-data result (docs/REPORT.md §7.5, criterion (c)) says (b) fails on PhysioNet 2012. C3 as stated should therefore be treated as not new, consistent with a NO_GO on the method; any novelty would have to come from (a) plus a positive empirical result, neither of which C3 currently contains.

prior_work.title: Robust Design and Evaluation of Predictive Algorithms under Unobserved Confounding (Rambachan, Coston, Kennedy), arXiv 2212.09844 v6, Nov 2025 (earlier title: 'Counterfactual Risk Assessments under Unmeasured Confounding')
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded this session and text extracted with pymupdf. I read the abstract, the introduction, Assumption 2.1, Lemma 2.1 (closed-form sharp bounds on perf(s;beta)), Sec. 4 (linear-fractional programs made linear via Charnes-Cooper, debiased cross-fitted estimators), footnote 8 (the 'identification breakdown point Gamma*', estimated as the smallest Gamma whose (1-alpha) confidence set contains 0) and App. E.1 (the MSM odds-ratio bound Lambda and its link to Assumption 2.1).
prior_work.how_it_covers: It partially identifies any 'overall performance' functional perf(s;beta)=E[beta0(X;s)+beta1(X;s)Y*]. beta0 and beta1 are arbitrary researcher-chosen functions of X. The bounds hold when P(Y*=1|X,D=0) may differ from P(Y*=1|X,D=1) within bounding functions, and the MSM odds-ratio (Lambda) model is one case. The sharp bounds are closed form: the extreme delta is chosen by the sign of beta1(X). For binary Y, the loss difference of two fixed predictors f1(x_obs,m), f2(x_obs,m) always has the form a(x_obs,m)+b(x_obs,m)Y. So C3's sharp bound on R_T(f1)-R_T(f2) under an odds-ratio model is exactly this lemma, with D relabeled as source vs. target pattern m and X coarsened to x_obs(m). The paper also has LP formulations for class-specific metrics, doubly robust inference with CIs, and the breakdown value Gamma* for a performance DIFFERENCE (an income-group disparity, with Gamma*=1.69 reported). C3's 'breakdown Gamma*' and 'LP' components are therefore already here.

refutations.residual_gap:
Every methodological component of C3 is published. Sharp bounds on a linear-in-Y performance functional under an odds-ratio/MSM model, with closed-form extremes by the sign of beta1 and LP versions: Rambachan-Coston-Kennedy. A two-model risk-difference interval that is tighter than differencing, with bootstrap CIs: Guerdan et al. The breakdown value Gamma* for a performance difference: Rambachan footnote 8. Tilting P_T(Y|X) against a labeled source in the source-labeled, target-unlabeled transport design, anchored to target prevalence: Steingrimsson et al. 2024. Target-moment constraints to sharpen bounds: Nie-Imbens-Wager. Outcome-dependent acquisition odds-ratio tilts for deployment loss under a changed measurement policy, and pattern-specific tilts with elicited ranges: Zamanian et al. 2024 and 2023. For binary Y, the loss difference of two predictors is a(x_obs,m)+b(x_obs,m)Y. C3's bound is therefore Rambachan's Lemma 2.1 with D relabeled as (source vs. target pattern m) and X coarsened to x_obs(m), plus one linear prevalence constraint. No new estimator, identification result or sharpness argument is needed.

I found no single paper that applies this machinery to missing INPUT modalities with (a) a nominal P_S(Y|x_obs(m)) obtained by marginalising a fully observed source, (b) a separate cohort-selection parameter Gamma_S next to the acquisition parameter Lambda_M (C3 as stated has only one tilt, so this is not in C3 either), and (c) an empirical check of whether the ranking breakdown Gamma* separates artificial-dropout from natural-missingness rankings on real data. The remaining gap is an instantiation and empirical audit, not a methods contribution. C3 should be presented as an application of Guerdan/Rambachan/Steingrimsson bounds, citing them, and not as a new 'acquisition-aware model selection' method.

Two caveats. First, the prevalence constraint uses target label information (P_T(Y)); if target labels are public, the partial-identification framing does not apply at all. Second, the search was limited: the WebSearch budget was already exhausted, so I searched through the Europe PMC REST API, arXiv listing search and Crossref, while Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited. A 2025-2026 conference paper that applies MSM difference bounds specifically to feature-acquisition shift could have been missed.

refutations.residual_gap:
I found no prior work, in missing-data statistics, clinical prediction methodology, multimodal EHR ML, time-series imputation, neuroimaging or recommender systems, that runs a controlled real-data audit of the following kind:

- It fixes one eligible population and one prediction cutoff.
- It evaluates the same trained models under two regimes: (a) artificial modality/panel dropout at matched rates on the fully observed subset, and (b) natural record-availability masks on the full eligible population, with labels available in both.
- It quantifies ranking agreement with pairwise risk-difference sign tests and CIs, or with Kendall tau.
- Before attributing any flip to selective acquisition, it tests whether the flip disappears once simple nulls are removed. The nulls are (i) reweighting the complete-case subset to the eligible population, i.e. the S effect, and (ii) prevalence or class-balance adjustment.

The pieces exist separately:

- **The phenomenon itself** is already visible in published tables. On EHR+CXR: DrFuse, MedFuse A.4/A.6 and CareBench. On connectomes: Liang et al. 2024. In recommender systems, with the label as the missing variable: Marlin & Zemel 2009.
- **The null-explanation tools are standard.** Case-mix benchmarks come from Vergouwe 2010 and Debray 2015; selection weighting from Corbin et al. and ICYM2I; prevalence reweighting from standard label-shift methods.
- **The 'synthetic vs natural transfer' audit template** is Taori et al. 2020.
- **Selection and prevalence as explanations** are explicitly named but untested in DAMS (Zhou et al.) on eICU. The authors call for exactly this testbed as future work.

What is genuinely new is therefore the combination of design and domain. That is an empirical audit contribution of at most moderate size, not a method. It must be framed as a controlled test that cites these works, and not as the discovery that rankings flip.

Because PhysioNet 2012 target labels are fully public, the audit is an empirical check. No non-identifiability claim applies to it.

If the repository's own results show that flips vanish after S-reweighting or prevalence adjustment, that finding is itself the contribution. It would also mean a NO_GO for any mechanism-level claim.

Search limits: the WebSearch budget was already used up, so searches ran through arXiv full-text search, Europe PMC (MEDLINE plus preprints) and Crossref. Papers outside those indexes, such as some IEEE or ACM venues without preprints, may have been missed. That is the reason for medium rather than high confidence.

It does not compare rankings between them (no rank correlation or pairwise test), reports no label prevalence, and runs no reweighting or class-balance adjustment.

prior_work.verification: I downloaded the arXiv PDF and extracted the text in this pass. prior_work.how_it_covers: It names, as an untested hypothesis, the alternative explanations that C4 tests: cohort selection and prevalence or label shift rather than the missingness mechanism, for why missingness-shift methods fail on real eICU data. refutations.residual_gap:
No verified prior work runs C4's controlled audit. What is missing is a design that: (i) fixes one eligible population and one prediction cutoff on real data; (ii) evaluates the SAME trained models under artificial modality dropout on the complete-case subset, matched to the natural rate or pattern, and under natural missingness on the full eligible population; (iii) compares the two rankings with pairwise risk-difference sign tests and CIs, e.g. a Kendall tau plus the count of significant flips; and (iv) tests the null explanations first, namely class-balance (prevalence) adjustment and S-reweighting or DR adjustment on observed covariates, before attributing the remaining flips to label-dependent recording.

The pieces all exist separately: the phenomenon in published tables (DrFuse, MedFuse, CareBench, Berkelmans), protocol-dependence of artificial masks on PhysioNet 2012 itself (Qian et al.), a selection or prevalence explanation stated but untested (DAMS Discussion) or shown only for complete-case imputation comparisons (Roy et al. 2026), and the correction and decomposition tools (ICYM2I IPW; Feng et al. 2024).

C4's novelty is therefore an empirical audit and replication with null-explanation controls. It is not a methodological contribution, and it must cite all of the above. Two further points narrow it:
- The repository's own result is largely negative. Dropout ranking reproduces the natural ranking with tau 0.63-0.77, there is about 1 significant flip per run, about half of those are recovered by class balance, and 17/20 cross-ICU flips are recovered by DR.
- In PhysioNet 2012, M is record availability, not verified acquisition, so any claim about 'selective acquisition' in C4 must be phrased as a claim about recording.

Search caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so coverage relied on arXiv full-text search, Europe PMC, Crossref and direct PDF reads. CHIL/MLHC/KDD papers that are not on arXiv could have been missed.

prior_work.title: When Does Multimodal Learning Help in Healthcare? A Benchmark on EHR and Chest X-Ray Fusion (CareBench), arXiv 2602.23614, 2026
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded and text-searched in this session (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 5.4 'Robustness to Modality Missingness', Fig. 2, Tables 1 and 3).
prior_work.how_it_covers: The same model zoo is evaluated on two sets: a matched subset with complete modalities (7,149 stays) and a naturally missing base cohort (26,947 stays, about 75% without CXR). A separate controlled sweep then raises CXR missingness synthetically from 0% to 80%. Rankings visibly change: the EHR-only Transformer beats many fusion models on the base cohort, and InfoReg/AUG lead there. So the paper shows that complete-case results, synthetic sweeps and natural-cohort results disagree. It does not fix one eligible population, compare the artificial and natural regimes as a ranking test, give pairwise CIs, or test whether the disagreement comes from cohort selection (matched subset vs base cohort) or from outcome prevalence.

prior_work.title: MedFuse: Multi-modal fusion with clinical time-series data and chest X-ray images (Hayat, Geras, Shamout), MLHC 2022, arXiv 2207.07027
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded and text-searched in this session (Sec. 5.1-5.3, App. A.4, A.5, A.6).
prior_work.how_it_covers: App. A.4 randomly drops CXR from the paired test set, and AUROC falls as the drop rate rises. App. A.6 instead adds naturally CXR-absent (uni-modal) test samples, and in-hospital-mortality AUROC rises. This is a direct artificial-vs-natural contrast on real data, with opposite signs. It covers one model only, not a ranking. It offers no explanation beyond noting that only 18.8% and 26.2% of samples are paired. There is no selection or prevalence analysis.

prior_work.title: Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (Zhou, Balakrishnan, Lipton), AISTATS 2023, arXiv 2211.02093
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded in this session. The real-data experiment paragraph and the Discussion were read verbatim.
prior_work.how_it_covers: The eICU two-hospital experiment applies source re-masking and reweighting adjustments to a naturally missing target, and they fail. The Discussion names 'selection bias (very different cohort), label shift, or changes in prevalences of disease' as likely reasons but does not test them. It says 'Finding appropriate real world empirical testbeds and analyzing sensitivity to assumption violations are important directions for future work.' So the explanatory hypothesis in C4 is already stated, and the test is explicitly left open.

prior_work.title: Prediction of Survival Outcomes under Clinical Presence Shift: A Joint Neural Network Architecture (Jeanselme, Martin, Sperrin, Peek, Tom, Barrett), arXiv 2508.05472, 2025
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded and Sec. 6 (weekend-effect case study) read in this session.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Uses a natural experiment on real MIMIC-III data (weekday to weekend admission) where test ordering differs. It compares how models that use or ignore the observation process transport, measured as transfer loss, and model rankings differ between the random split and the shifted setting. It treats the outcome gap as a target shift, handled by evaluating on the same test set, and subsamples to control training size. It covers a real natural observation-process shift with model comparison and some confound control. It has no artificial dropout arm and no S vs M decomposition.

prior_work.title: Compatibility of Missing Data Handling Methods across the Stages of Producing Clinical Prediction Models (Tsvetanova et al.), arXiv 2504.06799, 2025
prior_work.verification: Full PDF downloaded in this session. Sec. 4 (NCORR empirical example) and the limitations were read verbatim.
prior_work.how_it_covers: Defines validation bias against deployment performance across handling methods. However, the real NCORR analysis uses natural missingness only, and the paper says: 'Because fully observed NCORR data were not available, we were unable to evaluate the estimand corresponding to deployment requiring complete data.' There is no comparison with artificial dropout on real data.
